questions.stem: Incremental budgeting is based on:
options: Starting from a zero base each period
The previous period's budget or actual figures plus or minus adjustments
questions.rationale: Incremental budgets roll forward last year's numbers, which can perpetuate inefficiency.

questions.stem: In zero-based budgeting, each budget item must:
options: Rise each year by the rate of inflation
Be justified from scratch for the new period
Be approved by the external auditor
Equal the amount spent last year
questions.rationale: ZBB challenges every cost, which can reduce waste but takes more time.

questions.stem: A rolling budget is one that:
options: Is never changed during the budget year
Ignores the actual results of earlier periods
Is updated regularly by adding a new period as the oldest period ends
Is prepared only once a year and then fixed
questions.rationale: Rolling budgets keep a constant planning horizon and respond to change.

questions.stem: A key advantage of participative budgeting is:
options: There is never any budgetary slack
It always produces the lowest possible costs
Greater motivation and commitment from managers
The budget can be set much faster
questions.rationale: People are more likely to accept targets they helped set, though budgetary slack can occur.

questions.stem: Budgetary slack means:
options: Budgets are set too tightly to achieve
The budget is prepared late in the period
Managers deliberately set easier targets than necessary
Cash is left unused at the year end
questions.rationale: Building in slack makes performance easier to achieve and can reduce efficiency.

questions.stem: Which type of budget is prepared by adjusting for actual activity?
questions.rationale: A flexed budget compares like with like.

questions.stem: Budgeted sales are 5,000 units at £40 with variable cost £22. Actual sales are 5,400 units at £39 with variable cost £22. What is the sales volume contribution variance?
questions.rationale: Standard contribution £18 × (5,400 − 5,000) = £7,200 favourable.

questions.stem: Budgeted sales are 5,000 units at £40. Actual sales are 5,400 units at £39. What is the sales price variance?
Standard overhead per hour is £6 and budgeted hours are 10,000. Actual overhead is £63,000 for 9,600 hours. What is the total variable overhead expenditure variance?
questions.rationale: Flexed budget = 9,600 × £6 = £57,600. Actual £63,000. Difference = £5,400 adverse.

questions.stem: A material usage variance is more likely to be caused by:
options: A price increase from the main supplier
A fall in sales volumes during the period
A change in the wage rate for staff
questions.rationale: Usage variance relates to quantity used for the actual output.

questions.stem: Adverse labour efficiency and adverse material usage variances might be linked by:
options: A change in the selling price of the product
Poorly trained staff causing wastage and slow work
A fall in the price of materials bought
questions.rationale: Operational problems can produce related variances.

questions.stem: Interdependence of variances means:
options: Variances are always unrelated to each other
Only price variances need to be investigated
All variances in a period are favourable
One variance may be caused by, or offset, another
questions.rationale: For example, buying cheaper material (favourable price) may increase waste (adverse usage).

questions.stem: Budgeted fixed overhead is £60,000 for 12,000 hours (£5 per hour). Actual fixed overhead is £62,500 for 12,400 hours. What is the fixed overhead expenditure variance?
questions.rationale: Budget £60,000 − actual £62,500 = £2,500 adverse.

questions.stem: Net present value (NPV) is the:
options: Total of the undiscounted cash flows of a project
Number of years needed to recover the investment
Average annual accounting profit of a project
Present value of cash inflows less the initial investment
questions.rationale: Positive NPV adds value to the business.

questions.stem: A project costs £50,000 and gives cash inflows of £20,000 a year for 3 years. The 10% discount factor for 3 years' annuity is 2.487. What is the NPV?
A project has a positive NPV at the cost of capital. The decision should be to:
questions.rationale: A positive NPV means the return exceeds the required return.

questions.stem: A project costing £60,000 has cash inflows of £25,000, £25,000 and £30,000 in years 1 to 3. What is the payback period?
questions.rationale: After 2 years £50,000 recovered. Remaining £10,000 ÷ £30,000 = 0.33. Payback 2.33 years.

questions.stem: A project costs £100,000 with residual value £10,000. Average annual profit is £18,000. What is the accounting rate of return on average investment?
A disadvantage of the payback method is that it:
options: Uses accounting profit rather than cash flows
Is too complicated for managers to understand
Ignores cash flows after the payback period and the time value of money
Cannot be calculated for most projects
questions.rationale: Payback is simple but ignores overall profitability.

questions.stem: The internal rate of return (IRR) is the discount rate at which:
options: ARR equals the cost of capital
questions.rationale: A project is acceptable if the IRR is above the required return.

questions.stem: Which cash flow should be ignored in investment appraisal?
questions.rationale: Depreciation is a non-cash accounting charge.

questions.stem: £10,000 will be received in 3 years. The discount factor at 8% for year 3 is 0.794. What is the present value?
A company has 5,000 labour hours (the limiting factor). Product X gives £24 contribution for 4 hours and product Y £21 for 3 hours. Which should be prioritised?
options: Product X, higher contribution per unit
Product Y, contribution of £7 per hour versus £6
questions.rationale: Rank by contribution per limiting factor unit: X = £6, Y = £7.

questions.stem: A special order requires 200 kg of material already in stock, which cost £5 per kg. It has no other use except scrap at £2 per kg. What is the relevant cost?
questions.rationale: The relevant cost is the opportunity cost, the scrap value 200 × £2 = £400.

questions.stem: A special order uses 200 kg of material that would need to be replaced at £6 per kg. The stock cost £5 per kg. What is the relevant cost?
questions.rationale: If the material will be replaced, the relevant cost is the replacement cost: 200 × £6 = £1,200.

questions.stem: A division can shut down a product line with contribution of £20,000 but avoidable fixed costs of £25,000. What is the effect on profit of shutting it?
questions.rationale: Closing loses £20,000 contribution but saves £25,000 fixed cost, net gain £5,000.

questions.stem: In a make or buy decision, which cost is irrelevant?
questions.rationale: Costs that continue whichever option is chosen do not affect the decision.

questions.stem: A company can buy a part for £14 or make it at variable cost £11 and apportioned fixed overhead £4 (all fixed overhead is unavoidable). What should it do for 10,000 parts?
questions.rationale: Relevant cost of making is £11 against £14 buying, saving £3 × 10,000 = £30,000.

questions.stem: Cost-plus pricing sets the selling price by:
options: Adding a mark-up to the cost of the product
Setting price at the lowest cost
questions.rationale: A fixed margin or mark-up is added to unit cost.

questions.stem: A product costs £60 and the business adds a 25% mark-up. What is the selling price?
A product's target selling price is £90 and the required margin is 30% of price. What is the target cost?
In market skimming pricing, a business:
options: Always matches the prices of its competitors
Sets a high initial price and reduces it over time
Prices its products at cost with no mark-up
Sets a low initial price to gain market share
questions.rationale: It captures high prices from early adopters.

questions.stem: Penetration pricing is used to:
options: Signal luxury quality with a high price
Gain market share with a low initial price
Maximise profit early in the product's life
Remove an unprofitable product from the market
questions.rationale: A low entry price attracts customers quickly.

questions.stem: Which are the four perspectives of the balanced scorecard?
options: Financial, customer, internal processes, learning and growth
Profit, loss, cash flow and tax
questions.rationale: Kaplan and Norton's balanced scorecard balances financial and non-financial measures.

questions.stem: Return on investment (ROI) for a division with profit £60,000 and capital employed £400,000 is:
A division has profit £60,000, capital employed £400,000 and the group's cost of capital is 12%. What is the residual income?
A KPI should be:
options: Hard to measure so it cannot be gamed
Unrelated to the strategy of the business
Specific, measurable and linked to objectives
Vague enough to cover many objectives
questions.rationale: Good KPIs help management monitor progress towards goals.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-financial performance indicator?
questions.rationale: Non-financial measures cover quality, customers, staff and processes.

questions.stem: Divisional managers are judged on ROI. Why might a manager reject a project with a return of 14% when the division earns 20% ROI and the company's cost of capital is 10%?
options: It has a negative NPV at the company's cost of capital
ROI cannot be calculated for new projects
Accepting it would reduce the division's ROI even though it is beneficial to the company
It would breach the company's ethics rules
questions.rationale: ROI can cause dysfunctional decisions. Residual income avoids this.

questions.stem: A transfer price should ideally:
options: Be set each year by the external auditor
Maximise the profit of the selling division only
Promote decisions that are good for the whole organisation
Be set equal to zero for all transfers
questions.rationale: Goal congruence is the key aim.

questions.stem: A selling division has spare capacity and variable cost of £15 per unit. What is the minimum transfer price?
questions.rationale: With spare capacity there is no lost contribution, so the minimum is marginal cost.

questions.stem: An activity-based budget allocates overheads according to:
options: The actual overhead costs of last year
Cost drivers such as number of orders or set-ups
questions.rationale: ABB links resources to the activities that cause cost.

questions.stem: Which budgeting approach is most likely to uncover unnecessary spending?
questions.rationale: ZBB makes every cost justify itself.

questions.stem: A disadvantage of incremental budgeting is that it:
options: Needs no historical data to be prepared
Takes far longer to prepare than other methods
Cannot be used in a growing business
questions.rationale: Last year's spending is assumed to be necessary.

questions.stem: Imposed budgets are set by senior management. A common risk is:
options: Budgets that are too easy to achieve
Lack of commitment from the managers who must achieve them
Excessive slack built in by managers
questions.rationale: Targets that are not accepted can reduce motivation.

questions.stem: Feedback control in budgeting means:
options: Predicting the future results before they happen
Setting the budget at the start of the year
Comparing actual results with budget after the event and taking corrective action
Ignoring variances until the year end
questions.rationale: Feed-forward control looks ahead; feedback looks at past performance.

questions.stem: Which budget is typically prepared first when sales demand is the limiting factor?
questions.rationale: Other budgets are driven from the sales budget.

questions.stem: A company budgets fixed overheads of £120,000 for the year, spread evenly. Actual overhead for the first quarter is £34,000. What is the quarterly variance?
questions.rationale: Budget for a quarter is £30,000. Actual £34,000 is £4,000 over.

questions.stem: Beyond budgeting suggests:
options: Using rolling forecasts and relative targets instead of fixed annual budgets
Carrying out no review of performance
questions.rationale: It aims to be more adaptive.

questions.stem: Budgeted sales mix is 60% A and 40% B. Actual total sales are the same but 70% A and 30% B. If A earns higher margin than B, what is the likely effect on profit?
questions.rationale: A shift towards the higher-margin product raises average profit.

questions.stem: Standard variable overhead rate £5 per hour. Actual hours 2,100 and actual cost £10,200. What is the variable overhead expenditure variance?
questions.rationale: Standard cost for 2,100 hours = £10,500. Actual £10,200. Favourable by £300.

questions.stem: Standard hours for actual output 2,000; actual hours 2,100; standard variable overhead rate £5 per hour. What is the variable overhead efficiency variance?
questions.rationale: 100 extra hours × £5 = £500 adverse.

questions.stem: A planning variance arises when:
options: Sales volumes are higher than expected
The original standard was unrealistic compared with the revised, achievable standard
Prices of materials fall during the year
Staff work faster than the standard time
questions.rationale: It separates the effect of poor planning from operational performance.

questions.stem: An operating variance measures performance against:
questions.rationale: It shows what managers could control.

questions.stem: Budgeted fixed overhead absorption rate is £10 per unit based on 6,000 units. Actual output is 6,300 units. What is the fixed overhead volume variance?
questions.rationale: (6,300 − 6,000) × £10 = £3,000 favourable: more overhead was absorbed than budgeted.

questions.stem: Which is the most appropriate response to a significant adverse variance that is controllable?
options: Ignore it because it cannot be changed now
Investigate the cause and take corrective action
Blame the finance team for the result
Change the budget so the variance disappears
questions.rationale: Controllable variances should be addressed by the responsible manager.

questions.stem: A project costs £80,000 and yields £30,000 a year for 4 years. The 8% annuity factor for 4 years is 3.312. What is the NPV?
Two projects have positive NPVs, A £12,000 and B £20,000. They are mutually exclusive. Which should be chosen?
options: Neither, because they cannot both be done
A, because it is the less risky project
B, because it has the higher NPV
Both, because both have positive NPVs
questions.rationale: Higher NPV adds more value.

questions.stem: In capital rationing, projects may be ranked using the:
options: Gross profit margin of each project
questions.rationale: It shows value created per unit of scarce capital.

questions.stem: A project has an NPV of £15,000 and an initial investment of £60,000. What is the profitability index?
Which of these is a non-financial factor in investment appraisal?
questions.rationale: Qualitative factors can influence decisions.

questions.stem: Working capital invested at the start of a project and recovered at the end is treated as:
options: A cash outflow at the start and an inflow at the end
Treated as a profit at the start of the project
Ignored because it is not a cost of the project
Charged as depreciation over the project's life
questions.rationale: It is a cash flow in the project.

questions.stem: Which of these is a relevant cash flow for a new machine?
options: Interest on the loan used to finance it
Head-office costs that do not change
Additional operating cash inflow after tax from the project
questions.rationale: Financing costs are reflected in the discount rate, and non-cash items are ignored.

questions.stem: Inflation increases cash flows in future years. When doing NPV in money terms, the discount rate should be:
options: A real rate that excludes inflation
A money (nominal) rate that includes inflation
questions.rationale: Match cash flows and discount rate: nominal with nominal.

questions.stem: A project has an IRR of 14% and the cost of capital is 10%. The decision is to:
questions.rationale: IRR exceeds the required return.

questions.stem: Contribution per unit is £10 and each unit uses 2 kg of a scarce material. What is the contribution per kg?
A company with a limiting material of 4,000 kg has products P (contribution £12 per unit, 3 kg) and Q (£16, 5 kg). What is the contribution if all material is used on the better product?
options: £16,000 from P, as £4 per kg beats £3.20 per kg

questions.stem: A sunk cost is:
options: A cost already incurred that cannot be recovered
A cost that relates only to the next period
A cost that is relevant to the decision
A cost that will be incurred in the future
questions.rationale: It is ignored in decisions.

questions.stem: Which of the following should be included in a relevant cost calculation for labour that is fully employed?
options: Nothing, because wages are always sunk
Only the basic wages paid to the staff
The wages already paid last period
questions.rationale: Opportunity cost matters when labour is scarce.

questions.stem: Spare labour is available and already paid £20 per hour. A new job needs 100 hours. What is the relevant labour cost?
questions.rationale: If idle labour is paid regardless, there is no extra cost.

questions.stem: A product has variable cost £14 and a target contribution margin of 30% of price. What is the price?
questions.rationale: Variable cost is 70% of price. £14 ÷ 0.7 = £20.

questions.stem: Which pricing approach is most suitable for a product with strong brand loyalty and few substitutes?
questions.rationale: Customers are willing to pay more.

questions.stem: Price discrimination involves:
options: Always giving a discount to every customer
Setting a single price for all customers
Pricing every product below its cost
Charging different customers different prices for the same product
questions.rationale: It works when markets can be segmented.

questions.stem: A loss leader strategy:
options: Avoids all competition in the market
Sets very high prices to deter customers
Always results in an overall loss for the business
Sells one product below cost to attract customers to buy others
questions.rationale: It aims to increase total profit through other sales.

questions.stem: Return on capital employed (ROCE) is:
questions.rationale: It shows return on long-term funding.

questions.stem: Which perspective of the balanced scorecard looks at 'how do customers see us?'
questions.rationale: Measures include satisfaction and retention.

questions.stem: Which perspective focuses on innovation and staff skills?
questions.rationale: Examples are training hours and employee turnover.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of a leading indicator?
options: The closing cash balance at the year end
Annual revenue reported in the accounts
Last year's profit for the year
questions.rationale: Leading indicators predict future performance.

questions.stem: Benchmarking involves:
options: Comparing performance with best practice or competitors
Setting budgets for the coming year
questions.rationale: It identifies areas for improvement.

questions.stem: A transfer price is set at full cost plus 20%. A disadvantage is that it:
options: May not encourage efficiency or goal congruence
Has no administration cost to operate
Is always the optimal price for the group
questions.rationale: Cost-plus can pass on inefficiencies.

questions.stem: In a not-for-profit organisation, the '3Es' of performance are:
questions.rationale: They measure value for money.

questions.stem: Economy in value for money means:
options: Maximising the price charged for services
Achieving the stated objectives of the organisation
Obtaining inputs at the lowest cost for the required quality
questions.rationale: Efficiency relates output to input. Effectiveness relates outputs to objectives.

questions.stem: A budget that is prepared after considering input from the managers who must achieve it is described as:
questions.rationale: Participation increases ownership of targets.

questions.stem: In a flexible budget, which cost is NOT adjusted for changes in activity within the relevant range?
questions.rationale: Only variable costs move with activity.

questions.stem: A budget for 10,000 units has materials £50,000 and fixed overhead £30,000. What is the flexed budget at 12,000 units?
Budgetary control is the process of:
options: Comparing actual results with the budget and taking action on differences
questions.rationale: It involves monitoring and corrective action.

questions.stem: A cash budget helps a manager to:
options: Plan borrowing or investment of surplus funds
questions.rationale: It shows timing of cash flows.

questions.stem: Budgeted sales were 2,000 units at £50 and actual were 1,900 at £50. What is the sales volume variance in revenue?
questions.rationale: 100 fewer units × £50 = £5,000 adverse.

questions.stem: Standard contribution is £12 per unit. Budget 5,000 units. Actual sales 4,600 units. What is the sales volume contribution variance?
questions.rationale: 400 fewer units × £12 = £4,800 adverse.

questions.stem: A fixed overhead expenditure variance is the difference between:
questions.rationale: It measures overspend or underspend.

questions.stem: Which of the following might cause an adverse sales price variance?
options: Discounts offered to win more orders
questions.rationale: Selling at lower prices than standard.

questions.stem: A company expects a favourable materials price variance because of bulk buying. A likely trade-off is:
options: Higher holding costs and risk of obsolescence
questions.rationale: Buying more can increase storage cost.

questions.stem: A project costs £100,000 and returns £35,000 each year for 4 years. What is the payback period?
The 10% discount factors for years 1 to 3 are 0.909, 0.826 and 0.751. A project costs £20,000 and returns £8,000 each year for 3 years. What is the NPV?
questions.rationale: PV of inflows = £8,000 × 2.486 = £19,888. NPV = £19,888 − £20,000 = −£112, so the project is marginally unacceptable.

questions.stem: Which would increase the NPV of a project?
questions.rationale: A lower discount rate increases present values.

questions.stem: The accounting rate of return uses:
options: Accounting profit rather than cash flows
questions.rationale: ARR is based on profit and investment.

questions.stem: Why is the time value of money important?
options: Cash received sooner is worth more than cash received later
questions.rationale: Discounting reflects the opportunity cost of waiting.

questions.stem: A company can make 4,000 units but demand is 5,000. Which is the limiting factor?
questions.rationale: Capacity limits output.

questions.stem: A relevant cost for a decision is:
questions.rationale: Only differences between options matter.

questions.stem: Qualitative factors in a decision to outsource might include:
questions.rationale: Non-financial factors can be decisive.

questions.stem: A business uses full cost-plus pricing with a 20% mark-up on a total cost of £50. What is the price?
Target costing starts from:
options: The price customers will pay and works back to the allowable cost
questions.rationale: Target cost = target price − target margin.

questions.stem: A product's price elasticity of demand is high. A price cut will:
options: Increase revenue as demand rises proportionately more
questions.rationale: Elastic demand responds strongly.

questions.stem: Residual income is:
options: Profit less a charge for capital employed
questions.rationale: It reflects the cost of capital.

questions.stem: Division profit £90,000, capital employed £600,000, cost of capital 10%. What is the ROI and RI?
A key limitation of using only financial measures is:
options: They ignore factors such as quality and customer satisfaction
questions.rationale: A balanced set of measures is better.

questions.stem: Value for money in public services is measured by:
questions.rationale: These are the three Es.

questions.stem: A beyond-budgeting approach replaces fixed targets with:
options: Relative performance measures and rolling forecasts
questions.rationale: It focuses on adaptability.

questions.stem: Standard costing is used to:
options: Set expected costs and measure variances against them
questions.rationale: Standards support control.

questions.stem: A budget based on 20,000 units has total costs of £340,000 (fixed £100,000). What is the flexed budget at 25,000 units?
Which of the following is a behavioural problem with budgets?
options: Managers pad budgets to make targets easy
questions.rationale: Budgetary slack.

questions.stem: A capital budget is used to plan:
questions.rationale: It covers long-term expenditure.

questions.stem: Standard overhead absorption £8 per hour; actual hours 3,200; standard hours for output 3,000. What is the efficiency variance?
questions.rationale: 200 extra hours × £8 = £1,600 adverse.

questions.stem: Budgeted production 1,000 units; actual 1,100. Budgeted fixed overhead £20,000 (£20 per unit). What is the fixed overhead volume variance?
questions.rationale: 100 extra units × £20 = £2,000.

questions.stem: Material mix variance arises when:
options: The proportions of materials used differ from standard
questions.rationale: It relates to the blend.

questions.stem: Which person is most likely to be responsible for a materials price variance?
questions.rationale: Price relates to buying.

questions.stem: Variance investigation costs should be weighed against:
options: The expected benefit of correcting the cause
questions.rationale: Cost-benefit approach.

questions.stem: A project has cash flows: −£50,000 now and £18,000 per year for 4 years. What is the payback period?
A project has NPV of £6,000 at 10% and −£4,000 at 20%. By linear interpolation, the IRR is approximately:
If the NPV is zero, the project's return equals:
questions.rationale: IRR equals the discount rate.

questions.stem: Which factor would NOT be included in cash flows for NPV?
questions.rationale: It is non-cash.

questions.stem: A £100,000 asset gives £30,000 per year for 5 years with no residual value. The simple accounting rate of return on initial investment (depreciation straight-line) is:
The discounted payback period is:
options: Payback based on discounted cash flows
questions.rationale: It takes time value into account.

questions.stem: A company can buy a component for £10 or make it with variable cost £7 and fixed cost £3 (unavoidable). What should it do?
questions.rationale: Relevant cost of making is £7 only.

questions.stem: A product has a negative contribution. It should be:
options: Considered for discontinuation unless strategic benefits exist
questions.rationale: It reduces profit.

questions.stem: A company has 10,000 kg of material available. Product X needs 5 kg and earns £40; Y needs 2 kg and earns £22. Which earns more per kg?
questions.rationale: X £8/kg, Y £11/kg.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT relevant to a shutdown decision?
questions.rationale: They continue anyway.

questions.stem: A product costs £30 with a 40% mark-up. What is the price?
A target price is £80 and the required margin is 25% of price. The target cost is:
A firm uses price skimming for a new gadget. The most likely reason is:
options: To reduce price later to zero
Early adopters will pay a premium
questions.rationale: High initial price then lowers.

questions.stem: A price is set by reference to competitors' prices. This is:
questions.rationale: It looks outward.

questions.stem: ROI = profit £45,000; capital employed £300,000. What is ROI?
Which perspective of the balanced scorecard includes on-time delivery?
questions.rationale: It reflects process performance.

questions.stem: Residual income for a division with profit £70,000, capital £500,000 and cost of capital 12% is:
Transfer pricing at market price is most suitable when:
questions.rationale: Market prices reflect opportunity cost.

questions.stem: Efficiency in value for money is the relationship between:
questions.rationale: It measures how well resources are converted.

questions.stem: The main purpose of an external audit of a company's financial statements is to:
options: Calculate the tax payable by the company
Prevent all fraud in the company
Prepare the accounts for the directors
Give an independent opinion on whether they show a true and fair view
questions.rationale: Auditors express an opinion but the directors prepare the statements.

questions.stem: Reasonable assurance in an audit means:
options: Assurance relating to cash balances only
A high but not absolute level of assurance
No assurance is given to users
Absolute certainty that the accounts are correct
questions.rationale: Because of testing and inherent limitations, absolute assurance is impossible.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a limited-assurance engagement?
questions.rationale: A review provides negative assurance, less than an audit.

questions.stem: Who appoints the external auditor of a company?
questions.rationale: Auditors are appointed by shareholders to be independent of management.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a service that is NOT an assurance engagement?
options: A review of interim financial information
A statutory audit of financial statements
Preparing financial statements from the client's records
questions.rationale: Compilation and bookkeeping do not give assurance.

questions.stem: Which of these makes an audit report 'unmodified'?
options: The auditor disagrees with the accounts
A limitation has been placed on the scope
The financial statements show a true and fair view
A material uncertainty exists over going concern
questions.rationale: An unmodified (clean) opinion has no qualification.

questions.stem: An auditor cannot obtain sufficient evidence about a material balance but concludes the effect is not pervasive. The opinion is:
options: Disclaimer, as no opinion can be formed
Adverse, stating the accounts are misleading
Unmodified, with no change to the report
questions.rationale: A material but not pervasive limitation leads to a qualified opinion.

questions.stem: Financial statements are materially and pervasively misstated. The auditor gives:
questions.rationale: An adverse opinion says the statements do not give a true and fair view.

questions.stem: Materiality in audit is:
options: A limit set by tax rules
The fee agreed with the client
Any error at all, however small
The size of a misstatement that could influence users' decisions
questions.rationale: It guides planning and the evaluation of misstatements.

questions.stem: Audit risk is made up of:
options: Inherent risk, control risk and detection risk
Fraud risk and error risk only
questions.rationale: Audit risk = inherent × control × detection risk.

questions.stem: Inherent risk is the risk that:
options: A balance is misstated before considering controls
A client leaves for another audit firm
The auditor fails to detect a misstatement
Controls detect an error in the system
questions.rationale: It depends on the nature of the item, for example complex estimates.

questions.stem: If controls over a balance are strong, the auditor assesses control risk as:
options: Higher, so more testing is needed
Zero, so no testing is needed
Lower, so less substantive testing may be needed
questions.rationale: Effective controls reduce the risk of material misstatement.

questions.stem: If an auditor wants to reduce detection risk, they should:
options: Reduce the size of the sample tested
Do less testing on the balance
Perform more or better substantive testing
questions.rationale: Detection risk is under the auditor's control through the nature, timing and extent of tests.

questions.stem: Which of these is a typical planning procedure?
options: Signing the audit report on completion
Posting journals to the client's ledger
Understanding the client's business and its risks
Writing the financial statements for the client
questions.rationale: Understanding the entity is the basis for assessing risks.

questions.stem: Overall materiality is set at 1% of revenue of £8,000,000. What is materiality?
Which of the following is the most reliable type of audit evidence?
options: Internally generated documents with no checks
Evidence obtained directly by the auditor from external sources
questions.rationale: External, written and directly obtained evidence is generally more reliable.

questions.stem: Which procedure tests completeness of liabilities?
options: Reviewing post year-end payments and supplier statements
Inspecting documents showing ownership of assets
Observing the inventory count at the year end
questions.rationale: Unrecorded liabilities may be found by looking at payments after the year end.

questions.stem: An auditor traces a sample of items from the stores to the inventory listing. This tests:
questions.rationale: Physical to record tests whether everything that exists is recorded.

questions.stem: An auditor selects items from the inventory listing and inspects the items in the warehouse. This tests:
questions.rationale: Record to physical tests that recorded items really exist.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of external confirmation?
options: Re-performing a calculation made by the client
Carrying out analytical review of the ledger
Reviewing the budgets prepared by management
Writing to customers to confirm balances
questions.rationale: Receivables circularisation gives evidence from third parties.

questions.stem: Analytical procedures in audit involve:
options: Comparing and analysing relationships in financial data
Inspecting the contracts held by the client
Counting the inventory at the year end
questions.rationale: Unusual movements or trends point to potential misstatement.

questions.stem: Why is inventory cut-off testing performed?
options: To check the VAT charged on purchases
To check the unit values of the inventory
To make sure inventory movements are recorded in the correct period
To verify the identity of the staff counting
questions.rationale: Cut-off errors misstate cost of sales and inventory.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a substantive procedure?
options: Walking through a process to understand it
Assessing the tone set by senior management
Drawing a flowchart of the accounting system
Vouching a sample of sales invoices to the ledger
questions.rationale: Substantive tests check the amounts and disclosures themselves.

questions.stem: A test of control may involve:
options: Valuing the property held by the company
Counting the receivables balance at the year end
Inspecting whether purchase orders are authorised
questions.rationale: Tests of controls check that a control operated effectively.

questions.stem: An auditor tests a sample of 25 transactions and finds 1 error. The population is £500,000 and the sample £50,000 with error £1,000. What is the projected error (extrapolated by value)?
Auditor independence means the auditor is:
options: An employee of the client company
Always a shareholder of the client
Paid in shares of the client company
Free from influences that compromise objectivity
questions.rationale: Independence is crucial for credibility.

questions.stem: Which of the following threatens auditor independence?
options: Owning shares in the client company
questions.rationale: A financial interest is a self-interest threat.

questions.stem: The auditor prepares the client's accounts and then audits them. This creates a:
questions.rationale: Auditing one's own work is not objective.

questions.stem: An engagement letter sets out:
options: The scope, responsibilities and terms of the engagement
The year end figures of the company
The budget of the client for the year
The audit opinion on the financial statements
questions.rationale: It clarifies the responsibilities of both parties.

questions.stem: Going concern is relevant to the audit because:
options: It is not relevant to the audit at all
The accounts are prepared assuming the business will continue and the auditor must assess this
Auditors guarantee that the company will survive
It reduces the level of materiality used
questions.rationale: If material uncertainty exists the auditor must consider disclosure and the report.

questions.stem: The management representation letter is:
options: An invoice issued by the auditor for the audit
A report sent to HMRC by the company
A written confirmation from management of matters relevant to the audit
A statutory return filed at Companies House
questions.rationale: It supports other evidence but cannot replace it.

questions.stem: A key audit matter (KAM) in the audit report is:
options: A matter of most significance in the audit of the current period
A minor adjustment made to the accounts
An item relating to tax only
questions.rationale: KAMs are reported for listed companies and tell users about the areas of greatest risk.

questions.stem: Which type of audit is required by law for most UK companies above size thresholds?
questions.rationale: Statutory audits are required by the Companies Act for larger companies.

questions.stem: Internal audit differs from external audit because it:
options: Is required by law for all companies
Is performed only by the shareholders
Gives an opinion on the true and fair view
Is performed for management and covers a wide range of risks and controls
questions.rationale: Internal audit's scope is determined by management and the board.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a stakeholder who relies on the audit report?
questions.rationale: Audit reports add credibility for users of the financial statements.

questions.stem: An auditor's report on a small company with exemption from audit would be:
questions.rationale: Small companies meeting criteria can claim audit exemption.

questions.stem: True and fair view is a concept meaning that the accounts:
options: Meet the requirements of tax law only
Are accurate to the exact penny
Give a faithful presentation and are free from material misstatement
questions.rationale: It is a matter of overall judgement, not precision.

questions.stem: The auditor's responsibility for fraud is to:
options: Obtain reasonable assurance that the accounts are free from material misstatement due to fraud or error
Ignore fraud risk during the audit
Report all fraud to the shareholders only
questions.rationale: Management is primarily responsible for prevention and detection.

questions.stem: Where an auditor believes fraud may have occurred and law requires it, they should:
options: Delete the working papers about it
Ignore it and continue with the audit
Consider reporting to the appropriate authority
questions.rationale: Confidentiality does not stop statutory or legal reporting duties.

questions.stem: An audit risk assessment would consider an increase in complex estimates as:
questions.rationale: Estimates are subjective and prone to misstatement.

questions.stem: A new, unproven accounting system raises which risk?
questions.rationale: Untested systems may not prevent errors.

questions.stem: Performance materiality is set:
options: Equal to the profit for the year
Below overall materiality to reduce the chance of uncorrected misstatements exceeding materiality
questions.rationale: It provides a safety margin.

questions.stem: A company's profit before tax is £500,000 and the auditor uses 5% as the materiality benchmark. What is overall materiality?
Which of these is a typical benchmark for materiality in a profit-making company?
questions.rationale: Revenue, total assets and profit are common benchmarks.

questions.stem: An audit strategy sets out:
options: The holiday plan for audit staff
The client's budget for the next year
The overall scope, timing and direction of the audit
questions.rationale: The plan then details procedures.

questions.stem: Using the work of internal audit can help external auditors to:
options: Charge a higher fee to the client
Avoid carrying out the audit at all
Reduce the extent of their own procedures where internal audit is competent and objective
questions.rationale: Reliance is a judgement based on quality.

questions.stem: Which assertion is tested by confirming that recorded receivables are genuine amounts owed?
questions.rationale: Existence means assets, liabilities and equity exist at the date.

questions.stem: Which assertion is tested by checking whether all sales have been recorded?
questions.rationale: Completeness tests for omissions.

questions.stem: To test valuation of inventory, an auditor would:
options: Check cost records and compare with net realisable value
Count the number of staff employed
Review the VAT return for the period
questions.rationale: Inventory is valued at the lower of cost and NRV.

questions.stem: To test rights and obligations over a property, the auditor would inspect:
options: Title deeds or land registry documents
questions.rationale: Legal documents prove ownership.

questions.stem: Which evidence is generally more reliable?
options: Unsigned notes written by the client
questions.rationale: Originals are harder to alter.

questions.stem: Inquiry alone is generally:
questions.rationale: Inquiry must be corroborated by other procedures.

questions.stem: Re-performance means:
options: Asking a member of staff a question
Re-doing the accounts for the client
The auditor independently carrying out a procedure or control
questions.rationale: It is a reliable test of controls or calculations.

questions.stem: Observation of the inventory count by the auditor is evidence of:
options: The tax treatment of the inventory
The valuation of the inventory only
questions.rationale: It also helps test controls over counting.

questions.stem: An auditor uses a sample of 50 invoices from a population of 1,000. This is an example of:
questions.rationale: Sampling allows conclusions about the whole population.

questions.stem: Which of these is a non-statistical sampling method?
questions.rationale: Statistical methods involve random selection and evaluation using probability.

questions.stem: Cut-off testing for sales checks that:
options: Sales are recorded in the correct period
questions.rationale: Cut-off errors move income across periods.

questions.stem: A material uncertainty related to going concern that is adequately disclosed results in:
options: An unmodified opinion with a 'Material uncertainty related to going concern' section
questions.rationale: The auditor draws attention to the disclosure.

questions.stem: If management refuses to allow the auditor to access records, which opinion is likely?
options: Unmodified, with no change to the report
Qualified or disclaimer, depending on pervasiveness
Unmodified with an emphasis of matter
questions.rationale: A limitation on scope can lead to a qualified opinion or disclaimer.

questions.stem: An emphasis of matter paragraph is used to:
options: Replace the opinion on the accounts
Disclaim an opinion on the accounts
Qualify the opinion on the accounts
Draw attention to a matter already properly disclosed
questions.rationale: It does not modify the opinion.

questions.stem: The audit report is addressed to:
options: The directors of the company only
questions.rationale: The auditor reports to the owners.

questions.stem: After the audit, the auditor sends management a letter of weaknesses in internal control. This is called a:
questions.rationale: Management letters set out recommendations.

questions.stem: An auditor finds a misstatement of £8,000 which management refuses to correct. Materiality is £25,000. What is the most likely effect on the opinion?
options: No modification, as the item is below materiality
questions.rationale: Immaterial uncorrected misstatements are accumulated and evaluated, but do not alone modify the opinion.

questions.stem: Events after the reporting period are reviewed by the auditor up to:
options: The date of the audit report
questions.rationale: Subsequent events can affect the financial statements.

questions.stem: Which of these is a benefit of an audit to a company?
options: Increased credibility of the financial statements to lenders and investors
questions.rationale: Audit adds confidence but does not guarantee anything.

questions.stem: Assurance engagements involve three parties. These are:
options: The owner, the supplier and the customer
The auditor, HMRC and the bank
The practitioner, the responsible party and the intended users
questions.rationale: Each has a distinct role.

questions.stem: An audit report gives:
options: An opinion on the financial statements
questions.rationale: It provides assurance on the accounts.

questions.stem: A review engagement provides:
questions.rationale: Fewer procedures are performed than in an audit.

questions.stem: Under ISA 200, the overall objectives of the auditor include:
options: Obtaining reasonable assurance and reporting in line with findings
questions.rationale: These are the overall objectives.

questions.stem: Which of the following is part of understanding the entity in planning?
options: Its industry, regulatory environment and internal controls
questions.rationale: This helps identify risks of material misstatement.

questions.stem: An auditor may lower the audit risk by:
options: Increasing the amount of audit evidence obtained
questions.rationale: More evidence reduces detection risk.

questions.stem: Revenue is £10m and the auditor uses 0.5% of revenue as materiality. What is materiality?
Significant risks in an audit are those that:
questions.rationale: They often involve judgement or fraud.

questions.stem: An audit plan should be:
options: Updated if circumstances change during the audit
questions.rationale: Planning is iterative.

questions.stem: An auditor traces details from a delivery note to the sales invoice to test:
questions.rationale: It checks that all deliveries have been invoiced.

questions.stem: Inspecting a sample of invoices posted to the ledger tests:
questions.rationale: Vouching goes from ledger to documents.

questions.stem: An auditor sends confirmation requests to 20 customers and receives replies for 15. What should the auditor do about the five non-replies?
options: Perform alternative procedures, such as checking later receipts
questions.rationale: Alternative procedures provide evidence where confirmation fails.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of analytical review?
options: Comparing this year's gross margin with last year's
questions.rationale: It identifies unusual fluctuations.

questions.stem: A bank confirmation letter provides evidence of:
questions.rationale: It is externally generated evidence.

questions.stem: Audit evidence is considered sufficient when:
options: There is enough quantity to support the opinion
questions.rationale: Sufficiency is about quantity. Appropriateness is quality.

questions.stem: Where an auditor cannot attend the inventory count, they should:
options: Perform alternative procedures to obtain evidence over inventory
questions.rationale: Evidence must be sufficient and appropriate.

questions.stem: Test data in a computerised system is used to:
options: Check that the system processes transactions correctly
questions.rationale: It tests programmed controls.

questions.stem: Which of these is a safeguard to auditor independence?
questions.rationale: Rotation reduces familiarity risk.

questions.stem: An audit firm is paid a contingent fee based on the outcome of the audit. This creates a:
questions.rationale: Contingent fees for audits are generally prohibited.

questions.stem: An audit manager's spouse works as the finance director of the client. The main issue is:
options: Familiarity and self-interest threats to independence
questions.rationale: Close family relationships threaten objectivity.

questions.stem: Professional scepticism is:
options: A questioning mind and critical assessment of evidence
questions.rationale: It is essential throughout an audit.

questions.stem: A clean (unmodified) opinion states that the accounts give:
questions.rationale: That is the standard unmodified opinion.

questions.stem: An auditor disagrees with how an important item has been accounted for, which is material but not pervasive. The opinion is:
questions.rationale: A qualified opinion applies to material but not pervasive misstatement.

questions.stem: The auditor is unable to obtain evidence on many items and the possible effects are both material and pervasive. The opinion is:
questions.rationale: The auditor cannot form an opinion.

questions.stem: The directors' responsibilities statement and the auditor's report help readers to:
options: Understand who is responsible for preparing and who is responsible for reporting on the accounts
questions.rationale: They clarify roles.

questions.stem: A going concern disclosure in the notes is adequate and the auditor agrees. The report will:
options: Include a section on material uncertainty and remain unmodified
questions.rationale: The opinion is not modified if disclosure is adequate.

questions.stem: Which of these is a limitation inherent in an audit?
questions.rationale: Audits provide reasonable, not absolute, assurance.

questions.stem: Who is primarily responsible for preparing financial statements?
questions.rationale: Auditors express an opinion on them.

questions.stem: The objective of an external audit is to:
options: Express an opinion on the financial statements
questions.rationale: It adds credibility.

questions.stem: An agreed-upon procedures engagement:
options: Gives a true and fair opinion
Reports factual findings and gives no assurance opinion
questions.rationale: The user draws their own conclusions.

questions.stem: An exemption from audit for a small company applies if it meets conditions on:
options: Turnover, balance sheet total and employees
questions.rationale: Size thresholds determine exemption.

questions.stem: A preliminary analytical review during planning helps to:
questions.rationale: It highlights unusual relationships.

questions.stem: Overall materiality is £100,000. Performance materiality is set at 70%. What is performance materiality?
Audit risk is higher when:
options: Inherent risk and control risk are high
questions.rationale: Both increase the risk of misstatement.

questions.stem: An auditor identifies management override as a significant risk. The response includes:
options: Testing unusual journals and reviewing estimates
questions.rationale: ISA 240 requires specific procedures.

questions.stem: A first-year audit usually requires:
options: Extra work to understand the entity and opening balances
questions.rationale: Opening balances need assurance.

questions.stem: Which procedure is most appropriate to test the existence of fixed assets?
questions.rationale: Inspecting tangible assets gives reliable evidence.

questions.stem: Which procedure tests the completeness of purchases?
options: Tracing goods received notes to the purchases ledger
questions.rationale: Document to ledger tests omissions.

questions.stem: An auditor tests 60 items from a population worth £600,000. The sample value is £60,000 and errors total £1,800. What is the projected misstatement?
Audit evidence from a third party is generally:
options: More reliable than evidence from within the entity
questions.rationale: External sources are independent.

questions.stem: Substantive analytical procedures are most effective when:
options: Relationships are predictable and data is reliable
questions.rationale: Predictable relationships allow expectations.

questions.stem: The auditor reviews board minutes to:
options: Identify significant decisions and events affecting the accounts
questions.rationale: They provide context.

questions.stem: A significant receivable balance has no reply to a confirmation request. What is the best alternative procedure?
options: Examine subsequent cash receipts and supporting documents
questions.rationale: Subsequent receipts support existence.

questions.stem: An auditor who also does the client's bookkeeping faces a:
questions.rationale: Auditing own work.

questions.stem: Which would be a valid safeguard where a long relationship exists with the same audit client?
options: Rotation of the senior audit team
questions.rationale: Rotation addresses familiarity.

questions.stem: Confidentiality for auditors means they should:
options: Not disclose client information without permission or legal duty
questions.rationale: A fundamental principle.

questions.stem: A misstatement is material and pervasive. The opinion is:
questions.rationale: The accounts do not give a true and fair view.

questions.stem: The audit report must state:
options: The basis of the opinion and the auditor's responsibilities
questions.rationale: ISA 700 sets requirements.

questions.stem: Other matter paragraph is used to:
options: Draw attention to a matter other than those in the financial statements relevant to users
questions.rationale: It does not modify the opinion.

questions.stem: Management letters are sent to:
options: Management and those charged with governance
questions.rationale: They report control weaknesses.

questions.stem: The going concern basis is inappropriate and the accounts are still prepared on that basis. The opinion is:
questions.rationale: The accounts are materially and pervasively misstated.

questions.stem: A true and fair view opinion means the accounts are:
questions.rationale: Material misstatement is the key.

questions.stem: A business owned and run by one person who is personally liable for its debts is a:
questions.rationale: A sole trader has unlimited personal liability for business debts.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of a limited company?
options: It has no legal obligation to file accounts
It is a separate legal entity from its owners
questions.rationale: A company is legally separate from its shareholders, who generally have limited liability.

questions.stem: In a general partnership (not an LLP), partners are:
options: Jointly liable for the debts of the firm
Liable only up to their share capital
questions.rationale: Partners in a general partnership have unlimited personal liability.

questions.stem: A charity is mainly set up to:
options: Reduce the level of government debt
Provide financial returns to its owners
Achieve charitable purposes for public benefit
Maximise the profit paid to its shareholders
questions.rationale: A charity must operate for charitable purposes. Surpluses are reinvested rather than distributed.

questions.stem: Which type of organisation is usually owned by the government and funded by taxation?
questions.rationale: Public sector bodies deliver public services and are mostly funded by taxes.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes a franchise?
options: A business that is owned by the government
A business that is owned by its employees
A business licensed to use another business's brand and methods
A partnership formed between two charities
questions.rationale: A franchisee pays fees to use a franchisor's brand and system.

questions.stem: A social enterprise is best described as a business that:
options: Does not need to keep accounting records
Trades to achieve social or environmental objectives
Pays all of its profits to shareholders
Is owned and funded by the state
questions.rationale: Social enterprises trade like businesses but reinvest profit to achieve their social purpose.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of operating as a limited company rather than a sole trader?
options: No tax is payable on company profits
Accounts never have to be made public
Owners' personal assets are generally protected
questions.rationale: Limited liability protects shareholders' personal assets, but companies have extra duties including filing accounts.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an internal stakeholder?
questions.rationale: Employees work inside the organisation, while customers, HMRC and lenders are external.

questions.stem: Which stakeholder is mainly interested in whether a business can repay a loan?
questions.rationale: Lenders focus on the business's ability to meet interest and capital repayments.

questions.stem: HMRC's main interest in a business is:
options: That tax is calculated, reported and paid correctly
That customers are satisfied with products
That staff turnover is kept low
questions.rationale: HMRC is a regulator and tax collector.

questions.stem: Shareholders of a company are mainly interested in:
options: Profit and the return on their investment
Traffic levels around the local premises
questions.rationale: Shareholders invest to earn returns through dividends and share price growth.

questions.stem: A supplier who sells goods on credit is interested in the business primarily because of:
options: Its marketing strategy for next year
Its profit margin and nothing else
Its ability to pay invoices on time
Its charitable donations during the year
questions.rationale: Suppliers are exposed to credit risk and want to be paid.

questions.stem: A conflict between stakeholders arises when:
options: Shareholders want higher dividends but employees want higher pay
HMRC issues a tax code to an employee
A customer buys a product at the listed price
All stakeholders want the same outcome from the business
questions.rationale: Both groups claim a share of the same limited profits.

questions.stem: Which of these is a task of the finance function?
questions.rationale: The finance function records transactions, prepares reports and supports decisions.

questions.stem: The main purpose of management accounts is to:
options: Meet filing requirements at Companies House
Help managers make decisions and monitor performance
questions.rationale: Management accounts are for internal use and are not a legal requirement.

questions.stem: Financial accounts are mainly prepared for:
options: Employees who want to check their pay
External users such as shareholders and HMRC
Only the internal managers of the business
Competitors who want to compare performance
questions.rationale: Financial accounts follow regulations and are prepared for external parties.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a typical duty of a financial controller?
options: Recruiting staff for the sales team
questions.rationale: The financial controller manages accounting and reporting.

questions.stem: Why must accounting records be kept for a minimum period (for example 6 years for limited companies in the UK)?
options: To meet legal and tax requirements
To reduce the depreciation charged each year
To increase the profit shown in the accounts
To avoid the need to charge VAT
questions.rationale: HMRC and company law require records to be retained for set periods so they can be inspected.

questions.stem: A cash-flow forecast would normally be prepared by the finance function to:
options: Record the sales made in the past period
Plan whether the business will have enough cash in future periods
Calculate the depreciation on non-current assets
Report the profit for the year to HMRC
questions.rationale: A cash flow forecast helps identify future shortfalls or surpluses.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a fundamental principle of the AAT Code of Professional Ethics?
questions.rationale: The five principles are integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality, and professional behaviour.

questions.stem: Confidentiality means an accountant should:
options: Always report client matters to the press
Not disclose client information without proper authority or legal duty
Share information about clients with friends
Never share any information with the client
questions.rationale: Information must be kept private unless there is permission or a legal or professional duty to disclose.

questions.stem: An accountant's friend asks them to hide some income from HMRC. Which principle is mainly threatened?
questions.rationale: Integrity means being straightforward and honest and not being associated with false or misleading information.

questions.stem: An accountant accepts an expensive gift from a client who is awaiting a decision. Which threat does this create?
questions.rationale: A gift can influence judgement because of personal benefit.

questions.stem: A client pressures an accountant to change a figure by threatening to take their work elsewhere. This is an:
questions.rationale: Intimidation means being deterred from acting objectively because of threats.

questions.stem: An accountant prepares the accounts and is then asked to review their own work as part of the same engagement. Which threat arises?
questions.rationale: Reviewing one's own work reduces objectivity.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a possible safeguard against an ethical threat?
options: Accepting the gift and recording it later
Ignoring the issue and carrying on as normal
Having work reviewed by another member of staff
Telling the client about the concern only
questions.rationale: Independent review is a common safeguard that reduces the threat to objectivity.

questions.stem: Sustainability in business means:
options: Meeting present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs
Ignoring the environmental impact of activities
Reducing prices to win more customers
Maximising short-term profit above all else
questions.rationale: Sustainable organisations balance economic, social and environmental concerns.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of an environmental sustainability action?
questions.rationale: Environmental sustainability reduces resource use and pollution.

questions.stem: Which is an example of social sustainability?
options: Paying fair wages and ensuring safe working conditions
Paying dividends to the shareholders each year
Using recycled paper for all printing
Reducing the electricity used in the offices
questions.rationale: Social sustainability relates to employees, customers and communities.

questions.stem: Which law protects personal data held by organisations in the UK?
options: The Bribery Act on its own
The Consumer Rights Act on its own
The Companies Act 1985 on its own
UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018
questions.rationale: Organisations must collect, hold and use personal data lawfully and securely.

questions.stem: A business suspects a customer is laundering money. What is the correct action?
options: Ignore the concern and carry on trading
Report the concern to the appropriate person, such as the MLRO, without tipping off the customer
Delete the records relating to the customer
Tell the customer that a report is being made
questions.rationale: Money laundering regulations require suspicions to be reported internally. Tipping off is an offence.

questions.stem: Which law makes it an offence to give or receive bribes?
options: Health and Safety at Work Act 1974
questions.rationale: The Bribery Act 2010 criminalises bribery and failing to prevent it.

questions.stem: Under the Equality Act 2010, which of the following is a protected characteristic?
questions.rationale: Protected characteristics include age, disability, race, religion, sex and sexual orientation.

questions.stem: Employers must provide a safe workplace. Which Act sets out this duty?
options: Finance Act 2024 and its tax rules
Health and Safety at Work Act 1974
Companies Act 2006 and its reporting rules
questions.rationale: The 1974 Act sets the main duties on employers for health and safety.

questions.stem: Which method of communication is best for a formal record that a manager has instructed a change to a process?
options: A text from a personal phone
questions.rationale: Written communication provides a clear and auditable record.

questions.stem: Good communication in a finance team includes:
options: Long, vague reports with little detail
Clear, accurate and timely information to the right person
Sending all data to every member of staff
Delaying deadlines until staff are ready
questions.rationale: Communication should be clear, relevant and delivered when needed.

questions.stem: A manager has asked for sales data by Friday, but you will be late. What is the best action?
options: Ask a colleague to say the data was sent
Tell the manager as soon as possible and agree a new date
Send incomplete data without explaining it
Say nothing and hope the manager does not notice
questions.rationale: Early, honest communication allows the manager to plan.

questions.stem: Which spreadsheet function would add a column of numbers in cells B2 to B10?
questions.rationale: SUM adds a range of cells. B2+B10 would add only two cells.

questions.stem: A spreadsheet cell contains =A1*B1. What happens if the formula is copied down a row?
questions.rationale: Relative references change when copied to a new row.

questions.stem: To stop a cell reference changing when it is copied, you should use:
options: A named table covering the range
A relative reference such as A1
A text box placed over the cell
questions.rationale: The dollar signs fix the row and column.

questions.stem: The main objective of most private sector businesses is to:
options: Employ as many people as possible
Make a profit for their owners
questions.rationale: Private businesses aim to generate profit, though they may have other objectives too.

questions.stem: Which of these is a typical objective of a not-for-profit organisation?
options: Provide a service within its budget
questions.rationale: Not-for-profit organisations focus on their purpose, not profit distribution.

questions.stem: A limited liability partnership (LLP) gives members:
options: Limited liability but with partnership-style tax treatment
No liability to pay any tax
Unlimited personal liability for the debts
questions.rationale: An LLP is a separate legal entity, but members are taxed as partners.

questions.stem: Which type of business is owned by its customers or employees and run for mutual benefit?
questions.rationale: Co-operatives are owned and controlled democratically by their members.

questions.stem: A public limited company (plc) can:
questions.rationale: A plc may sell shares to the public and is subject to stricter rules.

questions.stem: In which sector does a local authority operate?
questions.rationale: Local authorities are government bodies funded by taxation.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes the voluntary sector?
options: The Armed Forces and emergency services
High street banks and building societies
Listed companies traded on the stock exchange
questions.rationale: The voluntary sector includes charities and not-for-profit groups.

questions.stem: Which sector produces raw materials such as coal and crops?
questions.rationale: The primary sector extracts or grows raw materials. Secondary manufactures. Tertiary provides services.

questions.stem: A car manufacturer is part of which sector of industry?
questions.rationale: Manufacturing turns raw materials into products.

questions.stem: A hairdresser is part of which sector of industry?
questions.rationale: Services are part of the tertiary sector.

questions.stem: Why might a business choose to operate as a limited company rather than a partnership?
options: To avoid filing returns with Companies House
To remove the need to prepare accounts
To limit the owners' personal liability for business debts
To avoid paying corporation tax on profits
questions.rationale: Limited liability protects owners' personal assets but adds reporting duties.

questions.stem: Which stakeholder is most interested in job security and working conditions?
questions.rationale: Employees depend on the organisation for their livelihood.

questions.stem: Which stakeholder is mainly interested in product quality, value and after-sales service?
questions.rationale: Customers want good quality and fair prices.

questions.stem: Local communities are stakeholders because they are affected by a business's:
options: Its range of products for customers
The terms of its bank loan
questions.rationale: Noise, pollution, jobs and local spending affect communities.

questions.stem: A manager wants a larger bonus for hitting profit targets and shareholders want a higher dividend. This is an example of:
options: A legal requirement under company law
questions.rationale: Both claims compete for the same profit.

questions.stem: A department that deals with recruitment, training and staff welfare is:
questions.rationale: HR manages people.

questions.stem: Which department is responsible for producing and recording the accounts?
questions.rationale: The finance department keeps records and reports.

questions.stem: A hierarchy shows:
options: Levels of authority and reporting lines in an organisation
The stock levels held in each store
The prices charged for each product
The tax rates applied to profits
questions.rationale: An organisation chart displays who reports to whom.

questions.stem: The finance department's role in supporting managers includes:
options: Hiring the cleaners for the premises
Providing budgets, forecasts and performance reports
Designing the logo and branding of the business
Making the products that are sold to customers
questions.rationale: Management accounting information supports decisions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a statutory (legal) duty of a limited company's directors?
options: Set up a website for the business
Hold monthly social events for staff
Prepare annual accounts and file them at Companies House
questions.rationale: Companies must prepare and file accounts and confirmation statements.

questions.stem: Which authority collects VAT and income tax?
questions.rationale: HM Revenue & Customs administers most UK taxes.

questions.stem: Companies House is the registrar of:
questions.rationale: It holds company registration details and filed accounts.

questions.stem: Which of these tasks might a payroll clerk do?
options: Audit the annual accounts of the business
Calculate wages, deductions and prepare payslips
Set the budget for the next year
questions.rationale: Payroll deals with pay, tax and NIC.

questions.stem: A budget is:
options: A financial plan for a future period
questions.rationale: Budgets set targets for income and expenditure.

questions.stem: Accurate and timely information is important because it:
questions.rationale: Decisions are only as good as the data behind them.

questions.stem: Which is an example of using accounting information to monitor performance?
options: Painting the walls of the office
Comparing actual sales with budgeted sales
Writing a staff handbook for new starters
questions.rationale: Variance reporting compares actual and plan.

questions.stem: A colleague tells you they falsified an expense claim. What should you do?
options: Help your colleague to cover it up
Ignore it and say nothing to anyone
Post about it on social media
questions.rationale: Integrity requires you to act on known wrongdoing through proper channels.

questions.stem: A client offers you a very large gift after you complete their accounts. The most appropriate response is to:
options: Decline it and tell your manager
Hide the gift from your firm
Ask the client for more in future
Accept it quietly and keep it to yourself
questions.rationale: Gifts can threaten objectivity.

questions.stem: Professional behaviour means:
options: Complying with laws and avoiding conduct that discredits the profession
Always agreeing with whatever clients request
Ignoring deadlines when work is busy
Maximising profit for the firm at all costs
questions.rationale: It is one of the five AAT fundamental principles.

questions.stem: You discover an error that reduces tax payable. Your manager tells you not to correct it. What is the correct action?
options: Raise it with a more senior person and seek advice, and do not take part in the error
Delete the evidence of the error
Say nothing and let the return go ahead
Send the return as it is without checking
questions.rationale: Integrity and compliance with law come first.

questions.stem: The Companies Act 2006 requires company records to be kept for at least:
questions.rationale: Retention periods vary, but 6 years is typical for company accounting records.

questions.stem: Which law covers how businesses must treat consumers?
questions.rationale: The Act sets rights on goods, services and digital content.

questions.stem: Under the National Minimum Wage rules, employers must:
options: Pay all wages in cash only
Pay at least the legal minimum hourly rate
Pay every worker exactly the same rate
Pay wages only once a year
questions.rationale: The minimum rate depends on the worker's age.

questions.stem: Which body regulates the use of personal data in the UK?
questions.rationale: The ICO enforces data protection law.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a business reducing its carbon footprint?
questions.rationale: Lower emissions support environmental sustainability.

questions.stem: Recycling paper in the office is an example of:
options: A tax saving for the business
An audit procedure carried out by auditors
questions.rationale: It reduces waste and resource use.

questions.stem: A fair trade policy supports sustainability by:
options: Avoiding the need for an audit
Cutting the wages paid to suppliers
Ensuring suppliers receive fair prices and conditions
Increasing the profit of the business only
questions.rationale: It supports social and economic sustainability in the supply chain.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to present a comparison of monthly sales over a year?
questions.rationale: Visuals make trends easy to see.

questions.stem: When writing a formal email to a customer you should:
options: Write in capital letters for emphasis
Send it without checking it first
Use a polite, professional tone and check accuracy
questions.rationale: Professional communication protects the organisation's reputation.

questions.stem: An email attachment containing confidential payroll data should be:
options: Printed and left on the desk
questions.rationale: Confidential data should be protected.

questions.stem: Which function finds the average of values in A1 to A10?
questions.rationale: AVERAGE returns the arithmetic mean of a range.

questions.stem: In a spreadsheet, cell A1 contains 200 and B1 contains 5. What does =A1/B1 return?
Which feature would you use to find all invoices over £1,000 in a list?
questions.rationale: Filters show only rows meeting criteria.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between a sole trader and a partnership?
options: A sole trader must prepare audited accounts
A partnership must be registered at Companies House
A sole trader has limited liability but a partnership does not
A partnership has two or more owners sharing profits and liability
questions.rationale: A sole trader has one owner. A general partnership has at least two.

questions.stem: Which of these is a feature of a public limited company (plc) but not a private limited company (Ltd)?
options: It may offer its shares to the general public
It has limited liability for shareholders
It is a separate legal entity
questions.rationale: Limited liability, separate legal identity and filing apply to both.

questions.stem: Shareholders of a limited company receive a share of profits as:
questions.rationale: Dividends are distributions of profit to shareholders.

questions.stem: A sole trader's profits are taxed as:
options: The personal income of the owner
questions.rationale: The business is not a separate legal entity.

questions.stem: A company's profits are subject to:
questions.rationale: Limited companies pay corporation tax on profits.

questions.stem: Which of these is a typical objective of a public sector organisation?
options: Provide services that meet public needs within budget
questions.rationale: Public bodies are accountable to the public and funded from taxes.

questions.stem: A business that wants to raise capital by selling shares to many investors is most likely to be a:
questions.rationale: Only a plc can offer shares to the public.

questions.stem: A company's main materials provider has a stake in the business as an:
questions.rationale: Suppliers are outside the organisation.

questions.stem: Customers are interested in a business mainly because they want:
options: Good products and services at a fair price
questions.rationale: Customers want value and reliability.

questions.stem: Which stakeholder invests money in a company and expects a return?
questions.rationale: Shareholders are the owners of the company.

questions.stem: A manager is a stakeholder because they are interested in:
options: Business performance, job security and rewards
questions.rationale: Managers are internal stakeholders affected by performance.

questions.stem: A company closes a factory to cut costs. Which stakeholder is most likely to oppose this?
questions.rationale: Jobs and local economic impact are affected.

questions.stem: A department that deals with buying raw materials and supplies is:
questions.rationale: Purchasing sources goods and services.

questions.stem: The marketing department is mainly responsible for:
options: Promoting products and understanding customer needs
questions.rationale: Marketing sells and promotes.

questions.stem: Which function is responsible for making products?
questions.rationale: Production turns inputs into outputs.

questions.stem: A small span of control means a manager:
questions.rationale: Narrow spans mean closer supervision.

questions.stem: Delegation means:
options: Giving authority for tasks to a subordinate while keeping accountability
questions.rationale: Managers remain accountable for delegated work.

questions.stem: The financial accounts of a limited company must be filed with:
questions.rationale: Filed accounts are available to the public.

questions.stem: Which of these is a task of the credit control function?
questions.rationale: Credit control manages receivables.

questions.stem: Bookkeeping is mainly about:
questions.rationale: It is the foundation for the accounts.

questions.stem: A management report to the board is most useful if it is:
questions.rationale: Decisions depend on prompt, reliable information.

questions.stem: Which of these would a finance team use to compare actual performance against plan?
questions.rationale: Variance analysis explains differences from budget.

questions.stem: A colleague asks to see a confidential client file for no business reason. You should:
questions.rationale: Information should only be shared with authorised people.

questions.stem: Which fundamental principle is breached by deliberately recording a false sale?
questions.rationale: Honesty and truthfulness are core to integrity.

questions.stem: An accountant who keeps their skills up to date through training is following:
questions.rationale: Ongoing learning maintains competence.

questions.stem: You are asked to approve an expense that you know is private. What should you do?
options: Refuse and report it through the proper channel
questions.rationale: Acting with integrity includes challenging inappropriate requests.

questions.stem: Whistleblowing is when an employee:
questions.rationale: Whistleblowers are protected by law in many cases.

questions.stem: Which law regulates the minimum employee pension provision in the UK?
questions.rationale: Employers must enrol eligible workers into a pension.

questions.stem: A contract of employment must be given to employees:
options: In writing, as a statement of terms
questions.rationale: Employees have a legal right to a written statement of terms.
