questions.stem: Why might a business hold a bank account in a foreign currency?
options: To match foreign currency receipts and payments and reduce conversion costs
To earn lower interest on its balances
To avoid paying tax on income
To avoid all exchange rate risk
questions.rationale: Natural hedging reduces exposure.

questions.stem: A treasury policy typically sets out:
options: The marketing rules for the business
The prices of the products sold
How cash, borrowing and risk should be managed
questions.rationale: A policy ensures consistent, controlled treasury decisions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a typical control over cash handling?
options: Daily banking of receipts and regular reconciliations
Letting one person handle every step
Leaving takings in the till overnight
questions.rationale: These controls reduce loss and fraud.

questions.stem: Cash management should be consistent with which ethical principle when advising a client on investments?
options: Maximising the fees earned by the adviser
questions.rationale: Advice must be based on proper knowledge and the client's needs.

questions.stem: Opening cash £8,000. Sales receipts £42,000. Payments: wages £18,000, suppliers £20,000, rent £3,000, loan repayment £4,000. What is the closing cash?
Which is a difference between profit and cash flow?
options: Profit includes capital purchases but cash flow does not
Cash flow includes capital purchases and loan repayments but profit does not
Cash flow includes depreciation as a cash cost
They are always equal in every period
questions.rationale: Timing and non-cash items cause differences.

questions.stem: A business buys goods on 60 days' credit and sells them on 30 days' credit. Compared with paying immediately, what is the effect on cash?
options: The business receives cash from customers 30 days before it pays the supplier
The business is always overdrawn as a result
The business pays 30 days before it is paid
There is no effect on the cash position
questions.rationale: Supplier credit longer than customer credit helps cash flow.

questions.stem: A cash flow forecast shows a shortfall of £15,000 in month 4. Which is a short-term way to cover it?
questions.rationale: Overdrafts are flexible short-term finance.

questions.stem: Which of these items should be excluded from a cash flow forecast?
options: Wages paid to staff each month
Loan repayments due in the period
questions.rationale: A provision is a non-cash accounting adjustment.

questions.stem: Sales are £20,000 in May. 40% are paid in May, 50% in June and 10% in July. How much cash is received in June from May sales?
Cash flow forecasts should be updated:
options: Never, once the forecast is approved
Only when asked to by HMRC
Regularly as new information becomes available
Only at the end of the financial year
questions.rationale: Forecasts are only useful when they reflect current expectations.

questions.stem: A positive cash balance in a forecast period might allow a business to:
options: Increase the amount of credit sales
Invest surplus funds short term or repay debt
questions.rationale: Surpluses should be used effectively.

questions.stem: Receivables days 50, inventory days 70, payables days 40. What is the cash operating cycle?
Revenue is £1,460,000 and receivables are £200,000. What are receivables days (365-day year)?
Which action is most likely to improve working capital?
options: Paying suppliers earlier than the due date
Reducing the credit period given to customers
Increasing the amount of inventory held
Offering longer credit terms to customers
questions.rationale: Collecting cash faster reduces the need for finance.

questions.stem: Which ratio measures the ability to meet short-term debts with the most liquid assets?
questions.rationale: Quick ratio excludes inventory.

questions.stem: Current assets are £60,000 including inventory £20,000. Current liabilities are £40,000. What is the quick ratio?
A business with high inventory days may be exposed to:
questions.rationale: Holding stock ties up cash.

questions.stem: Economic order quantity (EOQ) balances:
questions.rationale: The EOQ minimises total inventory costs.

questions.stem: Taking a 3% discount for payment in 15 days instead of 45 days has an annualised implied cost of about:
Factoring receivables can improve:
options: The gearing ratio of the business
The inventory turnover of the business
The revenue earned by the business
Cash flow by releasing cash earlier
questions.rationale: Factors advance a percentage of invoice value.

questions.stem: Which source of finance usually has the lowest cost for a company?
options: Retained profit, which has no cost at all
Secured bank loan, because debt is cheaper than equity
questions.rationale: Debt is cheaper as lenders carry less risk and interest is tax deductible.

questions.stem: Retained earnings are:
options: A bank loan taken out by the company
A government grant paid to the company
questions.rationale: Retained profit is reinvested.

questions.stem: A company issues 200,000 new £1 shares at £2.50 each. How much cash is raised?
A rights issue offers new shares to:
options: New investors only, at a discount
The general public through an offer
Existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings
The directors of the company only
questions.rationale: It reduces dilution risk.

questions.stem: A mortgage on commercial property is:
questions.rationale: The property is security for the loan.

questions.stem: Hire purchase differs from a finance lease because:
options: Ownership never passes to the buyer
It needs no deposit or payments
It is a type of government grant
Ownership usually passes to the buyer after the final payment
questions.rationale: HP leads to ownership.

questions.stem: A bank offers a 10-year loan of £100,000 at 6% with interest-only payments. What is the annual interest?
Crowdfunding is:
options: An overdraft facility from a bank
A loan from a high street bank
Raising small amounts from many investors online
A form of tax relief for investors
questions.rationale: It can be donation, reward, debt or equity based.

questions.stem: Business angels are:
options: Wealthy individuals who invest in early-stage companies
Banks that lend to small businesses
questions.rationale: They provide capital and often advice.

questions.stem: £5,000 is invested at 3% compound interest for 3 years. What is the closing value, to the nearest £?
An overdraft of £20,000 costs 11% a year. What is the interest for 2 months?
The effective annual rate is higher than the nominal rate when interest is:
options: Compounded more than once a year
questions.rationale: More frequent compounding increases the effective rate.

questions.stem: When interest rates rise, the market value of fixed-rate bonds usually:
questions.rationale: Fixed coupons become less attractive.

questions.stem: A business has £50,000 surplus cash for 3 months. A deposit pays 4% a year. What interest is earned (simple)?
A UK company buys goods for €40,000 at £1 = €1.15. What is the cost in sterling (to the nearest £)?
A weaker pound makes UK exports:
options: Free of tax for overseas buyers
Unchanged in price for overseas buyers
questions.rationale: Foreign buyers need less of their currency to buy pounds.

questions.stem: A UK company will receive $100,000 in 3 months. The current rate is £1 = $1.30. The forward rate is £1 = $1.28. What is the sterling receipt using the forward contract?
Hedging is:
options: Reducing exposure to a risk such as exchange rate movements
questions.rationale: Examples are forward contracts and options.

questions.stem: Which of these is a key aim of cash management?
options: Holding no cash at all at any time
Having enough liquidity while earning a return on surplus funds
questions.rationale: Balance liquidity, safety and return.

questions.stem: A company is considering paying a supplier early to get a discount. It should compare the discount rate with:
options: Its share price on the stock market
The cost of borrowing or the return on surplus cash
questions.rationale: If the implied return is higher than alternatives, early payment is worthwhile.

questions.stem: A company's treasury policy limits investments to institutions with high credit ratings. This reduces:
questions.rationale: Highly rated banks are less likely to default.

questions.stem: Segregation of duties in treasury means:
options: The person who arranges deals does not also approve and record them
Dealing is not restricted in any way
One person carries out every step of a deal
No records need to be kept of deals
questions.rationale: It lowers fraud and error risk.

questions.stem: A business expects sales of £90,000 in June, 40% received in the month and 60% a month later. May sales were £80,000. What is cash received from sales in June?
A forecast shows closing cash in March of £6,500 and April receipts of £20,000, payments of £24,000. What is closing cash in April?
Which of these would improve a cash flow forecast the most?
questions.rationale: Faster collection increases receipts.

questions.stem: Why might a profitable business have negative cash flow?
options: Because of investment in assets and growth in working capital
questions.rationale: Profit does not equal cash.

questions.stem: A sensitivity analysis on a cash forecast tests:
options: How cash changes if key assumptions change
questions.rationale: It identifies risk.

questions.stem: Which item is a cash outflow?
questions.rationale: Wages are paid in cash.

questions.stem: Cost of sales is £730,000 and inventory is £100,000. What are inventory days (365 days)?
Working capital ratio of 2:1 means:
options: Current assets are twice current liabilities
questions.rationale: It is the current ratio.

questions.stem: A just-in-time system relies heavily on:
options: Reliable suppliers and accurate demand forecasting
questions.rationale: Stock is delivered when needed.

questions.stem: Which action reduces the cash operating cycle?
options: Extending the payment period to suppliers (within agreed terms)
questions.rationale: More supplier credit funds working capital.

questions.stem: A business offers 1.5% discount for payment in 10 days instead of 40 days. What is the approximate annualised rate?
Which source is suitable for short-term working capital?
questions.rationale: It is flexible and repayable on demand.

questions.stem: A debenture is:
options: A long-term loan often secured on company assets
questions.rationale: Debenture holders are creditors.

questions.stem: Sale and leaseback is when a business:
options: Sells an asset and leases it back to release cash
questions.rationale: It converts an asset into cash.

questions.stem: A company has gearing (debt/(debt+equity)) of 25% and issues more debt. Gearing will:
questions.rationale: More debt raises the debt proportion.

questions.stem: Government grants may be available to support:
questions.rationale: Grants have conditions attached.

questions.stem: Trade credit is:
options: Credit given by suppliers allowing delayed payment
questions.rationale: It is a free source of short-term finance if paid on time.

questions.stem: Peer-to-peer lending connects:
options: Borrowers directly with individual lenders online
questions.rationale: It is an alternative finance source.

questions.stem: Simple interest on £8,000 at 5% for 18 months is:
£20,000 is invested for 3 years at 6% compound interest. What is the value after 3 years?
A bank pays 2% interest on a £25,000 deposit for a year. What interest is earned?
Inflation reduces the:
questions.rationale: Money buys less over time.

questions.stem: The risk that interest rates rise and increase borrowing costs is:
questions.rationale: Fixed-rate loans reduce this risk.

questions.stem: A UK company sells goods to the US for $65,000 at £1 = $1.30. What is the sterling value?
A UK company has to pay €30,000 when £1 = €1.20. What is the sterling cost?
A UK importer will pay $200,000 in 3 months. If the dollar strengthens against the pound by that date, the sterling cost will:
questions.rationale: More pounds are needed to buy dollars.

questions.stem: Which is a way to reduce exchange rate risk on a future dollar payment?
questions.rationale: Forward contracts fix the rate.

questions.stem: A cash pooling arrangement between group companies helps to:
options: Reduce overall borrowing and interest costs
questions.rationale: Surpluses offset deficits.

questions.stem: A company's liquidity policy sets:
options: Minimum cash or facility levels to meet obligations
questions.rationale: It protects against cash shortfalls.

questions.stem: A company invests surplus cash in a deposit with a bank rated highly. The main risk reduced is:
questions.rationale: Highly rated banks are less likely to default.

questions.stem: A business forecasts cash receipts of £62,000 and payments of £68,000 in a month. Opening cash is £10,000. What is closing cash?
Which of these would be a one-off cash outflow in a cash flow forecast?
questions.rationale: Capital items are not regular.

questions.stem: A business buys goods for £30,000 on 45 days' credit, sells for £48,000 on 60 days' credit. If sales and purchases occur on day 0, what is the timing of the net cash flow?
options: Pays suppliers on day 45, receives customers on day 60
questions.rationale: The business funds the gap of 15 days.

questions.stem: A cash deficit that is short-term could be financed by:
questions.rationale: It matches the short-term need.

questions.stem: A cash flow forecast should include VAT payments because:
options: VAT is a cost of sales
VAT is a cash outflow to HMRC
questions.rationale: VAT payments affect cash.

questions.stem: Cash in the bank at the start of the month plus receipts less payments equals:
questions.rationale: It is the basic cash calculation.

questions.stem: Which would improve cash by releasing working capital?
questions.rationale: Lower inventory frees cash.

questions.stem: A high payables period may indicate:
options: Use of supplier credit as a source of finance
questions.rationale: It could also signal liquidity strain.

questions.stem: Revenue £2,190,000 and receivables £300,000. What are receivables days (365)?
Which is a symptom of overtrading?
options: Rapid sales growth with a large overdraft
questions.rationale: Growth outpaces funding.

questions.stem: Offering a settlement discount to customers aims to:
questions.rationale: It improves cash flow.

questions.stem: Which ratio is a measure of efficiency in collecting debts?
questions.rationale: Lower is generally better.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of an overdraft?
options: Repayable on demand and variable interest
questions.rationale: It is flexible but can be withdrawn.

questions.stem: A company borrows £200,000 at 7% interest-only for 5 years. Tax is 25%. What is the annual post-tax cost of interest?
The main advantage of a bank loan over equity is:
questions.rationale: Lenders have no ownership rights.

questions.stem: Venture capital is most likely to be provided to:
questions.rationale: Investors seek high returns.

questions.stem: Debt finance requires the company to:
options: Pay interest and repay the principal
questions.rationale: It is a contractual obligation.

questions.stem: £5,000 is invested at 8% per year with interest compounded half-yearly (4% per half-year) for 1 year. What is the value?
An investment with higher risk is expected to offer:
questions.rationale: Risk and return are linked.

questions.stem: A fixed-term deposit is useful for:
options: Surplus cash not needed for a known period
questions.rationale: It locks in funds for a higher rate.

questions.stem: Liquidity risk is the risk of:
options: Not being able to meet payments when due
questions.rationale: Cash may not be available.

questions.stem: A UK business is due to pay SEK 500,000 when £1 = SEK 12.5. What is the sterling cost?
The pound strengthens against the euro. A UK importer buying from the eurozone will pay:
options: Less sterling for the same euro cost
questions.rationale: Each pound buys more euros.

questions.stem: A UK exporter will receive US$ in 3 months. To avoid exchange rate risk it could:
options: Enter a forward contract to sell the dollars
questions.rationale: A forward fixes the rate.

questions.stem: A natural hedge arises when a business:
options: Matches foreign currency receipts and payments
questions.rationale: Exposure is reduced without instruments.

questions.stem: A treasury policy might set limits on:
options: Counterparty exposure and types of investment
questions.rationale: It controls risk.

questions.stem: The main role of a treasury function is to manage:
questions.rationale: It supports liquidity.

questions.stem: A company has a floating rate loan. Which risk does it face?
questions.rationale: Higher rates increase interest.

questions.stem: Why should treasury duties be separated between those who arrange deals and those who record them?
options: To reduce the risk of fraud and errors
questions.rationale: It is segregation of duties.

questions.stem: Which statement shows a company's assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time?
questions.rationale: The statement of financial position (balance sheet) is a snapshot at the reporting date.

questions.stem: A company issues 100,000 £1 ordinary shares at £1.50 each. What is credited to share premium?
questions.rationale: Nominal value £100,000 goes to share capital. The excess of £0.50 × 100,000 = £50,000 is share premium.

questions.stem: A company has 400,000 £1 ordinary shares. It makes a 1 for 4 bonus issue from retained earnings. What is the increase in share capital?
questions.rationale: 1 new share for every 4 held = 100,000 shares at £1 nominal. Share capital rises by £100,000 and retained earnings fall by the same amount.

questions.stem: A rights issue is made of 1 new share for every 2 held. The company has 600,000 £1 shares and the issue price is £1.20. What cash is raised if all rights are taken up?
questions.rationale: 300,000 new shares × £1.20 = £360,000. Share capital rises £300,000 and share premium £60,000.

questions.stem: Which of the following is shown in the statement of changes in equity?
questions.rationale: The SOCE shows profit for the year, other comprehensive income, share issues and dividends.

questions.stem: Where is a revaluation surplus on property recorded?
options: In share capital as new shares issued
Other comprehensive income and a revaluation reserve in equity
As a liability in the statement of financial position
In profit or loss as other income
questions.rationale: A surplus on revaluation is recognised in OCI and accumulated in equity, not taken to profit.

questions.stem: A company declares and pays an ordinary dividend of £0.10 per share on 2,000,000 shares. What is the effect?
options: Profit for the year falls by £200,000 and cash falls by £200,000
Retained earnings fall by £200,000 and cash falls by £200,000
Share capital falls by £200,000 and cash falls by £200,000
Liabilities rise by £200,000 and cash is unchanged
questions.rationale: Dividends are a distribution of profit and are not an expense in profit or loss.

questions.stem: A company has an 8% loan of £500,000 throughout the year. What is the finance cost for the year?
questions.rationale: £500,000 × 8% = £40,000, shown in finance costs.

questions.stem: Preference shares that carry a fixed dividend and are redeemable are normally classified as:
options: Equity, with the dividend as a distribution
Liabilities, with the dividend as a finance cost
questions.rationale: Redeemable preference shares meet the definition of a financial liability under IAS 32.

questions.stem: Under IAS 2, inventory is valued at:
options: The expected selling price of the inventory
The higher of cost and net realisable value
The lower of cost and net realisable value
The cost of replacing the inventory today
questions.rationale: Inventory must not be carried above the amount expected to be recovered.

questions.stem: Inventory cost £18,000 can be sold for £20,000 after repairs costing £3,500 and selling costs of £1,000. At what value should it be held?
Which of these costs can be included in inventory under IAS 2?
options: Storage costs not needed in production
Production overheads based on normal capacity
questions.rationale: Only costs of bringing inventory to its present location and condition are included.

questions.stem: Under IAS 16, which of these is capitalised as part of the cost of a non-current asset?
questions.rationale: Costs directly attributable to bringing the asset to its working condition are capitalised.

questions.stem: A machine costing £100,000 has a 10-year life. After 4 years it is revalued to £90,000 with remaining life of 6 years and no residual value. What is the revaluation surplus?
questions.rationale: Carrying amount = £100,000 − 4 × £10,000 = £60,000. Revalued to £90,000, so surplus = £30,000.

questions.stem: Following the revaluation of a machine to £90,000 with 6 years left, what is the annual depreciation?
A provision should be recognised under IAS 37 when:
options: A contingent asset exists at the reporting date
A loss is merely possible in future
There is a present obligation, an outflow is probable and it can be reliably estimated
Management intends to spend money in future
questions.rationale: All three conditions must be met.

questions.stem: A possible obligation where the outflow is not probable should be:
options: Recognised in full as a provision
Recorded as revenue in the period
questions.rationale: Contingent liabilities are disclosed unless the possibility of outflow is remote.

questions.stem: After the year end, but before the accounts are approved, a customer owing £12,000 at the reporting date goes into liquidation. How is this treated under IAS 10?
options: An adjusting event: write off or provide against the receivable
A non-adjusting event, so disclose only
An event requiring a reduction in share capital
Not an event, so ignore it
questions.rationale: It provides evidence of conditions at the reporting date, so the accounts are adjusted.

questions.stem: A fire destroys a warehouse after the year end. Under IAS 10 this is:
options: A prior-period error to be corrected
An event that is ignored in the accounts
An adjusting event requiring the accounts to be changed
A non-adjusting event, disclosed if material
questions.rationale: The condition did not exist at the reporting date, so only disclosure is required.

questions.stem: Under IFRS 15, revenue is recognised when:
options: Cash is received from the customer
The invoice is printed and sent
The contract is signed by both parties
questions.rationale: Revenue is recognised as control of goods or services passes to the customer.

questions.stem: A company sells a 12-month service subscription for £2,400 on 1 October. Its year end is 31 December. How much revenue is recognised in the year?
questions.rationale: 3 months of 12 = £2,400 × 3/12 = £600. The remainder is contract liability (deferred income).

questions.stem: Research costs under IAS 38 are:
questions.rationale: Research cannot be capitalised. Development costs can be if criteria are met.

questions.stem: A change in accounting policy is applied retrospectively. A change in accounting estimate is applied:
questions.rationale: Estimates (such as useful life) are changed from the date of the change, not restated.

questions.stem: Which section of the statement of cash flows includes the purchase of a machine?
questions.rationale: Capital expenditure on non-current assets is an investing cash flow.

questions.stem: Operating profit is £120,000. Depreciation is £30,000, inventory increased by £12,000, receivables increased by £8,000 and payables increased by £5,000. What is cash generated from operations?
A company issues shares for cash. Where is this shown in the statement of cash flows?
questions.rationale: Raising or repaying capital is a financing cash flow.

questions.stem: Why is depreciation added back to profit when calculating cash from operations?
questions.rationale: Depreciation reduces profit but does not use cash.

questions.stem: Opening property, plant and equipment was £400,000, closing £460,000, depreciation £50,000 and there were no disposals. What were the additions (cash paid to buy assets)?
questions.rationale: Closing 460 = opening 400 + additions − depreciation 50, so additions = 460 − 400 + 50 = £110,000.

questions.stem: A company profit on disposal of an asset is £8,000 and proceeds are £30,000. What is shown in investing activities?
options: £30,000 inflow, with the £8,000 profit deducted in operating reconciliation
questions.rationale: The proceeds are an investing inflow. The profit is a non-cash adjustment in the operating section.

questions.stem: A parent has control of a subsidiary when it holds:
options: More than 50% of the voting rights (or otherwise controls it)
Any shares in the other company at all
At least 20% of the voting rights
Only preference shares in the other company
questions.rationale: Control, normally over 50% of votes, requires consolidation.

questions.stem: Parent pays £600,000 for 80% of a subsidiary with fair value net assets of £500,000. NCI is measured at its proportionate share of net assets. What is goodwill?
A subsidiary has net assets of £650,000 at the year end and the parent owns 80%. What is the non-controlling interest (proportionate method, ignoring goodwill)?
Parent sold goods to a subsidiary for £60,000 (cost £40,000). Half remain in the subsidiary's inventory at year end. What is the unrealised profit adjustment?
questions.rationale: Profit £20,000 × 50% unsold = £10,000, deducted from group inventory and retained earnings.

questions.stem: Parent revenue is £800,000, subsidiary revenue is £300,000 and intra-group sales are £50,000. What is consolidated revenue?
questions.rationale: £800,000 + £300,000 − £50,000 = £1,050,000. Intra-group sales are eliminated.

questions.stem: A subsidiary profit for the year is £100,000 and the parent holds 75%. What is the profit attributable to NCI?
A company holds 30% of another company and has significant influence but not control. How is it accounted for in group accounts?
options: As an associate using the equity method
questions.rationale: Between 20 and 50% with significant influence usually indicates an associate.

questions.stem: Gross profit margin is calculated as:
questions.rationale: It shows the percentage of sales left after cost of sales.

questions.stem: Revenue is £500,000 and cost of sales is £300,000. What is the gross profit margin?
Current assets are £180,000 (including inventory £60,000) and current liabilities are £90,000. What is the quick (acid test) ratio?
Operating profit is £120,000. Equity is £800,000 and non-current liabilities are £200,000. What is the return on capital employed?
Revenue is £730,000 and trade receivables are £120,000. What is the receivables collection period (365-day year)?
Cost of sales is £438,000 and inventory is £73,000. What is the inventory holding period (365-day year)?
Cost of sales is £438,000 and trade payables are £54,000. What is the payables payment period (365-day year, using cost of sales)?
Operating profit is £60,000 and finance costs are £15,000. What is interest cover?
Non-current liabilities are £300,000 and equity is £700,000. What is gearing (non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities))?
Gross margin has fallen from 40% to 34% while revenue has risen. Which is a possible explanation?
options: Depreciation charges fell during the year
Selling prices cut or input costs have risen
questions.rationale: Gross margin is affected by selling price and direct costs, not overheads.

questions.stem: A high current ratio of 3.5 might indicate:
options: A lower level of profit than last year
A high level of gearing in the company
Inefficient use of working capital, such as excess inventory or cash
Liquidity problems in meeting short-term debts
questions.rationale: A very high ratio may reflect idle resources, though it also suggests liquidity strength.

questions.stem: A limitation of ratio analysis is that:
options: It can predict the future exactly
It is always forward looking and predictive
It requires no judgement from the user
It depends on historical figures and accounting policies that can differ between companies
questions.rationale: Ratios should be compared over time and against similar organisations and used with other information.

questions.stem: A company has 500,000 £1 ordinary shares and share premium of £80,000. It issues 100,000 new shares at £1.80. What is the share premium account balance afterwards?
Which of these can the share premium account be used for?
questions.rationale: Share premium is a non-distributable reserve.

questions.stem: Retained earnings at the start of the year were £120,000. Profit for the year was £45,000 and dividends paid were £20,000. What is the closing balance?
A company with 2,000,000 £0.50 shares declares a dividend of 3p per share. What is the total dividend?
In a company's statement of profit or loss, income tax expense is shown:
questions.rationale: Profit after tax = profit before tax − income tax expense.

questions.stem: Profit before tax is £200,000 and tax is calculated at 25%. What is profit after tax?
A company underestimated last year's tax by £3,000. How is the difference treated this year?
options: Included in this year's tax expense
questions.rationale: A change in estimate is dealt with in the current period.

questions.stem: Which of the following is shown in other comprehensive income?
questions.rationale: OCI includes revaluation gains.

questions.stem: Directors' remuneration is disclosed in:
options: The notes to the financial statements
The bank statement of the company
It is not disclosed to anyone
questions.rationale: Companies must disclose director pay.

questions.stem: A company's capital is divided into:
questions.rationale: Shares represent ownership.

questions.stem: Which reserve cannot be used to pay dividends?
questions.rationale: Unrealised surpluses are not distributable.

questions.stem: Under IAS 16, depreciation of a non-current asset starts when:
options: The asset is available for use
questions.rationale: Depreciation begins when the asset is in the location and condition for use.

questions.stem: Land is normally:
options: Not depreciated because it has an unlimited life
Expensed in the year of purchase
Depreciated over a period of 50 years
Depreciated each month on a reducing balance
questions.rationale: Land generally has an indefinite life.

questions.stem: A building costing £500,000 includes land of £100,000. The building has a 40-year life and no residual value. What is annual depreciation?
questions.rationale: Depreciable amount £400,000 ÷ 40 = £10,000.

questions.stem: Under IAS 16, subsequent expenditure that extends the life of an asset is:
questions.rationale: Betterment costs add to the asset.

questions.stem: A company changes from FIFO to AVCO for inventory valuation. This is a:
options: Change treated as a dividend to shareholders
Error corrected as a prior period adjustment
Change in accounting estimate applied prospectively
Change in accounting policy applied retrospectively
questions.rationale: A policy change requires restatement of comparatives.

questions.stem: A £60,000 error in last year's profit is discovered. The correct treatment under IAS 8 is:
options: Restate the comparatives and opening balances
Charge it to this year's income statement only
questions.rationale: Material prior period errors are corrected retrospectively.

questions.stem: Under IAS 37 a provision is measured at:
options: The most optimistic estimate of the amount
Zero until payment is actually made
The best estimate of the expenditure required to settle the obligation
The highest possible amount that might be paid
questions.rationale: Provisions are best-estimate liabilities.

questions.stem: A contingent asset should be:
options: Disclosed only if an inflow is probable
questions.rationale: Contingent assets are not recognised until virtually certain.

questions.stem: A company is being sued for £200,000. Its lawyers say there is a 70% chance it will lose and the best estimate of the loss is £150,000. What is the correct treatment?
questions.rationale: An outflow is probable and can be estimated, so a provision is required.

questions.stem: A government grant for purchasing an asset is normally:
options: Recognised immediately in full as income
Recognised as income over the life of the asset
Deducted from share capital in equity
Ignored in the accounts of the company
questions.rationale: IAS 20 matches grants to the related costs.

questions.stem: Under IFRS 16, a lessee generally recognises:
options: Only a rent expense in profit or loss
Nothing in the statement of financial position
A right-of-use asset and a lease liability
Only a liability for the lease payments
questions.rationale: Most leases are brought onto the balance sheet.

questions.stem: Under IAS 38 a company can capitalise development costs when:
options: It wants to increase the profit for the year
The costs are small in amount
Technical feasibility and probable future benefits can be demonstrated
At any time during the project
questions.rationale: Capitalisation requires specific criteria to be met.

questions.stem: Inventory is written down to NRV. What is the effect on profit?
options: There is no effect on profit
Profit is reduced by the write-down
Profit is increased by the amount of the write-down
Equity is increased by the write-down
questions.rationale: The loss is recognised in cost of sales.

questions.stem: Using the indirect method, an increase in trade payables is:
questions.rationale: More credit from suppliers keeps cash in the business.

questions.stem: An increase in trade receivables of £15,000 is:
questions.rationale: Cash is tied up in receivables.

questions.stem: Operating profit £90,000; depreciation £20,000; profit on disposal £5,000; decrease in inventory £7,000. What is cash generated from operations (other items nil)?
Interest paid is shown under:
options: It is not shown in the statement of cash flows
Equity in the statement of changes in equity
questions.rationale: IAS 7 allows operating or financing classification.

questions.stem: Dividends paid are usually classified as:
questions.rationale: Dividends are a return to owners.

questions.stem: Opening cash £15,000; net cash from operating £60,000; investing (£40,000); financing £10,000. What is the closing cash?
Cash equivalents are:
options: Inventory that can be sold quickly
Short-term, highly liquid investments easily converted to cash
Land that can be sold on the open market
questions.rationale: Typically maturing within 3 months.

questions.stem: In consolidation, the investment in a subsidiary in the parent's own statement of financial position is:
options: Included in group inventory at cost
Doubled so that it is shown twice
questions.rationale: Consolidation replaces the investment with the subsidiary's assets and liabilities.

questions.stem: A parent owns 80% of a subsidiary. In the consolidated statement of profit or loss the subsidiary's revenue is included:
questions.rationale: Full consolidation includes 100% of the subsidiary's income and expenses, with NCI shown separately.

questions.stem: A subsidiary has dividends payable to the parent of £10,000. In consolidation this is:
options: Shown as a liability of the group
Added to the profit of the group
questions.rationale: Intra-group balances cancel on consolidation.

questions.stem: The parent's receivables include £25,000 owed by a subsidiary, and the subsidiary's payables include the same amount. What is the effect on consolidated receivables?
questions.rationale: Intra-group balances are eliminated from both sides.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an intra-group transaction?
options: A sale made to an external customer
A loan received from an outside bank
A payment made to an external supplier
A sale from a parent to its subsidiary
questions.rationale: Transactions within the group must be eliminated.

questions.stem: A subsidiary sold goods to the parent for £80,000 at cost plus 25%. All the goods are still in the parent's inventory at the year end. What is the unrealised profit to eliminate?
NCI is shown in the consolidated statement of financial position:
questions.rationale: NCI represents equity not owned by the parent.

questions.stem: When a parent acquires a subsidiary, the subsidiary's assets are included in the group accounts at:
options: Fair value at the acquisition date
questions.rationale: Fair value measurement is used in acquisition accounting.

questions.stem: Goodwill arising on acquisition is:
options: Tested annually for impairment and not amortised under IFRS 3 and IAS 36
Amortised over a period of 5 years
questions.rationale: IFRS requires annual impairment testing.

questions.stem: An associate is accounted for using:
questions.rationale: The investor includes its share of the associate's profit.

questions.stem: Gross profit £240,000 and revenue £800,000. What is the gross margin?
Operating profit £96,000 and revenue £800,000. What is the operating margin?
Current assets £250,000 and current liabilities £125,000. What is the current ratio?
Revenue £1,000,000 and net assets £500,000. What is the asset turnover?
questions.rationale: Revenue ÷ net assets = 2.0.

questions.stem: ROCE is 15% and operating margin is 10%. What is the asset turnover (capital employed turnover)?
questions.rationale: ROCE = margin × asset turnover, so 15% ÷ 10% = 1.5.

questions.stem: A fall in the current ratio from 2.1 to 1.2 suggests:
questions.rationale: Less current-asset cover for short-term debts.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of comparing two companies' ratios?
options: They may use different accounting policies
Companies are always the same size
questions.rationale: Policy differences distort comparability.

questions.stem: A company's inventory days have risen from 40 to 65 while revenue is unchanged. This could indicate:
questions.rationale: More stock is held for the same sales.

questions.stem: Gearing has risen from 25% to 45%. Which statement is most likely?
questions.rationale: More debt means higher fixed interest commitments.

questions.stem: Dividend cover is calculated as:
questions.rationale: It shows how many times profit covers the dividend.

questions.stem: Earnings per share is:
options: Equity divided by the profit for the year
Dividends paid divided by the share price
Revenue divided by the number of shares
Profit attributable to ordinary shareholders ÷ number of ordinary shares
questions.rationale: EPS measures profitability per share.

questions.stem: Profit after tax £180,000 and 600,000 ordinary shares. What is EPS?
Price earnings (P/E) ratio is:
options: Dividend per share divided by the price
Profit divided by revenue for the year
EPS divided by the market price per share
questions.rationale: It shows how many years of earnings the share price represents.

questions.stem: A company has profit before tax of £300,000. Tax is £75,000 and an ordinary dividend of £60,000 is paid. Opening retained earnings are £400,000. What are closing retained earnings?
A company issues 50,000 £1 shares at par to raise cash. What is the effect on equity?
questions.rationale: At par, all proceeds go to share capital.

questions.stem: A company with 800,000 £1 shares makes a 3 for 8 rights issue at £1.40. How much cash is raised if all are taken up?
A company's statement of profit or loss shows revenue £2m, cost of sales £1.2m, distribution costs £200,000, administrative expenses £300,000. What is the operating profit?
Finance costs are shown in the statement of profit or loss:
questions.rationale: Interest is deducted to reach profit before tax.

questions.stem: Equity in a company statement of financial position includes:
options: Share capital, share premium and retained earnings
questions.rationale: Equity is the owners' interest.

questions.stem: An interim dividend is:
options: Paid part-way through the financial year
Paid in advance of the year
questions.rationale: A final dividend is proposed after the year end.

questions.stem: A final dividend proposed after the year end but before the accounts are approved should be:
options: Disclosed but not recognised as a liability
questions.rationale: There is no obligation at the reporting date.

questions.stem: An asset is revalued upward by £25,000. Where is the gain recorded?
questions.rationale: Revaluation gains go to OCI and the revaluation reserve.

questions.stem: A property was revalued from £200,000 to £260,000 on 31 December. It had a 20-year remaining life. What is the annual depreciation based on the new value?
IAS 1 requires a complete set of financial statements to include:
options: Statement of financial position, profit or loss and OCI, changes in equity, cash flows and notes
questions.rationale: These are the primary statements.

questions.stem: A company sells goods with a right of return. Under IFRS 15, revenue is recognised for:
options: The amount expected not to be returned
questions.rationale: A refund liability is recognised for expected returns.

questions.stem: A company enters a 3-year service contract for £90,000, with services delivered evenly. How much revenue is recognised in year 1?
The fair value of an asset is:
options: The price received to sell it in an orderly transaction between market participants
questions.rationale: IFRS 13 defines fair value.

questions.stem: A machine with a carrying amount of £50,000 has a recoverable amount of £40,000. What is the impairment loss?
questions.rationale: Carrying amount less recoverable amount.

questions.stem: An impairment loss is recognised in:
questions.rationale: Unless it reverses a previous revaluation gain.

questions.stem: Profit before tax £60,000; depreciation £8,000; increase in receivables £10,000; increase in payables £4,000. What is cash generated from operations?
The proceeds from selling a non-current asset appear in:
questions.rationale: Disposals are investing cash flows.

questions.stem: Opening share capital £100,000, closing £140,000 (all issued at par for cash). What is the financing cash inflow?
Repayment of a bank loan is shown in:
questions.rationale: Loans are sources of finance.

questions.stem: In a consolidated income statement, the profit attributable to the owners of the parent excludes:
questions.rationale: NCI is shown separately.

questions.stem: Parent owns 75% of a subsidiary with net assets of £400,000 at the year end. NCI is measured at proportionate share. What is the NCI?
The parent sold goods costing £50,000 to the subsidiary for £70,000. Half remain in the subsidiary's inventory. What is the unrealised profit?
Which of the following is an indicator of significant influence?
options: Representation on the board and participation in policy decisions
questions.rationale: Associates are typically 20–50% owned with influence.

questions.stem: A company's revenue grows 15% while operating profit grows 5%. What does this suggest?
questions.rationale: Costs grew faster than revenue.

questions.stem: A business has a current ratio of 0.8. This suggests that:
questions.rationale: Below 1 means liquidity pressure.

questions.stem: Which ratio shows how many times operating profit covers finance costs?
questions.rationale: Higher interest cover indicates safer borrowing.

questions.stem: A fall in the quick ratio and a rise in inventory days together suggest:
questions.rationale: More cash tied up in inventory.

questions.stem: A company has equity: share capital £200,000, share premium £50,000, retained earnings £150,000. What is total equity?
A company earns profit after tax of £90,000 and declares dividends of £40,000. By how much do retained earnings increase?
A company with 1,000,000 £0.25 shares issues 250,000 new shares at £0.60. What is credited to share capital and share premium?
Which of these would reduce distributable reserves?
questions.rationale: Dividends are paid from retained earnings.

questions.stem: Corporation tax due within 12 months is shown as:
questions.rationale: It is payable within a year.

questions.stem: Ordinary shareholders are entitled to:
options: Dividends and votes at general meetings
questions.rationale: They are the residual owners.

questions.stem: An asset is carried at £70,000 after depreciation and its recoverable amount falls to £60,000. The impairment loss is:
questions.rationale: Carrying amount − recoverable amount.

questions.stem: IAS 16 requires property, plant and equipment to be recognised initially at:
questions.rationale: Cost includes directly attributable expenditure.

questions.stem: A company revalues a building from £400,000 (NBV) to £520,000. What are the entries?
questions.rationale: The gain goes to other comprehensive income.

questions.stem: Research costs are expensed because:
questions.rationale: IAS 38 requires expensing research.

questions.stem: A material error from a previous period is corrected by:
options: Writing it off to share capital
questions.rationale: IAS 8 applies.

questions.stem: A provision of £20,000 has been recognised. The actual cost turns out to be £18,000. How is the £2,000 treated?
questions.rationale: Changes in estimate go through profit or loss.

questions.stem: Under IFRS 15, a contract liability arises when:
options: The customer pays before the company performs
questions.rationale: Deferred income.

questions.stem: A post-year-end event confirming conditions at the year end is:
questions.rationale: Adjust the financial statements.

questions.stem: Which standard deals with inventories?
questions.rationale: IAS 2 sets out valuation rules.

questions.stem: Profit before tax £40,000, depreciation £12,000, increase in inventory £6,000, decrease in payables £3,000. Cash from operations?
Opening PPE £300,000, closing £340,000, depreciation £30,000, disposals at NBV £10,000. What were the cash purchases of PPE?
questions.rationale: Closing 340 = opening 300 + additions − 30 − 10, so additions = £80,000.

questions.stem: Tax paid is shown in:
questions.rationale: IAS 7 normally classes it as operating.

questions.stem: A bonus issue of shares is shown in the cash flow statement as:
questions.rationale: No cash is received.

questions.stem: Which method treats a 35% holding with significant influence?
questions.rationale: An associate.

questions.stem: Parent acquires 90% of a subsidiary for £360,000. Net assets at acquisition £350,000. NCI at proportionate share. Goodwill?
Intra-group trading means:
options: Sales between companies within the same group
questions.rationale: These must be eliminated on consolidation.

questions.stem: The consolidated statement of financial position shows the investment in subsidiary:
options: Replaced by the subsidiary's assets and liabilities
questions.rationale: It is eliminated.

questions.stem: Subsidiary profit for the year is £120,000 and the parent owns 60%. Profit attributable to NCI?
Operating profit £50,000, revenue £400,000. Operating margin?
Cost of sales £360,000 and inventory £60,000. Inventory turnover?
Trade payables £48,000 and cost of sales £384,000. Payables days (365)?
Gearing of 55% suggests:
options: A high proportion of debt in the capital structure
questions.rationale: Higher gearing means higher financial risk.

questions.stem: A higher inventory turnover usually indicates:
questions.rationale: Efficient stock management.

questions.stem: A fall in ROCE could be caused by:
options: Lower margin or lower asset turnover
questions.rationale: ROCE = margin × asset turnover.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a production overhead?
questions.rationale: Production overheads are indirect factory costs.

questions.stem: A worker earns £10.50 per hour and works 37.5 hours. What is the gross weekly pay?
A business has 250 units at £8 each and 150 units at £10 each. What is the total value using the actual cost of units on hand?
A company's total costs are £50,000 at 5,000 units and the variable cost per unit is £6. What are the fixed costs?
A job's direct costs are £2,000 and the business adds a profit margin of 20% on selling price. What is the price?
Overheads of £42,000 are absorbed at £6 per direct labour hour. How many hours were budgeted?
Production overhead absorbed is debited to:
questions.rationale: WIP is charged with absorbed overhead.

questions.stem: A cost centre is a:
options: Location, function or item for which costs are collected
questions.rationale: It helps in cost control.

questions.stem: Which payment method rewards an employee for each unit made?
questions.rationale: Pay is linked to output.

questions.stem: The value of inventory is reduced to NRV when:
questions.rationale: Prudence prevents overstating assets.

questions.stem: Overhead absorption is needed because:
options: Products must carry a share of indirect costs
questions.rationale: Full cost requires overheads.

questions.stem: A bakery costs £90 for 150 rolls. What is the cost per roll?
A cost that changes proportionately with output is:
questions.rationale: Total variable cost rises in proportion to output.

questions.stem: Basic pay is £12 per hour for 35 hours. Overtime for 8 hours is paid at double time. What is the gross pay?
Raw materials purchased on credit are debited to:
questions.rationale: Raw materials inventory increases.

questions.stem: A machine costs £50,000, has a residual value of £5,000 and a useful life of 5 years. What is the annual straight-line depreciation?
A van cost £24,000 and is depreciated at 25% per year on the reducing balance method. What is the depreciation charge in year 2?
A machine costs £30,000 and is depreciated at 20% straight line on cost. After 3 years, what is the net book value?
questions.rationale: Annual depreciation £6,000. Accumulated after 3 years £18,000. NBV = £12,000.

questions.stem: What is the double-entry for the annual depreciation charge?
options: Debit depreciation expense, credit accumulated depreciation
Debit accumulated depreciation, credit depreciation expense
Debit asset cost, credit depreciation expense
questions.rationale: The charge is an expense. The credit builds up the provision against the asset.

questions.stem: Depreciation is charged to:
options: Spread the cost of a non-current asset over its useful life
Save cash to replace the asset in future
Reduce the tax payable on profits to nil
Reflect the current market value of the asset
questions.rationale: Depreciation is an application of the accruals concept, matching cost to the periods benefiting.

questions.stem: A machine costing £40,000 is depreciated at 10% a year straight line. At the start of year 5 it is sold for £22,000. What is the profit or loss on disposal?
questions.rationale: Accumulated depreciation after 4 years = 4 × £4,000 = £16,000. NBV = £24,000. Proceeds of £22,000 are below NBV, so there is a loss of £2,000.

questions.stem: A machine cost £60,000 and has accumulated depreciation of £36,000. It is sold for £28,000. What is the profit or loss on disposal?
Which entry transfers the cost of a disposed asset (£60,000) to the disposals account?
questions.rationale: The asset account is cleared by crediting cost, with the matching debit in the disposals account.

questions.stem: Which of the following is capital expenditure?
questions.rationale: Capital expenditure acquires or improves non-current assets. Repairs and running costs are revenue expenditure.

questions.stem: The purchase price of a machine is £20,000 plus £1,500 delivery and £500 installation. Annual maintenance is £700. What is the cost to be capitalised?
questions.rationale: Capitalise purchase price, delivery and installation: £22,000. Maintenance is revenue expenditure.

questions.stem: An accrual is:
options: An expense incurred but not yet paid
Income that has been received in advance
A debt that a customer will not pay
A payment made in advance of the period it relates to
questions.rationale: Accruals recognise costs in the period they relate to, even if unpaid.

questions.stem: Rent paid during the year is £12,000. At the year end £3,000 of rent relates to the next year. What is the rent expense?
questions.rationale: £12,000 less the prepayment of £3,000 = £9,000.

questions.stem: The electricity bill paid in the year is £4,800. £900 is owed for the final quarter. What is the electricity expense?
Insurance paid on 1 April for the year to 31 March is £7,200. The year end is 31 December. What is the prepayment at the year end?
questions.rationale: 3 months (January–March) × £600 = £1,800 relates to the next year.

questions.stem: Rent income received in the year is £8,000. £1,500 relates to the next year. What is the rent income for the year?
questions.rationale: Income received in advance (£1,500) is deferred, so income = £8,000 − £1,500 = £6,500.

questions.stem: Where does an accrual appear in the statement of financial position?
questions.rationale: An accrual is an amount owed at the year end.

questions.stem: A business has paid £2,000 for next year's software licence. How should this be shown at the year end?
options: As an expense of this year
questions.rationale: A prepayment is a benefit paid for but not yet received, shown as an asset.

questions.stem: An irrecoverable debt is:
options: A discount given to a customer for early payment
An amount owed by a customer that will not be paid
A payment received from a customer in advance
An amount owed by the business to a supplier
questions.rationale: It is written off as an expense.

questions.stem: A debt of £700 is written off. What is the effect on profit?
questions.rationale: Irrecoverable debts are an expense, and receivables decrease.

questions.stem: Receivables are £84,000. An allowance of 3% is required. There was no previous allowance. What is the charge to profit?
The allowance for doubtful debts last year was £2,000. This year it is required to be £2,600. What is the effect on profit?
questions.rationale: Only the increase in the allowance (£600) is charged to the income statement.

questions.stem: A debt previously written off is unexpectedly received. Which entry is correct?
options: Debit irrecoverable debts expense, credit bank
Debit bank, credit irrecoverable debts recovered (income)
questions.rationale: The recovery is income as the original expense has already been charged.

questions.stem: Receivables of £50,000 include a debt of £2,000 that is certain to be irrecoverable. An allowance of 4% is applied to the remainder. What is the allowance?
In which statement is gross profit calculated?
questions.rationale: Gross profit = revenue − cost of sales.

questions.stem: Opening inventory £8,000, purchases £60,000, closing inventory £11,000. What is the cost of sales?
Sales £120,000, sales returns £4,000, cost of sales £70,000. What is gross profit?
questions.rationale: Net sales £116,000 − cost of sales £70,000 = £46,000.

questions.stem: Gross profit is £46,000. Expenses are £31,000. What is the net profit?
Purchases £60,000, carriage inwards £2,000, purchases returns £1,500, opening inventory £8,000, closing inventory £11,000. What is the cost of sales?
Where is carriage outwards shown in the financial statements?
options: In the statement of financial position as an asset
As an expense in the statement of profit or loss
questions.rationale: Carriage outwards is a distribution cost, not part of cost of sales.

questions.stem: Closing inventory is shown in:
options: Non-current assets in the statement of financial position only
Current liabilities in the statement of financial position
Equity in the statement of changes in equity only
Current assets in the statement of financial position, and deducted in cost of sales
questions.rationale: Closing inventory reduces cost of sales and appears as a current asset.

questions.stem: A sole trader's opening capital is £40,000, net profit £18,000, drawings £12,000 and capital introduced £5,000. What is closing capital?
Net assets of a sole trader are £51,000 at the year end. Opening net assets were £40,000. Drawings were £12,000 and no capital was introduced. What was the profit?
questions.rationale: Closing capital £51,000 = opening £40,000 + profit − £12,000, so profit = £23,000.

questions.stem: Which item is a current liability?
questions.rationale: Amounts due within 12 months, such as payables, are current liabilities.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a current asset?
questions.rationale: Office equipment is held for continuing use, so it is a non-current asset.

questions.stem: A partnership agreement normally sets out:
options: The depreciation method used for equipment
The rate of tax payable on partnership profits
The profit-sharing ratio, interest on capital and salaries
The VAT scheme used by the partnership
questions.rationale: Without a written agreement the Partnership Act 1890 applies, including equal profit shares.

questions.stem: Partners A and B share profits 3:2. Profit is £50,000. What is A's share?
A partnership has profit of £40,000. Partner A receives a salary of £8,000 and interest on capital of £2,000. The remainder is shared equally between A and B. What is A's total share?
Interest charged on a partner's drawings is:
options: An expense of the partnership business
Debited to the partner's current account and credited to the appropriation account
A reduction in the sales of the business
Added to the partner's capital account
questions.rationale: It adjusts the profit share, so it is part of the appropriation of profit.

questions.stem: A and B share profits equally. Goodwill of £30,000 is created when C joins. How is goodwill recorded for the existing partners before C is admitted?
options: Credit A £15,000 and credit B £15,000 in their capital accounts
Debit A £15,000 and debit B £15,000 in their capital accounts
Charge the £30,000 to the profit or loss account
Credit C £30,000 in C's capital account
questions.rationale: Goodwill belongs to the existing partners and is shared in the old profit-sharing ratio (1:1).

questions.stem: A partner's current account usually records:
options: Loans made to the partnership by the partner
Tax paid personally by the partner
The original capital invested by the partner only
Profit share, salary, interest and drawings
questions.rationale: The current account shows movements that are not changes to fixed capital.

questions.stem: The accounting concept that income and expenses are recorded when earned or incurred, not when cash moves, is:
questions.rationale: The accruals concept matches revenue and expenses to the period.

questions.stem: The business entity concept requires:
options: The business to be treated as separate from its owner
No depreciation to be charged on assets
Profits to be maximised in every period
Assets to be valued at their current market price
questions.rationale: Personal transactions of the owner are not recorded as business expenses; they are drawings.

questions.stem: The going concern concept assumes that:
options: Revenue is recorded only when cash is received
The business will be sold within the next year
The business will continue in operation for the foreseeable future
All assets are shown at their liquidation values
questions.rationale: If the business is not a going concern, assets must be valued differently.

questions.stem: Prudence means:
options: Not overstating assets or income and not understating liabilities or expenses
Ignoring losses that are unlikely to happen
Valuing all assets at their current market values
Maximising the profit reported in every period
questions.rationale: Prudence requires caution when judgements are needed.

questions.stem: A £15 stapler is treated as an expense, not a non-current asset. Which concept justifies this?
questions.rationale: The amount is too small to influence decisions, so capitalising it is not required.

questions.stem: A depreciation charge of £5,000 for the year has been omitted. Which statement is correct?
options: Profit is overstated and liabilities are understated
Profit is overstated and assets are overstated by £5,000
Profit is understated and liabilities are overstated
questions.rationale: Omitting depreciation overstates profit and the carrying amount of the asset.

questions.stem: A purchases invoice for £840 was posted to the purchases account as £480. The posting to payables was correct. What entry is needed in the suspense account?
questions.rationale: Purchases was understated by £360, so it must be debited, and suspense (which had a debit balance of £360) is credited.

questions.stem: A machine costing £48,000 has a residual value of £6,000 and a 7-year life. What is the annual straight-line depreciation?
A van costing £20,000 is depreciated at 30% reducing balance. What is the net book value after 2 years?

A machine costing £36,000 is bought on 1 October. The year end is 31 December. Annual straight-line depreciation is 10% of cost and is charged pro rata by month. What is the depreciation for the first year?

A company charges a full year's depreciation in the year of purchase and none in the year of disposal. A machine costing £10,000 at 20% straight line is bought in year 1 and sold in year 4. What is the accumulated depreciation at disposal?
questions.rationale: Years 1, 2 and 3 are charged: 3 × £2,000 = £6,000. No charge in the year of disposal.

questions.stem: An asset with cost £25,000 and accumulated depreciation £15,000 is part-exchanged for £12,000 as part of the purchase price of a new asset. What is the profit or loss on disposal?
questions.rationale: NBV £10,000. Part-exchange allowance £12,000. Profit £2,000.

questions.stem: Where is the profit on disposal of a non-current asset shown?
options: In the statement of financial position as an asset
In the statement of profit or loss as other income
questions.rationale: A profit on disposal is credited to the income statement.

questions.stem: The disposals account is debited with the asset's cost and accumulated depreciation is credited. What is the balance on the disposals account before proceeds?
options: Equal to the net book value
questions.rationale: Debit cost less credit accumulated depreciation leaves NBV.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a reason for charging depreciation?
options: To match cost to the periods that benefit
To show the market value of the asset
questions.rationale: Depreciation is an allocation of cost, not a valuation.

questions.stem: A non-current asset's carrying amount (NBV) is:
options: The cost of replacing the asset today
The market value at the reporting date
questions.rationale: NBV is the asset's cost less depreciation to date.

questions.stem: Plant cost £90,000 with residual value £10,000 and an 8-year life (straight line). After 3 years the remaining life is revised to 3 years with the same residual value. What is the new annual depreciation?
questions.rationale: NBV after 3 years = £90,000 − 3 × £10,000 = £60,000. (£60,000 − £10,000) ÷ 3 = £16,667. A change of estimate is applied from now on.

questions.stem: Telephone costs paid in the year were £2,400. The opening accrual was £300 and the closing accrual is £450. What is the expense for the year?
Insurance paid in the year was £5,000. The opening prepayment was £800 and the closing prepayment is £1,100. What is the expense?
Rent of £3,000 per quarter is paid in advance on 1 January, 1 April, 1 July and 1 October. The year end is 30 November. What is the prepayment at the year end?
questions.rationale: The October payment covers October–December. One month (December) is prepaid: £3,000 ÷ 3 = £1,000.

questions.stem: An accrual is recorded by:
questions.rationale: The expense is recognised and a liability is created.

questions.stem: A prepayment is recorded by:
questions.rationale: The expense is reduced and an asset is recognised.

questions.stem: Interest income received in advance of £600 is outstanding at the year end. What is the correct entry?
options: Debit deferred income £600, credit interest received £600
Debit interest received £600, credit deferred income £600
questions.rationale: Income that relates to the next period is removed from this period's income and held as a liability.

questions.stem: Commission paid to sales staff of £7,500 for the year includes £500 relating to the prior year. What is the commission expense for this year?
questions.rationale: Remove the £500 that belongs to last year.

questions.stem: Receivables are £60,000. A debt of £4,000 is to be written off and a 5% allowance is required on the remaining receivables. What is the total charge to profit (no previous allowance)?
The opening allowance is £1,500. The closing receivables are £50,000 and the allowance should be 4%. What is the movement in the allowance?
questions.rationale: Required allowance £2,000. The increase of £500 is charged to profit.

questions.stem: An allowance for doubtful debts is shown in the statement of financial position as:
options: A non-current asset of the business
A current liability owed to suppliers
questions.rationale: Net receivables = trade receivables less allowance.

questions.stem: Which statement about an allowance for doubtful debts is correct?
options: It is added to the sales figure for the year
It is an estimate and can be adjusted each year
It is a cash payment made to customers
It is exactly the same as writing off a debt
questions.rationale: Allowances recognise probable losses while write-offs deal with specific debts.

questions.stem: Receivables are £80,000 and the allowance is 3% of net receivables after writing off a debt of £2,000. What is the allowance?
Receivables of £30,000 less allowance of £1,200 are shown in the statement of financial position at:
Sales £210,000; opening inventory £14,000; purchases £120,000; carriage inwards £3,000; closing inventory £18,000. What is the gross profit?
Gross profit £91,000; wages £30,000; rent £12,000; depreciation £6,000; discount received £2,000. What is the net profit?
Which of the following is shown in the statement of financial position, not the statement of profit or loss?
questions.rationale: Closing inventory is a current asset.

questions.stem: Net profit is £45,000 and drawings are £18,000. Opening capital is £50,000. What is the closing capital?
A sole trader's statement of financial position shows non-current assets £60,000, current assets £30,000, current liabilities £12,000 and long-term loan £20,000. What is the capital?
In the statement of financial position, assets are usually listed in order of:
options: Alphabetical order of the account names
Value, with the largest first only
The date on which each asset was purchased
questions.rationale: Non-current assets are shown first, then current assets.

questions.stem: The extended trial balance includes columns for:
options: VAT due to and from HMRC only
The bank statement and cash book only
The owner's drawings and capital only
Adjustments, statement of profit or loss and statement of financial position
questions.rationale: The extended trial balance helps prepare financial statements from the ledger balances.

questions.stem: An adjustment for closing inventory of £15,000 is made in an extended trial balance. Which entries are made?
questions.rationale: The inventory asset is recognised and cost of sales is reduced.

questions.stem: Drawings are shown in the:
options: Current liabilities as an amount owed
Statement of financial position as a deduction from capital
Cost of sales as a direct cost
Statement of profit or loss as an expense
questions.rationale: Drawings reduce capital and are not an expense.

questions.stem: Where is a bank overdraft shown in the statement of financial position?
questions.rationale: An overdraft is repayable on demand.

questions.stem: A and B are partners sharing profits 2:1. The profit for the year is £45,000. What is B's share?
A and B share residual profits equally after B receives a salary of £10,000 and A receives interest on capital of £4,000. Profit is £50,000. What is B's total share?
A partner's drawings are debited to:
questions.rationale: Drawings reduce the amount the partner is owed.

questions.stem: A partnership agreement states interest on capital at 5%. Partner A has capital of £40,000. What is A's interest on capital?
If there is no partnership agreement, the Partnership Act 1890 provides that profits are shared:
questions.rationale: There are no salaries or interest on capital by default.

questions.stem: A partnership has an opening current account balance for A of £3,000 credit, share of profit £25,000 and drawings £22,000. What is the closing balance?
A machine costs £72,000, has a residual value of £12,000 and is depreciated over 5 years. After 2 years, what is the accumulated depreciation?
A car costing £16,000 is depreciated at 25% reducing balance. What is the charge in year 3?
A non-current asset cost £40,000 and was depreciated at 20% straight line for 3 years, then sold for £14,500. What is the profit or loss on disposal?
questions.rationale: Accumulated depreciation £24,000, so NBV £16,000. Proceeds of £14,500 are £1,500 below NBV, a loss on disposal.

questions.stem: Which account is credited when depreciation is charged for the year?
questions.rationale: The cost account is left unchanged.

questions.stem: An asset that is fully depreciated but still in use is:
options: Still shown at cost with accumulated depreciation equal to cost
questions.rationale: Net book value is zero (or residual value) but the asset remains in the register.

questions.stem: A business uses units of production depreciation. Machine cost £90,000, residual £10,000, total life 100,000 units, 18,000 units made this year. What is the charge?
Rent is paid quarterly in advance on 1 Jan, Apr, Jul and Oct at £2,400 each. The year end is 31 December. What is the rent expense for the year?
questions.rationale: Four quarters × £2,400 = £9,600, with no prepayment as the year end is a quarter end.

questions.stem: Annual insurance of £3,600 was paid on 1 August. The year end is 31 December. What is the prepayment?
questions.rationale: 7 months (January–July) of £300 per month = £2,100 relates to next year.

questions.stem: Wages for the last 3 days of the year (£900) have not been paid by the year end. What entry is needed?
questions.rationale: The expense belongs to this year and the amount owed is a liability.

questions.stem: A prepayment from last year was £400 and this year's is £550. Payments made were £4,000. What is the expense?
Closing accrual is £1,200 and the opening accrual was £800. Cash paid was £14,000. What is the expense?
Receivables at the year end are £75,000. A 4% allowance is needed. The opening allowance was £2,500. What is the charge to the statement of profit or loss?
questions.rationale: Required £3,000 less existing £2,500 = increase of £500.

questions.stem: A business has trade receivables of £60,000. Specific bad debts of £1,500 are to be written off and a general allowance of 2% is needed on the remainder. What is the total charge (no previous allowance)?
Which account is debited when a debt is written off?
questions.rationale: The expense is debited and receivables is credited.

questions.stem: The allowance for doubtful debts is reduced from £3,200 to £2,800. What is the effect?
questions.rationale: A reduction in the allowance increases profit.

questions.stem: Opening inventory £12,000, purchases £88,000, purchases returns £3,000, closing inventory £15,000. What is the cost of sales?
A business has revenue of £150,000 and cost of sales of £90,000. What is the gross profit margin?
Which of these would be shown under current liabilities?
questions.rationale: VAT payable is a short-term liability.

questions.stem: A sole trader has net assets of £84,000 at the year end. Capital at the start was £70,000, drawings £16,000 and no capital introduced. What was the profit?
questions.rationale: Closing capital £84,000 = £70,000 + profit − £16,000, so profit = £30,000.

questions.stem: Discount received is shown in the statement of profit or loss as:
questions.rationale: Discounts received reduce costs but are normally presented as income.

questions.stem: Carriage inwards is included in:
questions.rationale: It is a cost of bringing inventory to its location.

questions.stem: Which statement about the statement of financial position is correct?
options: It shows profit over a period
It shows assets, liabilities and capital at a specific date
questions.rationale: It is a snapshot at the year end.

questions.stem: A bank overdraft and a bank loan repayable in 5 years are classified, respectively, as:
questions.rationale: Overdrafts are repayable on demand. The loan is long term.

questions.stem: A and B are partners. B's interest on a capital of £50,000 at 6% is:
Net profit £60,000. A's salary £12,000. Interest on capital: A £3,000, B £2,000. Remaining profit shared A:B 3:2. What is B's total?
When a partner introduces additional capital, it is credited to:
questions.rationale: Capital introductions increase the capital account.

questions.stem: In the partnership appropriation account, which item is deducted from net profit before the residual is shared?
options: Partners' salaries and interest on capital
questions.rationale: These are appropriations of profit.

questions.stem: A business records revenue when goods are delivered, not when cash is received. Which concept is applied?
questions.rationale: Revenue is recognised when earned.

questions.stem: The consistency concept requires:
options: Using the same accounting policies from year to year
questions.rationale: It helps comparisons over time.

questions.stem: The money measurement concept means the accounts only include:
options: Items that can be measured in monetary terms
questions.rationale: Staff skills, for example, are not recorded.

questions.stem: A machine costing £45,000 with residual value £5,000 is depreciated over 8 years. What is the annual straight-line charge?
An asset costing £30,000 is depreciated at 20% reducing balance. What is the NBV after 3 years?
The depreciation charge for the year is £8,000. What is the effect on profit?
questions.rationale: Depreciation is an expense but not a cash flow.

questions.stem: A van is sold for £6,500. Its cost was £18,000 and accumulated depreciation £11,000. What is the profit or loss on disposal?
questions.rationale: NBV £7,000. Proceeds £6,500, a loss of £500.

questions.stem: Accumulated depreciation is shown in the statement of financial position as a:
options: Deduction from the cost of non-current assets
questions.rationale: It reduces carrying amount.

questions.stem: A machine costing £60,000 is depreciated at 10% on cost. A full year's charge is made in the year of purchase and none in the year of sale. It is sold in year 3 for £42,000. What is the profit or loss on disposal?
questions.rationale: Years 1 and 2 are charged: £12,000, so NBV £48,000. Proceeds £42,000 are £6,000 below NBV, a loss.

questions.stem: Electricity paid in the year £3,600. At the year end £400 is accrued and last year's accrual was £300. What is the expense?
Rent paid in the year £9,000. It includes £1,500 for the following year. What is the expense?
A business pays £4,800 for annual insurance on 1 September. The year end is 31 December. What is the expense for the year and the prepayment?
questions.rationale: 4 months = £1,600. The remaining 8 months £3,200 is prepaid.

questions.stem: An accrual increases:
questions.rationale: The expense is recognised before payment.

questions.stem: Income received in advance is shown as a:
questions.rationale: The business owes goods or services.

questions.stem: Receivables £40,000 with an allowance of 5%. What is the net receivables figure?
Opening allowance £1,800; closing receivables £60,000 with a 3% allowance. A debt of £600 is written off during the year. What is the total charge to profit?
questions.rationale: Write-off £600 plus allowance movement: new £1,800 less old £1,800 = nil. Total £600.

questions.stem: A customer who owed £900 has gone bankrupt and will pay nothing. The entry is:
questions.rationale: The debt is written off.

questions.stem: Net profit is £34,000. Opening capital £60,000, drawings £20,000. What is closing capital?
Closing inventory is understated by £5,000. What is the effect on gross profit and net assets?
options: Gross profit understated; net assets overstated
questions.rationale: Understated closing inventory increases cost of sales and reduces assets.

questions.stem: A fall in the value of inventory below cost requires:
questions.rationale: Inventory is valued at the lower of cost and NRV.

questions.stem: The statement of profit or loss covers:
questions.rationale: It shows performance over a year.

questions.stem: Where would a bank loan repayable in three years appear?
questions.rationale: It is repayable after more than one year.

questions.stem: Partner salary and interest on capital are examples of:
questions.rationale: They are not expenses of the business.

questions.stem: A and B are partners. A's capital is £60,000 and B's £20,000. Interest on capital is 5%. Profit after interest is shared equally. Total profit is £30,000. What is B's total share?
questions.rationale: Interest: A £3,000, B £1,000. Residual £26,000 shared equally gives £13,000 each. B = £13,000 + £1,000 = £14,000.

questions.stem: Partners' drawings are normally debited to:
questions.rationale: They reduce the balance owed to the partner.

questions.stem: Which concept says that revenue should be recognised when earned, not when cash is received?
questions.rationale: It matches revenue and costs to the period.

questions.stem: A business writes off an asset worth £8 because it is immaterial. This follows:
questions.rationale: Small items need not be capitalised.

questions.stem: A company expects to continue trading for the foreseeable future. This is the:
questions.rationale: It underpins the normal basis of preparation.

questions.stem: The historical cost concept means assets are recorded at:
questions.rationale: It is the basis for most assets.

questions.stem: The main purpose of internal controls is to:
options: Increase the amount of tax payable
Eliminate all risk from the organisation
Safeguard assets, prevent and detect error and fraud, and support reliable reporting
questions.rationale: Controls give reasonable, not absolute, assurance.

questions.stem: A preventive control is designed to:
options: Stop an error or fraud from occurring
Correct an error at a later date
Report an error to the external auditors
Detect an error after it has happened
questions.rationale: Examples include authorisation limits and passwords.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a detective control?
questions.rationale: Reconciliations identify errors after they have occurred.

questions.stem: Segregation of duties means:
options: Only managers are allowed to process payments
No one person controls all stages of a transaction
Staff share passwords to access systems
Every member of staff does every task
questions.rationale: It reduces fraud risk by requiring collusion to override.

questions.stem: In a small business only two people work in the accounts office. Which compensating control is most appropriate where segregation is impossible?
options: Remove all controls to speed up processing
Regular independent review of transactions by the owner or an external accountant
