Give both staff full access to all records
Delay reconciliations until the year end
questions.rationale: Management review compensates for limited segregation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a physical control?
questions.rationale: Physical controls restrict access to assets.

questions.stem: The control environment refers to:
options: The physical layout of the office
The attitude, awareness and actions of management regarding controls
The number of staff in the finance team
The accounting software used by the business
questions.rationale: A good control environment starts with an ethical tone from the top.

questions.stem: Authorisation limits mean that:
options: All spending in the business is banned
Spending above a set amount requires approval from a senior person
Staff can spend any amount they choose
Only cash payments can be made
questions.rationale: Limits ensure appropriate oversight of larger transactions.

questions.stem: A company has strong controls on sales but weak controls on purchases. The overall risk is best described as:
options: Weaknesses in one area can still allow material misstatement or fraud
There is no risk, as sales are well protected
The risk is eliminated by the sales controls
The overall risk is lower than average
questions.rationale: Controls must be considered across all key processes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a component of the fraud triangle?
questions.rationale: The fraud triangle is pressure, opportunity and rationalisation.

questions.stem: An employee in financial difficulty takes cash because they think they will pay it back. Which elements of the fraud triangle are shown?
questions.rationale: Financial difficulty is pressure. The belief they will repay is rationalisation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of fictitious supplier fraud?
options: An employee creating a fake supplier and paying invoices to their own account
Staff arriving late for work each day
Suppliers delivering goods late to the business
A VAT return being filed after the deadline
questions.rationale: A fake supplier is used to divert payments.

questions.stem: Teeming and lading involves:
options: Reconciling the bank balance each month
Using later receipts from customers to cover earlier stolen payments
Paying all suppliers on time and in full
questions.rationale: Cash from one customer is stolen and covered with receipts from another, delaying detection.

questions.stem: Which control best reduces the risk of payroll fraud involving ghost employees?
options: Combining the HR and payroll duties in one person
Independent verification of employees on payroll to HR records
Paying staff in cash to avoid bank fees
questions.rationale: Matching payroll to HR records, ideally by independent staff, identifies non-existent employees.

questions.stem: Red flags that might suggest fraud include:
options: High staff morale and low turnover
Budgets that are accurate to within 1%
Employees who never take holiday and resist sharing duties
Bank reconciliations completed quickly each month
questions.rationale: Fraudsters often need to be present to conceal their activities.

questions.stem: A cyber-security risk where staff receive fake emails asking them to share passwords is known as:
questions.rationale: Phishing uses deception to obtain credentials or payments.

questions.stem: A fraudster contacts the finance team posing as the CEO and demands an urgent payment to a new account. This is:
options: A contra entry between customer and supplier
Business email compromise (a type of impersonation fraud)
A routine payment to an approved supplier
questions.rationale: Staff should verify unusual requests using a known contact method.

questions.stem: A flowchart of the purchasing process is an example of:
questions.rationale: Process maps document steps to help identify risks and improve efficiency.

questions.stem: Which document is raised first in a typical purchasing cycle?
questions.rationale: Order of events: requisition, purchase order, delivery (GRN), invoice, payment.

questions.stem: The 'three-way match' in accounts payable compares:
options: Purchase order, goods received note and invoice
questions.rationale: A match confirms what was ordered, received and invoiced agree before payment is authorised.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an IT general control?
options: Counting the inventory in the warehouse
Restricting access to the accounting system by user role
Checking the total on a supplier invoice
questions.rationale: General controls apply across systems and include access, backups and change management.

questions.stem: Which is an application control in a payroll system?
options: A firewall protecting the whole network
An annual backup of all company data
A validation check to prevent entry of hours above 80 a week
A password policy for all users
questions.rationale: Application controls apply to specific processing, such as input validation.

questions.stem: A business backs up data daily and stores copies offsite. Which risk does this primarily address?
options: Loss of data from system failure, ransomware or disaster
Changes in tax law affecting the business
Late payment of invoices by customers
questions.rationale: Backups support recovery after loss or corruption of data.

questions.stem: Lean or process improvement aims to:
options: Add extra approval steps to every process
Increase the amount of paperwork needed
Duplicate work so errors are found
Remove waste and improve efficiency in a process
questions.rationale: Improvement can reduce cost and cycle time while keeping controls.

questions.stem: The Companies Act 2006 requires directors to:
options: Keep adequate accounting records and prepare true and fair accounts
Pay all of the profits out as dividends
questions.rationale: Directors are responsible for accounting records and financial statements.

questions.stem: Money laundering regulations require businesses to carry out:
questions.rationale: Identity checks and ongoing monitoring are core to the regulations.

questions.stem: Under money laundering rules, 'tipping off' means:
options: Warning a person that a report has been or may be made about them
Giving a gift to a customer or supplier
Keeping records of customer identity checks
Reporting a suspicion to the MLRO
questions.rationale: Tipping off is a criminal offence.

questions.stem: Which body is responsible for the UK Corporate Governance Code?
questions.rationale: The FRC sets the code, applying on a 'comply or explain' basis to listed companies.

questions.stem: 'Comply or explain' means that a company:
options: Is fined for every departure from the code
Must comply with every provision in all circumstances
Must follow code provisions or explain why it has not
Can ignore the code without giving reasons
questions.rationale: It allows flexibility but requires transparency.

questions.stem: Which person usually has the responsibility for preparing a company's financial statements?
questions.rationale: Directors prepare the accounts. Auditors give an opinion on them.

questions.stem: Which of these is a purpose of a whistleblowing policy?
options: To reduce the cost of the annual audit
To prevent staff from speaking about concerns
To help managers hide errors in the accounts
To allow staff to report concerns safely
questions.rationale: Employees are protected by law when making qualifying disclosures.

questions.stem: A data breach involving personal customer data must normally be reported to the ICO within:
options: 72 hours of becoming aware, where there is a risk to individuals
questions.rationale: UK GDPR requires notification within 72 hours where there is a risk to individuals' rights.

questions.stem: A manager asks you to delay recording a large invoice until next month to improve this month's results. What is the issue?
options: It is allowed under the prudence concept
It is a legitimate way to save tax
It breaches the integrity principle and the accruals concept
It is acceptable timing and within the rules
questions.rationale: Deliberately misstating periods is misleading and unethical.

questions.stem: Which ethical safeguard may be created by the profession, legislation or regulation?
questions.rationale: These are safeguards created by the profession or the law.

questions.stem: You are asked to prepare a client's accounts but you lack the knowledge to do so properly. What should you do?
options: Ask the client to fix any mistakes later
Decline the work or get appropriate help or training
Do the work anyway and hope for the best
questions.rationale: Professional competence and due care prevent work being done beyond competence.

questions.stem: Which control would best prevent the same invoice being paid twice?
options: Training staff on the use of software
An annual stock take of all inventory
Marking invoices as paid and checking for duplicates before payment
questions.rationale: Duplicate payment checks are a preventive control.

questions.stem: A bank reconciliation is performed by someone who does not process payments or receipts. This is an example of:
questions.rationale: Independent review improves detection of fraud and error.

questions.stem: Which control protects against unauthorised access to a payroll file?
options: Keeping paper files in a cupboard
Weekly team meetings in the finance office
Longer lunch breaks for payroll staff
questions.rationale: Access rights should be limited to those who need them.

questions.stem: A control that requires two signatures for payments above £10,000 is an example of:
questions.rationale: Dual authorisation prevents unauthorised large payments.

questions.stem: Rotating staff duties and compulsory holidays can help to:
options: Increase the level of staff absence
Reduce the VAT paid to HMRC
Detect fraud that depends on one person concealing it
Increase the profit of the business
questions.rationale: Others see the work and unusual items emerge.

questions.stem: Which of these is a limitation of internal controls?
options: They cost nothing to design and operate
They are always effective in every circumstance
They guarantee that no fraud will ever occur
They can be bypassed by management override or collusion
questions.rationale: Controls provide reasonable, not absolute, assurance.

questions.stem: An organisation has a policy for approving new suppliers and amending bank details. This helps to prevent:
options: High turnover among the finance staff
Fictitious supplier and payment diversion fraud
Bad debts from customers who do not pay
questions.rationale: Independent verification protects the supplier master file.

questions.stem: A cash count carried out by a manager who is independent of the cashier is a:
questions.rationale: It detects shortages after the event.

questions.stem: What is a corrective control?
options: An action to fix problems found, such as restoring data from a backup
A written policy statement issued to staff
A password that restricts access to the system
An approval signature on a purchase order
questions.rationale: Corrective controls restore normal operations.

questions.stem: A payroll clerk adds a non-existent worker and collects the pay. This is known as:
questions.rationale: Fictitious employees can be added when payroll is not verified.

questions.stem: Skimming refers to:
options: Taking cash before it is recorded in the accounts
Posting a transaction to the wrong account
Buying goods at a lower price than normal
Covering one theft with later customer receipts
questions.rationale: The sale is not recorded so the theft is hard to detect.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of management override of controls?
options: A routine password change by a user
A director instructing staff to post an unsupported journal
A training session on fraud awareness
A monthly bank reconciliation by an independent person
questions.rationale: Management can bypass controls and so is a high-risk area.

questions.stem: Which type of fraud involves false financial reporting to hit targets or meet loan covenants?
questions.rationale: Misstatement of results may be driven by pressure on management.

questions.stem: A company's bonus scheme pays managers solely on profit. Which part of the fraud triangle increases?
questions.rationale: Strong incentives create pressure to manipulate results.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a typical indicator of possible misappropriation of cash?
options: Unexplained cash shortages and altered records
Bank reconciliations done daily by an independent person
questions.rationale: Frequent differences and amended entries are warning signs.

questions.stem: A company discovers that an employee has stolen £5,000. The fraud policy should require:
options: Prompt investigation and reporting through the proper channels
Hiding the matter from the board and staff
Immediate promotion of the employee involved
Deleting the records relating to the theft
questions.rationale: A response plan ensures consistent treatment.

questions.stem: Cyber risk: ransomware is:
options: Malicious software that locks data until a payment is made
A fake invoice sent to the finance team
A tax avoidance scheme used by companies
An error made by the bank on a payment
questions.rationale: Backups and patching reduce the risk.

questions.stem: An employee falls for an email asking them to log in on a fake website. This is:
questions.rationale: Phishing steals credentials by impersonation.

questions.stem: In a sales cycle which document is used to confirm that goods have been dispatched?
questions.rationale: It is evidence goods have left.

questions.stem: To ensure that all goods dispatched are invoiced, a business should:
options: Check the payables ledger for each supplier
Count the cash held in the safe
Match dispatch notes to sales invoices
questions.rationale: This addresses completeness of revenue.

questions.stem: A credit limit check before accepting a customer order is a:
options: Preventive control in the sales cycle
questions.rationale: It reduces the risk of bad debts.

questions.stem: A process map helps an organisation to:
options: Calculate the tax due on its profits
Value the goodwill of the business
questions.rationale: Visualising steps highlights delays and risks.

questions.stem: A purchasing process allows one person to raise an order, receive goods and pay the supplier. What is the main weakness?
options: Payments to suppliers being made too slowly
Too many approvals slowing the process
questions.rationale: One person controls the whole process.

questions.stem: Which document is used to authorise payment for goods received?
options: A delivery note on its own
A customer order from a client
Approved supplier invoice matched to order and GRN
questions.rationale: Three-way matching supports payment authorisation.

questions.stem: Which of these is a typical cost of a poor system?
questions.rationale: Inefficient systems waste time and money.

questions.stem: Cloud accounting software introduces which key control consideration?
options: The cost of typewriters and stationery
Storage of large volumes of paper
Maintaining manual ledgers in the office
questions.rationale: Third-party hosting requires assurance over security.

questions.stem: A disaster recovery plan is designed to:
options: Restore systems and data after a major disruption
Increase the profits of the business
Reduce the fees paid for the audit
questions.rationale: It supports business continuity.

questions.stem: Who is responsible for establishing and maintaining a company's system of internal control?
questions.rationale: Directors are responsible; auditors review the controls relevant to the audit.

questions.stem: The three lines of defence model places risk ownership with:
options: External audit, which is the third line
questions.rationale: Second line oversees risk, third line (internal audit) gives independent assurance.

questions.stem: A company's risk appetite is:
options: The amount of risk it is willing to accept to achieve its objectives
The value of its shares on the market
The rate of tax it pays on its profits
The profit it expects to earn in a year
questions.rationale: Risk appetite guides decision making.

questions.stem: The Bribery Act 2010 includes an offence of:
options: Failing to prevent bribery by associated persons
Avoiding the requirement for an audit
Making excessive profit in a year
questions.rationale: Companies need adequate procedures.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an adequate procedure to prevent bribery?
options: A gifts and hospitality register and staff training
questions.rationale: Policies, training and monitoring help show reasonable steps.

questions.stem: A 'tone at the top' refers to:
options: The pricing policy set by the board
The salaries paid to senior staff
Management's attitude to ethics and controls
The noise level in the open-plan office
questions.rationale: Strong ethical leadership strengthens the control environment.

questions.stem: The money laundering reporting officer (MLRO) is responsible for:
options: Receiving internal reports and deciding whether to report to the NCA
Hiring staff for the finance team
Preparing the tax returns of the business
questions.rationale: Suspicions are reported through a suspicious activity report (SAR).

questions.stem: Which of these is a possible penalty for failing to keep adequate accounting records?
options: An exemption from the annual audit
A refund of VAT from HMRC
A reduction in the tax payable
questions.rationale: Directors have a legal duty to keep records.

questions.stem: Under UK GDPR, individuals have the right to:
options: Access the personal data held about them
questions.rationale: Subject access requests must be dealt with promptly.

questions.stem: A conflict of interest policy requires staff to:
options: Declare any personal interests that could affect decisions
Ignore decisions where they have an interest
questions.rationale: Disclosure allows the risk to be managed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a preventive control in the payroll system?
options: Requiring HR approval before a new starter is added
questions.rationale: Preventive controls stop errors before they occur.

questions.stem: An exception report highlights transactions that:
options: Fall outside normal parameters and need review
questions.rationale: It is a detective control.

questions.stem: Independent checking of inventory counts is a:
questions.rationale: It finds discrepancies after they have occurred.

questions.stem: Which control weakness is most serious in a purchasing system?
options: The same person can create suppliers and approve payments
questions.rationale: Combining these duties enables fictitious supplier fraud.

questions.stem: Limiting cash on the premises and banking daily is a:
questions.rationale: It reduces the loss if theft occurs.

questions.stem: Controls should be cost-effective, meaning:
options: The cost of the control should not exceed the benefit
questions.rationale: Design should be proportionate to the risk.

questions.stem: A control that reviews daily takings against till records is a:
questions.rationale: Reconciliations compare two sets of records.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes lapping?
options: Covering one customer's stolen payment with another customer's later payment
questions.rationale: Lapping delays detection of theft.

questions.stem: A company's accounts clerk has never taken a holiday in three years. This is:
options: A possible red flag for fraud
questions.rationale: Fraudsters often avoid absence to avoid discovery.

questions.stem: Fraud prevention is primarily the responsibility of:
options: Management and those charged with governance
questions.rationale: Auditors detect material fraud but do not prevent it.

questions.stem: A manager overrides controls to process a payment to a relative's company. Which fraud triangle element is most important?
questions.rationale: Management override is facilitated by weak governance.

questions.stem: A fraud response plan should include:
options: Who investigates, how evidence is preserved and who is informed
questions.rationale: A clear plan ensures consistent handling.

questions.stem: Bribery risk is highest when:
options: Dealing with agents or in high-risk countries without controls
questions.rationale: Risk assessments consider geography and intermediaries.

questions.stem: An organisation's order-to-cash cycle covers:
options: Receiving orders, delivering goods, invoicing and collecting payment
questions.rationale: It is the sales and receivables process.

questions.stem: A procure-to-pay process begins with:
questions.rationale: Order of events: requisition, order, receipt, invoice, payment.

questions.stem: A lengthy approval chain delays supplier payment and causes late fees. The best improvement is to:
options: Redesign the process to remove duplicate approvals while keeping key controls
questions.rationale: Efficiency should not compromise control.

questions.stem: System documentation, such as procedure manuals, helps to:
options: Ensure consistent operation and support training
questions.rationale: Clear procedures reduce errors.

questions.stem: A key benefit of using an integrated accounting system is:
options: Reduced duplication and better consistency of data
questions.rationale: One data source avoids reconciliation problems.

questions.stem: A firewall protects a network by:
questions.rationale: It is an IT security tool.

questions.stem: The UK Corporate Governance Code recommends that at least half of the board (excluding the chair) are:
questions.rationale: Independence supports oversight.

questions.stem: The audit committee should consist of:
options: Independent non-executive directors with financial expertise
questions.rationale: It monitors reporting and audit.

questions.stem: Anti-money laundering regulations require firms to carry out:
options: Risk assessments and customer due diligence
questions.rationale: Firms must know their customers.

questions.stem: A suspicious activity report (SAR) is submitted to:
questions.rationale: The MLRO decides whether to submit a SAR.

questions.stem: A data protection officer (DPO) is responsible for:
options: Advising on and monitoring data protection compliance
questions.rationale: UK GDPR requires a DPO in certain cases.

questions.stem: Which of these is a principle of UK GDPR?
options: Data should be kept no longer than necessary
questions.rationale: Storage limitation is a principle.

questions.stem: Directors' duties under the Companies Act 2006 include:
options: Promoting the success of the company and exercising reasonable care
questions.rationale: These are statutory duties.

questions.stem: An accountant is asked by a client to prepare accounts to a deadline that does not allow proper checks. What should they do?
options: Explain the risk and agree a realistic timetable
questions.rationale: Professional competence and due care require appropriate review.

questions.stem: An accountant is offered a lucrative consultancy by a client whose accounts they prepare. The main threat is:
questions.rationale: A personal financial interest may affect objectivity.

questions.stem: A budget-to-actual review by management is an example of:
questions.rationale: It finds differences after the event.

questions.stem: Which control helps ensure all sales invoices are recorded?
options: Sequential numbering of invoices and checking for gaps
questions.rationale: Gaps in sequence reveal missing documents.

questions.stem: A control that locks a user out after three incorrect password attempts is:
questions.rationale: It protects against unauthorised access.

questions.stem: A small business cannot afford segregation of duties. Which is the best compensating control?
options: Owner review of bank reconciliations and key reports
questions.rationale: Management oversight compensates.

questions.stem: Internal controls over cash receipts include:
questions.rationale: They reduce the risk of loss.

questions.stem: A control objective is:
options: What a control is designed to achieve
questions.rationale: For example, to ensure completeness.

questions.stem: Computer-generated exception reports are useful because they:
questions.rationale: They support monitoring.

questions.stem: Which is an example of asset misappropriation?
questions.rationale: Theft of assets.

questions.stem: Fraudulent financial reporting is often motivated by:
options: Pressure to meet targets or covenants
questions.rationale: Incentives influence behaviour.

questions.stem: An employee processes false refunds to their own account. Which control best detects this?
options: Independent review of refunds and exception reports
questions.rationale: It highlights unusual refunds.

questions.stem: A fraud risk assessment should be:
options: Updated regularly and reviewed by management
questions.rationale: Risks change over time.

questions.stem: Social engineering fraud typically relies on:
options: Manipulating people to disclose information or make payments
questions.rationale: Staff awareness is key.

questions.stem: A whistleblowing hotline helps by:
options: Providing a safe channel to report concerns
questions.rationale: It supports detection.

questions.stem: A business wants to speed up supplier payments without losing control. A suitable approach is:
options: Automating three-way matching and approval workflows
questions.rationale: Automation can maintain controls.

questions.stem: Data validation checks in a system, such as format and range checks, are:
questions.rationale: They check input accuracy.

questions.stem: Change management controls over IT systems aim to:
options: Ensure that changes are authorised, tested and documented
questions.rationale: They prevent unauthorised changes.

questions.stem: Which risk arises if one person can both amend supplier bank details and approve payments?
options: Fraudulent payments to a false account
questions.rationale: Segregation is needed.

questions.stem: A process owner is responsible for:
options: The design and performance of a business process
questions.rationale: They improve efficiency and control.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a corrective control in IT?
options: Restoring data from a backup after corruption
questions.rationale: It fixes a problem after the event.

questions.stem: The UK Corporate Governance Code applies on a basis of:
questions.rationale: Companies explain departures.

questions.stem: Which body regulates financial reporting and audit quality in the UK?
questions.rationale: It sets standards.

questions.stem: The board of a listed company establishes an audit committee. Its main purpose is to:
options: Provide independent review of financial reporting and controls
questions.rationale: It supports governance.

questions.stem: Under the Companies Act 2006 a director must avoid:
questions.rationale: It is a statutory duty.

questions.stem: Anti-bribery policies should include:
options: A ban on improper payments and a gifts register
questions.rationale: They support adequate procedures.

questions.stem: The ICO regulates:
questions.rationale: The Information Commissioner's Office.

questions.stem: An employer asks an accountant to backdate a document. The accountant should:
options: Refuse and escalate if pressure continues
questions.rationale: Backdating is dishonest.

questions.stem: A client asks an accountant to help structure a transaction that appears to have no purpose other than to evade tax. The accountant should:
questions.rationale: Evasion is illegal.

questions.stem: Professional behaviour includes:
options: Complying with relevant laws and avoiding discredit to the profession
questions.rationale: It is a fundamental principle.

questions.stem: A business has assets of £48,000 and liabilities of £15,500. What is the capital (owner's equity)?
questions.rationale: Capital = assets − liabilities = £48,000 − £15,500 = £32,500.

questions.stem: The owner introduces £5,000 cash into the business. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
options: Assets decrease by £5,000 and capital increases by £5,000
Capital increases by £5,000 with no effect on assets
Assets increase by £5,000 and liabilities increase by £5,000
Assets increase by £5,000 and capital increases by £5,000
questions.rationale: Cash (an asset) rises and the owner's claim on the business (capital) rises by the same amount.

questions.stem: A business buys a machine on credit for £4,000. What is the effect?
options: Liabilities decrease by £4,000 and assets increase by £4,000
Non-current assets increase by £4,000 and liabilities increase by £4,000
Non-current assets increase by £4,000 and cash decreases by £4,000
questions.rationale: A credit purchase creates a payable (liability) and a new asset. Capital is unchanged.

questions.stem: At the start of the year a sole trader has assets of £60,000 and liabilities of £22,000. During the year profit was £14,000 and drawings £9,000. What is closing capital?
questions.rationale: Opening capital £38,000 + profit £14,000 − drawings £9,000 = £43,000.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a liability?
questions.rationale: A bank loan is an amount the business owes. The other items are assets.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-current asset?
options: Goods held for resale to customers
Amounts owed to the business by customers
Cash held in the business bank account
A delivery van used for 5 years
questions.rationale: Non-current assets are held for long-term use in the business, not for resale or short-term conversion to cash.

questions.stem: Which entry increases an asset account?
questions.rationale: Assets and expenses increase with debits; liabilities, capital and income increase with credits.

questions.stem: A supplier is owed more money by the business. How is the payables account changed?
options: It is debited and credited equally
questions.rationale: Payables is a liability. Liabilities have credit balances so they increase with credits.

questions.stem: A business pays rent of £600 by bank transfer. What is the double-entry?
options: Debit rent payable £600, credit rent expense £600
questions.rationale: Rent is an expense (debit). Bank is an asset that falls, so it is credited.

questions.stem: A customer pays a £900 invoice by cheque. What is the double-entry?
questions.rationale: Cash received increases bank (debit). The customer's debt falls so receivables is credited. Sales were already recorded when the invoice was raised.

questions.stem: The owner takes £250 cash from the business for personal use. What is the double-entry?
questions.rationale: Drawings reduce the owner's equity and are debited to a drawings account, not to an expense.

questions.stem: A business buys goods for resale on credit from a supplier for £1,200 (ignore VAT). What is the double-entry?
questions.rationale: Purchases is debited. As the goods are bought on credit, the amount owed to the supplier is credited to payables.

questions.stem: A sale is made on credit for £800 plus VAT at 20%. What is the correct double-entry?
options: Debit sales £800, debit VAT £160, credit receivables £960
Debit receivables £960, credit sales £800, credit VAT £160
questions.rationale: The customer owes the gross £960. Sales is recorded net at £800 and the £160 VAT is a liability owed to HMRC.

questions.stem: A business returns goods costing £300 (net) to a supplier it bought from on credit. What is the double-entry (ignore VAT)?
options: Debit purchases returns £300, credit trade payables £300
Debit trade payables £300, credit purchases returns £300
Debit trade payables £300, credit sales returns £300
questions.rationale: The amount owed to the supplier falls (debit payables) and the returns are recorded in purchases returns (credit).

questions.stem: A debit balance on a bank account in the business's own ledger means the business has:
questions.rationale: The bank account in the ledger is an asset, so a debit balance means funds are held.

questions.stem: A business pays £2,000 of a £5,000 bank loan back by bank transfer. What is the entry?
questions.rationale: The liability reduces (debit) and the bank balance falls (credit). Only the interest element would be an expense.

questions.stem: A business buys a van for £12,000 paying £4,000 by bank and the rest on credit from the dealer. Which statement is correct?
options: Debit vehicles £4,000, debit payables £8,000, credit bank £12,000
Credit bank £4,000, credit payables £8,000, debit vehicles £12,000
Credit vehicles £12,000, debit bank £4,000, debit payables £8,000
questions.rationale: A split transaction: the asset is debited in full and the two sources of payment are credited.

questions.stem: Which book of prime entry records credit sales invoices issued to customers?
questions.rationale: The sales day book lists invoices issued on credit, which are then posted to the ledgers.

questions.stem: Which book of prime entry records credit notes received from suppliers?
questions.rationale: Credit notes received from suppliers for returned goods are listed in the purchases returns day book.

questions.stem: Which of these is recorded in the general journal?
options: A petty cash payment for stamps
A cheque received from a customer
Purchase of a non-current asset on credit
questions.rationale: The journal records unusual or non-routine transactions that do not belong in another book of prime entry, such as asset purchases and corrections.

questions.stem: A sales day book total shows net £5,000, VAT £1,000 and gross £6,000. Which ledger entry is correct?
questions.rationale: The total gross is debited to the sales ledger control (receivables). Sales and VAT are both credits.

questions.stem: Which document is used to record the supply of goods and services to a customer, requesting payment?
questions.rationale: An invoice sets out what was sold, the price, VAT and payment terms.

questions.stem: A credit note issued to a customer for returned goods is first recorded in the:
questions.rationale: Credit notes issued reduce what customers owe, so they go through the sales returns day book.

questions.stem: Which document would a customer send to a supplier to accompany a payment, showing which invoices are being paid?
questions.rationale: A remittance advice tells the supplier what the payment covers.

questions.stem: Which document does a supplier send to a customer at the end of the month showing invoices, credit notes and payments?
questions.rationale: A statement summarises the account and is useful for reconciling the supplier's balance.

questions.stem: A business sells goods for £500 net. VAT is charged at 20%. What is the total invoice amount?
An invoice shows a gross total of £1,440 including VAT at 20%. What is the VAT amount?
At the end of a quarter output VAT is £8,400 and input VAT is £5,100. What does the business do?
questions.rationale: Output VAT − input VAT = £3,300 payable to HMRC.

questions.stem: A business has output VAT of £2,000 and input VAT of £2,600 in a period. What is the position?
options: £600 is due to be reclaimed from HMRC
£600 is due to be paid to HMRC
No VAT position as it nets to nil
questions.rationale: Input VAT exceeds output VAT, so the business is owed a refund of £600.

questions.stem: Which account is used to record the VAT charged by a business on its sales?
questions.rationale: Output VAT is a liability to HMRC and is credited to the VAT account.

questions.stem: A trade discount of 10% is offered on a list price of £2,000 before VAT at 20%. What is the invoice total?
questions.rationale: Trade discount: £2,000 × 90% = £1,800 net. VAT £360. Total £2,160.

questions.stem: A customer is offered a 5% prompt payment discount on a net invoice of £4,000 plus VAT at 20%. The customer pays within the terms. How much do they pay?
questions.rationale: VAT is calculated on the discounted amount when the discount is taken: £4,000 × 95% = £3,800 + VAT £760 = £4,560.

questions.stem: In a subsidiary ledger, individual customer accounts are held in the:
questions.rationale: The sales ledger (receivables ledger) holds individual customer accounts.

questions.stem: A cheque received from a customer is first entered in the:
questions.rationale: Receipts and payments by bank are recorded in the cash book.

questions.stem: The opening bank balance is £3,200 (debit). Receipts of £1,800 and payments of £2,500 are made. What is the closing balance?
questions.rationale: £3,200 + £1,800 − £2,500 = £2,500. A positive total remains a debit balance.

questions.stem: The cash book shows a credit closing balance. What does this mean?
options: The cash book is incorrectly kept
The business has a surplus at the bank
The business is overdrawn at the bank
The bank owes the business money
questions.rationale: A credit balance in the cash book means payments exceed receipts, so the account is overdrawn.

questions.stem: Under the imprest system, petty cash is topped up each period by:
options: The amount remaining in the float
questions.rationale: The imprest method restores the float to its fixed amount by reimbursing what was spent.

questions.stem: The petty cash float is £150. Vouchers total £112 and cash in the box is £35. What is the discrepancy?
questions.rationale: Expected cash = £150 − £112 = £38. Actual £35. £3 is missing.

questions.stem: At the end of the month petty cash vouchers total £86 and the float is £200. How much is reimbursed from the bank to restore the imprest?
questions.rationale: Under the imprest system the reimbursement equals the total spent, restoring the original float.

questions.stem: Which is the correct double-entry for reimbursing a petty cash float of £86 from the bank?
questions.rationale: Petty cash is an asset. The top-up debits it and credits bank.

questions.stem: Which payment method involves the payer instructing their bank to transfer money directly to the payee's account?
questions.rationale: Bank transfers move funds electronically between accounts without the use of a paper cheque.

questions.stem: A cheque that has passed its date by more than six months is described as:
questions.rationale: A cheque presented more than six months after its date is stale and is normally refused by banks.

questions.stem: A customer's cheque is returned unpaid by the bank because of insufficient funds. How is this recorded?
questions.rationale: The original receipt is reversed: bank is credited and the customer's account is debited as they still owe the money.

questions.stem: A business receives a bank statement showing bank charges of £25 not yet in the cash book. What entry is needed?
questions.rationale: Bank charges are an expense and reduce the bank balance.

questions.stem: A trial balance is a list of:
questions.rationale: A trial balance lists all ledger balances to check that total debits equal total credits.

questions.stem: Which of these items normally has a credit balance in the trial balance?
questions.rationale: Income accounts such as sales have credit balances. Expenses and assets have debit balances.

questions.stem: In the trial balance, a business owner's personal withdrawals of cash are shown as a:
questions.rationale: Drawings reduce equity and are a debit balance in the trial balance.

questions.stem: Total debits are £84,200 and total credits are £83,700 in a trial balance. What does this indicate?
options: The accounts are correct and complete
An error has been made in recording or posting
The bank balance in the cash book must be wrong
Sales have been understated in the ledger
questions.rationale: A £500 difference between debits and credits shows at least one error that must be investigated.

questions.stem: A transaction was posted to the wrong account but with the correct debit/credit and amount. Will the trial balance still balance?
options: Only if it was an asset
questions.rationale: An error of commission posts the right amount to the wrong account of the same type, so the trial balance still balances.

questions.stem: A receivables account has debits of £7,400 and credits of £5,900. What is the balance carried down?
questions.rationale: Debits exceed credits by £1,500, so the account has a debit balance (the customer still owes £1,500).

questions.stem: A payables account has debits of £3,200 and credits of £4,700. What does the balance represent?
questions.rationale: Credits exceed debits, so the balance is a credit. The business still owes £1,500.

questions.stem: On which side of the ledger account is the balance brought down (b/d) recorded for an asset with a debit balance?
questions.rationale: The closing balance is carried down on the smaller side and brought down on the opposite side, which is the debit side for a debit balance.

questions.stem: Which of the following accounts normally has a credit balance?
questions.rationale: Liabilities, capital and income have credit balances.

questions.stem: Where are individual supplier accounts kept?
questions.rationale: The purchases (payables) ledger holds an account for each supplier.

questions.stem: A business pays wages of £1,800 by bank. What is the double-entry?
questions.rationale: Wages is an expense, so it is debited. Bank falls and is credited.

questions.stem: A business receives £150 interest from the bank and it is paid into the account. What is the double-entry?
questions.rationale: Interest received is income and so is credited. Bank increases and is debited.

questions.stem: A customer returns goods that were sold to them on credit for £250 (ignore VAT). What is the double-entry?
options: Debit sales returns £250, credit trade receivables £250
Debit trade receivables £250, credit sales returns £250
Debit purchases returns £250, credit trade receivables £250
questions.rationale: Sales returns is debited and the customer's balance is reduced by a credit to receivables.

questions.stem: The accounting equation after a business sells goods costing £600 on credit for £900 is affected by:
options: An increase in liabilities of £300 and no change in assets
An increase in assets of £900 and in liabilities of £900
A decrease in assets of £300 and in capital of £300
An increase in assets of £300 and an increase in capital of £300
questions.rationale: Receivables rise by £900 and inventory falls by £600, a net asset increase of £300, which is profit and increases capital.

questions.stem: A business pays an electricity bill of £420 by direct debit. Which accounts are affected?
questions.rationale: An expense is debited and the cash paid reduces bank, so bank is credited.

questions.stem: A discount given to a customer for paying promptly is called:
options: Bulk discount for buying large quantities
Trade discount given on the list price
Volume rebate paid at the end of the year
questions.rationale: Settlement discounts reward early payment. Trade discounts are reductions in list price.

questions.stem: A customer owing £2,000 pays £1,960 in full settlement within the discount period. What is the discount allowed?
questions.rationale: £2,000 − £1,960 = £40 discount allowed.

questions.stem: Discount allowed is shown in the accounts as:
questions.rationale: A discount allowed is a cost of encouraging prompt payment, so it is an expense.

questions.stem: Discount received from a supplier is shown in the accounts as:
questions.rationale: Discounts received reduce costs and are treated as income.

questions.stem: A supplier invoice is for £1,500. The business pays £1,470 and receives £30 discount. Which entry records the payment and discount?
options: Debit payables £1,500, credit bank £1,500 and discount received £30
Debit bank £1,470, credit payables £1,470, credit discount £30
Debit payables £1,470, credit bank £1,470 with no discount entry
Debit payables £1,500, credit bank £1,470, credit discount received £30
questions.rationale: The supplier's debt is cleared in full: bank pays £1,470 and the £30 balance is discount received.

questions.stem: A trade discount appears:
options: As a charge shown on the bank statement
On the invoice, reducing the price charged
Only in the cash book when payment is made
In the journal as a correction of an error
questions.rationale: Trade discounts are deducted on the invoice and are not recorded in the ledger accounts as a separate item.

questions.stem: Buying a new photocopier for use in the office for several years is:
questions.rationale: It provides benefit over more than one period, so it is capitalised as a non-current asset.

questions.stem: Paying for repairs to a delivery van is:
questions.rationale: Repairs maintain the asset and are expensed in the period.

questions.stem: Which of the following is capital income?
options: Rent received from letting a spare room
Proceeds from the sale of a non-current asset
Sales of goods in the normal course of trading
Interest received on the business bank account
questions.rationale: Capital income arises from non-trading transactions such as disposals or owner investment.

questions.stem: Which of these is revenue expenditure?
questions.rationale: Stationery is used up in the normal course of trading.

questions.stem: A business buys a van for £15,000 and pays £500 for the first full tank of fuel. How much is capital expenditure?
questions.rationale: The van is capital expenditure. The fuel is revenue expenditure.

questions.stem: A business pays £2,000 for the delivery and installation of a machine costing £18,000. What is the total capital expenditure?
questions.rationale: Delivery and installation costs needed to bring the asset into use are part of its cost.

questions.stem: Inventory is held by a business:
options: For use in the business for many years
questions.rationale: Inventory (stock) is a current asset held for sale.

questions.stem: Which item would be shown under current assets?
questions.rationale: Receivables are expected to be converted to cash within the year.

questions.stem: Which document is sent by a business to ask a supplier to provide goods?
questions.rationale: A purchase order is a formal request to a supplier.

questions.stem: A credit note is issued:
options: To reduce the amount owed by a customer, for example when goods are returned
To demand payment of an overdue invoice
To confirm that a payment has been received
To increase the amount a customer owes
questions.rationale: A credit note reverses part or all of an invoice.

questions.stem: Which document accompanies goods delivered and is signed by the customer as proof of receipt?
questions.rationale: The signed delivery note is evidence goods were delivered.

questions.stem: A supplier quotation is:
options: A bill for goods that have already been delivered
A statement of the price at which a supplier is willing to supply goods
An order sent by a customer for goods
A confirmation that a payment has been received
questions.rationale: A quotation is an offer to supply at a stated price and is not a demand for payment.

questions.stem: Which of the following should be shown on a credit note?
options: The owner's capital balance at the year end
The customer's bank password and account number
The business's tax return reference and tax due
A reference to the original invoice and the amount credited
questions.rationale: Credit notes should be cross-referenced so the ledger can be traced.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a bank paying-in slip?
options: To authorise a payment to a supplier from the account
To record cash and cheques paid into the bank account
To record the wages paid to staff each month
To place an order for stationery with a supplier
questions.rationale: It lists items banked and is the source document for the cash book receipts side.

questions.stem: Why should original documents such as invoices be retained?
options: They increase the profit shown in the accounts
They are evidence of transactions for audit and tax purposes
They are not needed once the entry is posted
They replace the need to keep ledger accounts
questions.rationale: Source documents support entries and must be kept for the required period.

questions.stem: Which of these is a source document for a cash purchase?
questions.rationale: A till receipt is evidence of the purchase and is used to record the payment.

questions.stem: Which payment method is best for a large urgent same-day transfer of funds?
questions.rationale: CHAPS transfers high-value sums on the same working day.

questions.stem: A standing order is:
options: A variable payment collected by the payee on request
A cash withdrawal made at a bank branch
A fixed payment made at regular intervals on the payer's instruction
A one-off cheque written to a supplier
questions.rationale: The payer instructs the bank to pay a fixed amount, such as rent, on set dates.

questions.stem: A direct debit differs from a standing order because:
options: The amount can vary and is collected by the payee
The amount is always fixed by the payer in advance
It can only be paid in cash at a branch
It cannot be cancelled once it has been set up
questions.rationale: A direct debit lets the payee collect varying amounts, for example a utility bill.

questions.stem: A business writes a cheque on 1 June and the supplier banks it on 4 June. When does the business's cash book record the payment?
options: 1 June, when the cheque is written
questions.rationale: The cash book records the transaction when the cheque is issued, which creates a timing difference with the bank statement.

questions.stem: A business pays a supplier by BACS. Which statement is true?
options: The payment requires a cheque to be signed
The payment normally clears within a few seconds
The payment usually takes about three working days to clear
The payment can only be made in cash
questions.rationale: BACS is a batch system with normal 3 working day cycle, unlike Faster Payments.

questions.stem: Which of these accounts has a debit balance in a trial balance?
questions.rationale: Expenses such as rent paid have debit balances.

questions.stem: Which of these errors will mean the trial balance does not balance?
options: Posting an entry to the wrong expense account
Posting a debit entry twice but the credit entry once
Recording a sale as a purchase
questions.rationale: A one-sided duplication changes only one side of the ledger, creating an imbalance.

questions.stem: The totals of a trial balance agree. This proves:
options: That total debits equal total credits
questions.rationale: Some errors, such as omissions and errors of principle, do not affect the balance.

questions.stem: A trial balance has total debits of £50,300 and credits of £50,000. A suspense account is opened. Which entry is made?
questions.rationale: Credits are short by £300, so a credit of £300 to suspense makes the totals agree.

questions.stem: A business has assets of £90,000 and capital of £62,000. What are its liabilities?
questions.rationale: Liabilities = assets − capital = £90,000 − £62,000 = £28,000.

questions.stem: The owner withdraws £1,500 of cash for personal use. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
options: Assets fall by £1,500 and capital falls by £1,500
Assets fall by £1,500 and liabilities fall by £1,500
Assets rise by £1,500 and capital rises by £1,500
Liabilities rise by £1,500 and capital falls by £1,500
questions.rationale: Cash leaves the business and the owner's claim on it is reduced by the same amount.

questions.stem: A business pays a supplier £2,000 owed to them from the bank. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
options: Liabilities fall by £2,000 and capital rises by £2,000
Assets fall by £2,000 and capital falls by £2,000
Assets rise by £2,000 and liabilities fall by £2,000
Assets fall by £2,000 and liabilities fall by £2,000
questions.rationale: Bank (an asset) and trade payables (a liability) both reduce, so capital is unchanged.

questions.stem: A sole trader earns a profit of £7,000 in the year and takes no drawings. What happens to capital?
questions.rationale: Profit adds to the owner's capital.

questions.stem: Which of these is a source of finance for the business owned by the owner?
questions.rationale: Capital is the amount invested by the owner. The other items are assets.

questions.stem: A business buys inventory for £700 cash. What is the double-entry?
questions.rationale: Purchases rise (debit) and cash falls (credit).

questions.stem: A business sells goods for £1,100 cash. What is the double-entry?
questions.rationale: Cash increases (debit) and sales income is credited.

questions.stem: A business pays insurance of £480 by cheque. What is the double-entry?
questions.rationale: Insurance is an expense (debit) and the bank balance falls (credit).

questions.stem: A business takes out a bank loan of £10,000 which is paid into its bank account. What is the double-entry?
questions.rationale: Bank increases (debit) and a liability to the lender is created (credit).

questions.stem: A sale on credit of £400 to a customer is made. What is the double-entry (ignore VAT)?
questions.rationale: The customer owes £400 (asset, debit) and sales income is credited.

questions.stem: The business pays a supplier £900 by BACS for goods previously bought on credit. What is the double-entry?
questions.rationale: The liability is reduced (debit) and bank falls (credit). Purchases were recorded when the goods were bought.

questions.stem: A business buys office furniture for £3,000 and pays by cheque. What is the double-entry?
questions.rationale: Furniture is a non-current asset, not an expense or purchase for resale.

questions.stem: A customer returns faulty goods that cost them £150 on credit. The business issues a credit note. What is the entry in the customer's account?
questions.rationale: The credit note reduces the amount owed, so it is a credit in the customer's account.

questions.stem: Which book of prime entry would a purchase of goods on credit be recorded in first?
questions.rationale: Credit purchase invoices are listed in the purchases day book.

questions.stem: Which entry records the total of the purchases day book (net £8,000, VAT £1,600, gross £9,600) in the general ledger?
options: Debit purchases £8,000, debit VAT £1,600, credit payables £9,600
Debit payables £9,600, credit purchases £8,000, credit VAT £1,600
questions.rationale: Purchases and input VAT are debited. The total owed to suppliers is credited.

questions.stem: A list of credit notes sent to customers is kept in the:
questions.rationale: Sales returns are recorded in the sales returns day book.

questions.stem: What is the VAT in a sales day book entry with a net amount of £2,500 at 20%?
Which of these is NOT a book of prime entry?
questions.rationale: A trial balance is a list of ledger balances, not a book of original entry.

questions.stem: A business's gross sales invoice total is £3,600 including 20% VAT. What is the net amount?
Output VAT for the quarter is £6,200 and input VAT is £7,100. What does the business do?
questions.rationale: Input VAT exceeds output VAT by £900, so a refund is due.

questions.stem: A zero-rated sale of £1,000 is made. What is the VAT charged?
questions.rationale: Zero-rated supplies carry VAT at 0%.

questions.stem: A business buys a standard-rated item for £480 net. What is the total paid including 20% VAT?
questions.rationale: VAT £96. Total £576.

questions.stem: Where are VAT amounts accounted for in the business's ledger?
options: VAT account in the general ledger
questions.rationale: The VAT account tracks amounts owed to or by HMRC.

questions.stem: Petty cash float is £200. Vouchers: stationery £34, travel £52, coffee £18, postage £26. How much cash should remain?
questions.rationale: Vouchers total £130. £200 − £130 = £70.

questions.stem: A petty cash voucher is:
options: A document that records a small payment from the petty cash box
questions.rationale: Vouchers support each payment and are authorised.

questions.stem: A petty cash book analysis shows total spent of £86, of which VAT is £6. Which entry records the VAT?
questions.rationale: Input VAT paid is reclaimable and debited to the VAT account.

questions.stem: Opening bank balance £1,200 overdrawn (credit). Receipts £3,500 and payments £1,800. What is the closing balance?
A business pays a supplier £600 by cheque. The cash book entry is:
questions.rationale: Payments reduce the bank balance, so they go on the credit side.

questions.stem: Which of these would have a credit balance in a trial balance?
questions.rationale: Discounts received are income and have credit balances.

questions.stem: The trial balance totals: debits £62,300, credits £62,300. Which error is still possible?
options: An addition error in one account only
A sale posted to the wrong customer's account
questions.rationale: Errors within the same class of accounts do not affect the trial balance totals.

questions.stem: A business pays carriage inwards of £120 by bank on goods bought. What is the double-entry?
questions.rationale: Carriage inwards is a cost of purchases and is debited. Bank falls and is credited.

questions.stem: A business pays carriage outwards of £75 in cash. What is the double-entry?
questions.rationale: Carriage outwards is a selling expense and is debited.

questions.stem: A customer who owes £300 pays by cheque and is allowed £6 discount. What is the cash book entry?
options: Debit bank £294 and debit discount allowed £6, credit receivables £300
Debit receivables £300, credit bank £294 and discount £6
questions.rationale: The customer's account is cleared in full; £6 is an expense.

questions.stem: A business buys goods for £2,000 on credit and returns £250 of them. What is the balance on the supplier's account?
questions.rationale: £2,000 − £250 = £1,750 still owed to the supplier.

questions.stem: The owner introduces a van worth £8,000 into the business. What is the double-entry?
questions.rationale: An asset and the owner's capital both increase.

questions.stem: A business sells a non-current asset on credit for £1,200. What is the debit entry?
questions.rationale: The buyer owes the business, so receivables is debited.

questions.stem: What does a credit balance on a supplier's account in the business's ledger show?
options: The business owes the supplier money
The supplier owes the business money
questions.rationale: Trade payables have credit balances.

questions.stem: Wages of £3,500 are paid by bank. Which accounts are debited and credited?
questions.rationale: Wages are an expense.

questions.stem: A business buys inventory on credit for £600 plus VAT at 20%. What is the credit entry in the payables account?
questions.rationale: The supplier is owed the gross amount £600 + £120 = £720.

questions.stem: Rent received of £400 from a tenant is paid into the bank. What is the double-entry?
questions.rationale: Rent received is income.

questions.stem: Which book of prime entry records the return of goods by a business to its supplier?
questions.rationale: Returns to suppliers are recorded in the purchases returns day book.

questions.stem: A business records a payment for office stationery of £30 from petty cash. Which book of prime entry is used?
questions.rationale: Small cash payments go through the petty cash book.

questions.stem: A summary of goods sent to credit customers with the date, customer and amount is the:
questions.rationale: It is the book of prime entry for credit sales.

questions.stem: The total of the sales returns day book (net £400, VAT £80, gross £480) is posted as:
options: Debit receivables £480, credit sales returns £400, credit VAT £80
Debit sales returns £400, debit VAT £80, credit receivables £480
questions.rationale: Returns reduce sales and output VAT, and reduce receivables.

questions.stem: A sales ledger account shows debit £5,000 and credit £3,200 at the month end. What is the balance?
questions.rationale: Debits exceed credits by £1,800.

questions.stem: A bank loan account shows credit balance of £12,000. This is a:
questions.rationale: A credit balance on a loan means the business owes the money.

questions.stem: In the nominal ledger, accounts record:
options: Income, expenses, assets, liabilities and capital
questions.rationale: The nominal (general) ledger holds all other accounts.

questions.stem: Which of these accounts is kept in the purchases ledger?
questions.rationale: The purchases ledger holds individual supplier accounts.

questions.stem: A business pays a bank loan instalment of £500 including £60 interest. What is the entry?
options: Debit loan £440, debit interest £60, credit bank £500
questions.rationale: Only the capital part reduces the loan. Interest is an expense.

questions.stem: A business spends £6,000 to extend its building. This is:
questions.rationale: It improves a non-current asset.

questions.stem: Painting an existing office to maintain it is:
questions.rationale: It maintains rather than improves an asset.

questions.stem: A business buys a machine for £9,000 and pays £400 for training staff to use it. How much should be capitalised?
questions.rationale: Staff training is revenue expenditure.

questions.stem: A petty cash float of £100 is reduced by payments of £68. What is the imprest top-up?
questions.rationale: The top-up equals the amount spent.

questions.stem: The petty cashier is responsible for:
options: Keeping the float, vouchers and the petty cash book
questions.rationale: Petty cash is administered by a petty cashier.

questions.stem: A business has assets £75,000 and liabilities £30,000. It makes a profit of £6,000 and the owner takes drawings of £2,000. What is the closing capital?
A business buys goods on credit for £3,000 and sells half for £2,500 cash. What is the overall effect on capital?
questions.rationale: Cost of goods sold £1,500; profit £1,000.

questions.stem: A trial balance includes: debits £47,500, credits £46,900. What is the difference and which side needs adjusting?
questions.rationale: Debits exceed credits by £600.

questions.stem: Under marginal costing, which costs are included in the cost of a unit?
questions.rationale: Marginal costing values inventory at variable cost. Fixed costs are charged to the period.

questions.stem: Opening inventory is 0. Production is 1,000 units and sales are 800 units. Fixed production overhead is £5,000. Which statement is true?
options: Absorption costing profit is lower than marginal costing profit by £5,000
The profits are the same under both methods
Marginal costing profit is higher than absorption costing profit by £1,000
Absorption costing profit is higher than marginal costing profit by £1,000
questions.rationale: 200 units are in closing inventory, each carrying £5 of fixed overhead under absorption costing (£1,000 deferred to next period).

questions.stem: Opening inventory is 500 units, production is 2,000 units and sales are 2,300 units. Fixed overhead is absorbed at £4 per unit. Compared with marginal costing, absorption costing profit is:
questions.rationale: Inventory fell by 300 units (500 to 200). Under absorption costing £4 × 300 = £1,200 of fixed overhead from earlier periods is charged in this period, so profit is lower.

questions.stem: Contribution per unit is:
options: Selling price − variable cost per unit
Selling price − total cost per unit
questions.rationale: Contribution covers fixed costs and then provides profit.

questions.stem: A product sells for £20 with variable costs of £12 per unit. What is the contribution to sales ratio?
questions.rationale: Contribution £8 ÷ price £20 = 40%.

questions.stem: Break-even point in units is calculated as:
questions.rationale: At break-even total contribution equals fixed costs.

questions.stem: Fixed costs are £48,000. Selling price is £25 and variable cost is £13 per unit. What is the break-even point in units?
questions.rationale: Contribution = £12. £48,000 ÷ £12 = 4,000 units.

questions.stem: Fixed costs are £48,000 and contribution per unit is £12. The business wants a profit of £24,000. How many units must it sell?
Fixed costs £48,000, selling price £25, variable cost £13. Budgeted sales are 5,200 units. What is the margin of safety in units?
questions.rationale: Break-even 4,000 units. 5,200 − 4,000 = 1,200 units.

questions.stem: The break-even point is 4,000 units and budgeted sales are 5,000 units. What is the margin of safety as a percentage of budget?
A business has a contribution to sales ratio of 40% and fixed costs of £60,000. What is the break-even revenue?
Which of these would reduce the break-even point?
options: A fall in the selling price
A rise in variable cost per unit
questions.rationale: Lower fixed costs means fewer units are needed to cover them.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a purpose of a budget?
questions.rationale: Budgets provide targets for planning and a benchmark for control.

questions.stem: Sales budget is 2,000 units. Opening inventory is 300 and the target closing inventory is 400. What is the production budget?
questions.rationale: Production = sales + closing inventory − opening inventory = 2,000 + 400 − 300 = 2,100.

questions.stem: Production is 2,100 units. Each unit needs 3 kg of material. Opening material inventory is 1,000 kg and the target closing is 1,500 kg. How many kg should be purchased?
questions.rationale: Usage 6,300 kg + closing 1,500 − opening 1,000 = 6,800 kg.

questions.stem: A principal budget factor is:
options: The largest single cost in the budget
The profit made in the previous year
The cash balance at the start of the year
The factor that limits the activity of the business
questions.rationale: It is often sales demand but can be materials, labour or machine capacity.

questions.stem: A flexible budget is used to:
options: Reduce costs automatically as activity falls
Fix the budget for the whole period in advance
Replace the cash budget with a simpler forecast
Compare actual results with a budget adjusted to the actual activity level
questions.rationale: A flexed budget allows like-for-like variance analysis.

questions.stem: Budgeted production is 1,000 units with variable costs of £6,000 and fixed costs of £4,000. What is the flexed budget cost for 1,200 units?
A cash budget shows March receipts of £30,000 and payments of £34,500. The opening balance is £8,000. What is the closing cash?

Credit sales: 60% of customers pay in the month after sale and 40% in the second month after sale. Sales were January £10,000 and February £12,000. How much cash is received in March from these two months' sales?
questions.rationale: February sales × 60% = £7,200 plus January sales × 40% = £4,000. Total £11,200.

questions.stem: A favourable variance means:
options: The budget itself was set incorrectly
Actual performance is better for profit than budget
Actual cost exceeded the budgeted cost
Actual sales were lower than the budget
questions.rationale: Favourable variances increase profit relative to the standard.

questions.stem: Budgeted sales were 1,000 units at £10. Actual sales were 1,000 units at £10.50. What is the sales price variance?
Budgeted material usage is 2 kg per unit at £5 per kg. Actual output 500 units used 1,100 kg. What is the material usage variance?
questions.rationale: Standard usage 1,000 kg. Excess 100 kg × £5 = £500 adverse.

questions.stem: Standard material price is £5 per kg. 1,100 kg were bought and used at a total cost of £5,830. What is the material price variance?
questions.rationale: Standard cost of 1,100 kg = £5,500. Actual £5,830. Difference £330 adverse.

questions.stem: Standard labour: 3 hours per unit at £12 per hour. Actual 400 units took 1,150 hours. What is the labour efficiency variance?
questions.rationale: Standard hours 1,200. Actual 1,150. Saving of 50 hours × £12 = £600 favourable.

questions.stem: The standard labour rate is £12 per hour. 1,150 hours were worked and the total paid was £13,225. What is the labour rate variance?
questions.rationale: Standard cost of 1,150 hours = £13,800. Actual cost £13,225. The difference of £575 is favourable.

questions.stem: An adverse variance should be investigated if:
options: It is material or shows a trend
It is any amount at all
questions.rationale: Management by exception focuses on significant variances.

questions.stem: A material price variance could be caused by:
options: A change in the volume of goods sold
Workers taking longer than the standard time
Buying from a different supplier at a different price
Using more material than planned in production
questions.rationale: Price variances relate to the price paid; usage variances relate to the quantity used.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a relevant cost for a decision?
options: A future cash flow that differs between options
A cost that is the same under all options
questions.rationale: Relevant costs are future, incremental cash flows.

questions.stem: A business spent £5,000 last year on market research. It must decide whether to launch a new product. Is the £5,000 relevant?
options: No, it is a sunk cost
Yes, it is a variable cost
Yes, it was spent on the product
Yes, because it is a fixed cost
questions.rationale: Past costs cannot be changed and do not affect future decisions.

questions.stem: A special order of 500 units is offered at £9 each. Variable cost is £7 per unit and there is spare capacity. Fixed costs are unchanged. What is the extra profit?
A business has 4,000 machine hours. Product A earns £30 contribution and needs 3 hours. Product B earns £28 and needs 2 hours. Which product should it favour to maximise profit?
options: Product A, because it uses more hours
Product B, because contribution per hour is £14 versus £10
Product A, because contribution per unit is higher
questions.rationale: Rank by contribution per scarce resource: A £10 per hour, B £14 per hour.

questions.stem: Opportunity cost is:
options: A cost that does not vary with output
The benefit lost by choosing one option instead of the next best
The cost of the chosen option only
A cost that has already been incurred
questions.rationale: It measures the value of the best alternative forgone.

questions.stem: A company makes 1,000 components a year at a variable cost of £8 each, plus £3,000 of fixed cost that would be avoided if it stopped making them. A supplier offers them at £9 each. What is the effect of buying instead of making?
questions.rationale: Make: £8,000 + £3,000 avoidable = £11,000. Buy: £9,000. Buying saves £2,000.

questions.stem: Total costs are £18,000 at 2,000 units and £24,000 at 3,500 units. What is the variable cost per unit (high-low)?
Total costs are £18,000 at 2,000 units and £24,000 at 3,500 units. What is the estimated total cost at 3,000 units?
Which of these is a step cost?
options: A supervisor needed for every 20 workers
Sales commission paid on each sale
questions.rationale: A step cost remains constant over a range and jumps at a threshold.

questions.stem: Which of these would be treated as a variable cost in a standard marginal costing system?
questions.rationale: Direct materials vary with output.

questions.stem: A cost of £8,000 comprises £5,000 fixed and £3,000 variable at 1,000 units. What is the total cost at 1,500 units?
questions.rationale: Variable = £3 per unit × 1,500 = £4,500. Fixed £5,000. Total £9,500.

questions.stem: Which method splits semi-variable costs into fixed and variable parts using the highest and lowest activity levels?
questions.rationale: The high-low method uses two data points.

questions.stem: Under marginal costing, fixed production overheads are:
options: Absorbed into the cost of each unit
Held in closing inventory until sold
Treated as a period cost charged in full to the period
questions.rationale: Marginal costing values inventory at variable cost only.

questions.stem: A business has opening inventory of 0, produces 5,000 units and sells 4,200. Fixed production overhead is £25,000. By how much does the absorption costing profit exceed the marginal costing profit?
questions.rationale: 800 units remain in closing inventory × £5 fixed overhead per unit = £4,000 deferred.

questions.stem: If production equals sales in a period (no change in inventory), profit under absorption costing is:
options: The same as under marginal costing
questions.rationale: Without a change in inventory, no fixed overhead is carried forward.

questions.stem: Selling price £30, variable cost £18, fixed costs £24,000 and sales 3,000 units. What is the marginal costing profit?
Which cost is included in a product's cost under absorption costing but not under marginal costing?
questions.rationale: Absorption costing adds a share of fixed production overhead.

questions.stem: Selling price £15, variable cost £9, fixed costs £18,000. What is the break-even sales revenue?
questions.rationale: Contribution per unit £6. Break-even units 3,000. 3,000 × £15 = £45,000.

questions.stem: Fixed costs £30,000, contribution £10 per unit. To make a profit of £20,000 how many units must be sold?
Which of these will increase the break-even point?
options: A rise in the selling price
A rise in contribution per unit
questions.rationale: More fixed costs require more contribution.

questions.stem: The margin of safety is:
options: Break-even sales minus actual or budgeted sales
Actual or budgeted sales minus break-even sales
questions.rationale: It shows how far sales can fall before a loss is made.

questions.stem: Contribution to sales ratio is 30%. Fixed costs are £45,000. Budgeted sales are £200,000. What is the margin of safety in £?
A break-even chart assumes:
options: Changing selling prices at different volumes
No fixed costs at any level of activity
Constant selling price and variable cost per unit
A mix of different products at different margins
questions.rationale: Simplifying assumptions make the analysis workable.

questions.stem: Budgeted sales are 4,000 units. Closing inventory target is 500 and opening inventory is 800. What is the production budget?
Each unit uses 2 hours of labour. Production is 3,700 units. How many labour hours are needed?
Labour hours required are 7,400 at £12 per hour. 5% of hours are lost to idle time that is paid for. What is the budgeted labour cost?
A master budget consists of:
options: Only the production budget for the period
Only the sales budget for the period
Only the cash budget for the period
The budgeted income statement, balance sheet and cash budget
questions.rationale: It consolidates all the functional budgets.

questions.stem: A budget committee typically:
options: Prepares the tax returns of the business
Audits the accounts at the year end
Records the transactions of the business
questions.rationale: It makes sure functional budgets are consistent.

questions.stem: A cash budget shows opening cash £5,000, receipts £28,000 and payments £36,500. What is the closing cash, and what does it signal?
Which of the following would not appear in a cash budget?
questions.rationale: Depreciation is non-cash.

questions.stem: A fixed budget is:
options: Always accurate whatever the activity level
Always adjusted for changes in activity
Prepared after the end of the period
Prepared for one level of activity and not adjusted
questions.rationale: Fixed budgets are poor for control when activity differs from plan.

questions.stem: A budget has variable costs of £5 per unit and fixed costs of £20,000 for 4,000 units. What would be the flexed budget for 5,000 units?
Standard cost £8 per unit, actual cost £8.40 per unit for 2,500 units. What is the total cost variance?
Standard direct material price £4 per kg. 2,000 kg bought for £7,600. What is the price variance?
questions.rationale: Standard cost £8,000 against actual £7,600 gives £400 favourable.

questions.stem: Standard usage is 2.5 kg per unit. 1,000 units were made using 2,600 kg at a standard price of £4. What is the usage variance?
questions.rationale: Standard usage 2,500 kg. Actual 2,600 kg. 100 kg × £4 = £400 adverse.

questions.stem: Sales: budget 800 units at £50. Actual 760 units at £52. What is the sales volume variance in revenue terms?
questions.rationale: (760 − 800) × £50 = £2,000 adverse. The price variance is (£52 − £50) × 760 = £1,520 favourable.

questions.stem: A favourable material price variance combined with an adverse usage variance might suggest:
options: Staff were more efficient than expected
Material prices rose during the period
questions.rationale: A low price may cause more waste.

questions.stem: Standard hours for actual output were 1,200 at £10. Actual hours worked were 1,260 and paid £12,978. What is the total labour variance?
questions.rationale: Standard cost = 1,200 × £10 = £12,000. Actual £12,978. Variance £978 adverse.

questions.stem: A variance report should be sent to:
options: Competitors who want to compare performance
The manager responsible for the area
HMRC as part of the tax return
questions.rationale: Responsibility accounting links variances to people who can act.

questions.stem: An adverse variance reduces:
questions.rationale: Adverse means worse than standard for profit.

questions.stem: A product has sales of £50,000, variable costs £30,000 and avoidable fixed costs £15,000. Should it be discontinued?
options: Yes, because it makes a loss on sales less variable costs
Yes, because the variable costs are too high
No, because it contributes £20,000 to profit after all costs
No, it contributes £5,000 after avoidable costs
questions.rationale: Contribution £20,000 less avoidable fixed £15,000 = £5,000 net benefit.

questions.stem: Which cost is irrelevant in deciding whether to accept a special order?
options: Existing fixed overhead that is not affected
Extra materials needed for the order
Extra delivery costs caused by the order
Extra labour needed for the order
questions.rationale: Only incremental costs matter.

questions.stem: A company has 3,000 machine hours and two products. A: contribution £20 per unit, 2 hours. B: contribution £18 per unit, 1.5 hours. Which gives the greater total contribution if all hours are used on one product?
questions.rationale: A earns £10 per hour (£30,000). B earns £12 per hour (£36,000).

questions.stem: A decision to make or buy should ignore:
questions.rationale: Costs that continue whichever choice is made are irrelevant.

questions.stem: Gross profit margin is 35% and revenue is £400,000. What is gross profit?
Net profit £30,000 on revenue £400,000. What is the net profit margin?
Sales per employee is a measure of:
questions.rationale: It relates output to a resource.

questions.stem: A business wants to improve gross margin from 30% to 35% on revenue of £100,000. What is the extra gross profit needed?
Which is a non-financial performance measure?
questions.rationale: Non-financial measures address service, quality and time.

questions.stem: A product has selling price £40, direct materials £12, direct labour £10 and variable overhead £4 per unit. What is the contribution per unit?
Sales are 6,000 units at £25. Variable cost is £15 per unit and fixed costs are £42,000. What is the profit?

Under absorption costing, closing inventory is valued at £9 per unit including fixed overhead of £3. 500 units are in closing inventory. What is the amount of fixed overhead deferred to the next period?
Which method of costing is better for short-term decisions such as accepting a special order?
questions.rationale: Marginal costing highlights contribution.

questions.stem: Fixed costs £36,000, selling price £18, variable cost £10. What is the break-even point in units?
