questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a sales ledger control account?
options: To record the VAT payable to HMRC each quarter
To check the accuracy of the individual customer accounts
To record the cash sales made by the business
To calculate the profit for the accounting period
questions.rationale: The control account total should agree to the sum of the individual receivables balances. Differences signal an error.

questions.stem: Which item is shown on the debit side of a sales ledger control account?
questions.rationale: Credit sales (gross, including VAT) increase receivables and are debited. Receipts, returns and write-offs are credits.

questions.stem: Opening receivables £14,500. Credit sales £62,000, cash received £58,300, sales returns £1,800. What is the closing balance on the sales ledger control account?
Opening payables £9,200. Credit purchases £41,000, payments to suppliers £39,500, discounts received £600, purchase returns £1,100. What is the closing payables control balance?
A sales ledger control account balance is £23,410 and the list of customer balances totals £23,140. What is the likely cause?
options: Customers have overpaid and are owed a refund
The control account is always right so no action is needed
An error in the control account or a customer account that must be investigated
VAT has been omitted from the list of customer balances
questions.rationale: A difference between the control account and the list of balances indicates an error that must be found.

questions.stem: Which item would appear on the credit side of a purchases ledger control account?
questions.rationale: Payables is a liability. Credit purchases increase it, so they are credited.

questions.stem: A contra entry of £400 is made between a customer who is also a supplier. What is the entry in the control accounts?
options: Debit cash £400, credit sales ledger control £400
Debit purchases ledger control £400, credit sales ledger control £400
No entry is needed in the control accounts
Debit sales ledger control £400, credit purchases ledger control £400
questions.rationale: The contra reduces both what the customer owes and what is owed to the same business as a supplier.

questions.stem: Control accounts are part of which ledger?
questions.rationale: Control accounts are kept in the general (main) ledger; the individual accounts are in the subsidiary ledgers.

questions.stem: A journal entry is used to record:
options: All cash sales made in the period
The daily petty cash payments to staff
Every credit sale made to customers
questions.rationale: The journal records transactions for which there is no other book of prime entry, such as correction of errors.

questions.stem: Which journal entry correctly writes off an irrecoverable debt of £200 plus VAT of £40 (VAT relief is available)?
options: Debit irrecoverable debts £200, debit VAT £40, credit receivables £240
questions.rationale: The expense is the net £200, VAT output tax is recovered by debiting the VAT account, and the receivable falls by £240.

questions.stem: A business buys a computer for £1,500 on credit from a supplier (ignore VAT). Which journal entry is correct?
questions.rationale: A non-current asset bought on credit is debited to the asset account. It is not recorded as purchases.

questions.stem: Why must every journal entry include a narrative?
options: To explain the reason for the entry and give an audit trail
To make sure the entry balances arithmetically
Because VAT regulations say it is required
To increase the value of the debit entry
questions.rationale: A narrative explains why the entry was made so it can be reviewed and traced.

questions.stem: A business owner transfers a personal car valued at £6,000 to the business as capital. Which journal entry is correct?
questions.rationale: The business gains an asset (debit) and the owner's capital increases (credit).

questions.stem: A business has previously posted the purchase of a non-current asset costing £3,000 to the purchases account. What is the correcting journal?
questions.rationale: Remove the cost from purchases (credit) and record it where it belongs, in non-current assets (debit).

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a bank reconciliation?
options: To record the sales made on credit terms
To calculate the profit for the period
To explain differences between the cash book and the bank statement
To check the accuracy of the VAT return
questions.rationale: It reconciles the business's own record of the bank balance to the bank's record.

questions.stem: Which of these would cause a difference between the cash book and the bank statement because of timing?
options: A direct debit not yet recorded
questions.rationale: Unpresented cheques have been written and entered in the cash book but not yet cleared by the bank. Other items are bank entries to be added to the cash book.

questions.stem: A cash book shows £5,300 debit. Bank charges of £45 and a direct debit of £120 appear on the statement but not in the cash book. What is the adjusted cash book balance?
A bank statement shows a balance of £8,150. There are unpresented cheques of £1,200 and outstanding lodgements of £900. What is the correct cash book balance?
A cash book balance after adjustments is £12,400. Unpresented cheques total £2,100 and outstanding lodgements are £1,350. What should the bank statement balance be?
A customer's standing order of £350 appears on the bank statement but is not in the cash book. What is the correct adjustment?
options: Debit sales ledger control £350, credit bank £350
Debit bank £350, credit sales ledger control £350
questions.rationale: Cash received increases the bank balance and reduces the amount owed by the customer.

questions.stem: A cheque for £540 paid to a supplier was entered in the cash book as £450. What is the adjustment to the cash book?
questions.rationale: A transposition error: the payment was understated by £90, so the cash book balance is overstated and must reduce.

questions.stem: A deposit recorded in the cash book but not yet shown on the bank statement is called:
questions.rationale: Receipts banked recently may not yet be credited by the bank.

questions.stem: A bank statement shows interest received of £18 which is not in the cash book. How is it recorded?
questions.rationale: Interest received increases bank and is income to the business.

questions.stem: A suspense account is used to:
options: Hold a temporary balance until errors are found and corrected
Record the permanent drawings of the owner
Hold the petty cash float for small payments
Record the VAT due to or from HMRC
questions.rationale: A suspense account holds the difference when the trial balance does not balance, until the cause is found.

questions.stem: A trial balance has credits of £500 more than debits. What entry is made to the suspense account?
questions.rationale: A debit is needed to make total debits equal credits.

questions.stem: Which error would NOT be revealed by a trial balance?
questions.rationale: A transaction omitted completely from the ledgers leaves debits and credits equal, so the trial balance still balances.

questions.stem: Rent paid of £800 was debited to the rates account. What type of error is this?
questions.rationale: Posted to the wrong account within the same class (expenses), so the trial balance still balances.

questions.stem: The purchase of a van was debited to the motor expenses account. What type of error is this?
questions.rationale: A non-current asset was treated as an expense, breaking an accounting principle (capital versus revenue).

questions.stem: Sales were recorded as £6,200 in the day book but the invoice total was £6,020. Both sides of the ledger were posted from the day book total. What type of error is this?
options: Transposition error in the trial balance only
questions.rationale: The wrong figure was entered in the original book and carried through both sides, so the trial balance still balances.

questions.stem: An error of £400 in debits was offset by a separate error of £400 in credits. This is known as:
questions.rationale: Two independent errors of equal and opposite size cancel out in the trial balance.

questions.stem: Discount allowed of £150 was wrongly debited to the discount received account instead of the discount allowed account. What is the correcting journal?
options: Debit discount allowed £150, credit discount received £150
Debit discount received £150, credit discount allowed £150
Debit discount allowed £300, credit discount received £300
questions.rationale: Reverse the wrong debit with a credit to discount received, and make the correct debit to discount allowed.

questions.stem: The trial balance does not balance. Debits exceed credits by £90. A suspense account is opened. Which entry is made?
questions.rationale: A credit of £90 to suspense makes total credits equal total debits.

questions.stem: Which deduction from an employee's gross pay is paid to HMRC and also based on earnings?
questions.rationale: PAYE income tax is deducted from pay and paid over to HMRC by the employer.

questions.stem: An employee has gross pay of £2,400. Income tax is £320, employee NIC is £150 and pension is £96. What is the net pay?
Which payroll cost is an expense of the employer, not deducted from the employee's pay?
options: Employee's National Insurance deducted from pay
Employee's own pension contribution from their wages
Employee's income tax collected through PAYE
questions.rationale: Employer NIC is an additional cost to the business on top of gross pay.

questions.stem: Gross wages £10,000. Employee deductions: tax £1,800, NIC £700, pension £400. Employer NIC £1,200. What is the total wages expense to the business?
questions.rationale: Employee deductions are part of gross pay. The expense = gross wages £10,000 + employer NIC £1,200 = £11,200.

questions.stem: Gross wages of £6,000 are paid. Net pay of £4,700 is paid to staff. Which account is credited with the liability to HMRC for tax and NIC?
options: Drawings account of the business owner
Bank account used to pay the net wages
Wages expense account in the statement of profit or loss
questions.rationale: The amounts deducted but not yet paid to HMRC are held as a liability until paid.

questions.stem: Which document does an employee receive each pay period showing gross pay, deductions and net pay?
questions.rationale: A payslip is issued each pay period. A P60 is the annual summary; a P45 is issued when someone leaves.

questions.stem: A P45 is issued to an employee:
options: At the end of the tax year
When they join the pension scheme
questions.rationale: A P45 records pay and tax to the leaving date and is given to the employee when employment ends.

questions.stem: Which action best separates duties to reduce the risk of fraud in the purchases system?
options: Different people order, receive and approve invoices for payment
Only the owner checks the bank statement
The same person raises orders and approves payment
Suppliers are paid without checking delivery
questions.rationale: Segregation of duties makes it harder for one person to commit and conceal fraud.

questions.stem: A business uses a goods received note (GRN). What does it confirm?
options: That a customer has placed an order for goods
Goods have been delivered and received
That the price on the invoice is correct
That the supplier has been paid for the goods
questions.rationale: A GRN is created on receipt of goods and is matched to the order and invoice before payment.

questions.stem: Checking a supplier invoice to the purchase order and goods received note before payment is called:
questions.rationale: Matching the order, GRN and invoice confirms that what was ordered was received and billed correctly.

questions.stem: Why are staff given passwords to access the accounting system?
options: To restrict access to authorised users only
To reduce the VAT payable by the business
To increase the sales made to customers
To speed up the posting of transactions
questions.rationale: Access controls help protect data and prevent unauthorised changes.

questions.stem: Which item would NOT appear in a sales ledger control account?
questions.rationale: Purchases relate to the purchases ledger control account.

questions.stem: Opening receivables £8,000; credit sales £30,000; receipts £27,500; discounts allowed £500. What is the closing balance?

The receivables control account balance is £12,640 but the list of customer balances totals £12,400. A sales invoice for £240 was entered in the sales day book but not posted to the customer's account. What is the correction?
questions.rationale: The control account is right because it was posted from the day book total. The individual account is missing a debit of £240.

questions.stem: Why is a control account useful?
options: It records the small payments made from petty cash
It replaces the need to prepare a trial balance
It calculates the depreciation on non-current assets
It helps locate errors in the ledger and deters fraud
questions.rationale: Control accounts provide an independent check on the subsidiary ledger.

questions.stem: Opening payables £12,500; credit purchases £48,000; payments £46,000; purchase returns £2,500. What is the closing balance?
In the purchases ledger control account, the cash book payments to suppliers are:
options: Posted to the sales ledger control
questions.rationale: Payments reduce the liability, so they are debited.

questions.stem: A contra of £700 is processed between a customer and supplier account but the entry in the purchases ledger control account was omitted. What is the effect?
options: The sales ledger control account will be understated
There will be no difference between the two figures
The purchases ledger control account will be £700 higher than the list of balances
The control account will be £700 lower than the list of balances
questions.rationale: The individual account was reduced but the control account was not, so the control account is overstated relative to the list.

questions.stem: A sales ledger control account is also called:
questions.rationale: The terms sales ledger and receivables ledger are interchangeable.

questions.stem: The owner withdraws £500 of inventory for personal use. Which journal entry is correct?
questions.rationale: Goods taken are a drawing and the cost is removed from purchases.

questions.stem: Which journal entry records the introduction of £10,000 capital by the owner into the business bank account?
questions.rationale: Bank increases (debit) and the owner's capital increases (credit).

questions.stem: A business writes off an irrecoverable debt of £360 including VAT of £60 (VAT relief claimed). Which statement is correct?
options: Debit irrecoverable debts £300, debit VAT £60, credit receivables £360
questions.rationale: The expense is the net amount. The VAT is recovered through the VAT account.

questions.stem: A journal opens a new business: debit bank £8,000, debit equipment £4,000, credit loan £3,000 and credit capital. What is the credit to capital?
questions.rationale: Debits £12,000 must equal credits. Capital = £12,000 − £3,000 = £9,000.

questions.stem: A journal entry corrects an error where £250 of rent was debited to insurance. Which entry is correct?
questions.rationale: The wrong debit to insurance is reversed (credit) and the correct debit to rent is made.

questions.stem: Which of these must be authorised before a journal is posted?
options: Routine totals from the sales day book
Cash sales recorded in the till each day
Journals correcting errors or adjusting accounts
Bank statements received from the bank
questions.rationale: Journals are open to misuse so they require authorisation and a clear narrative.

questions.stem: The cash book shows a bank balance of £2,400 debit. A dishonoured cheque of £300 from a customer appears on the bank statement. What is the updated cash book balance?
questions.rationale: A dishonoured cheque reverses the receipt: £2,400 − £300 = £2,100.

questions.stem: Cash book balance £6,800. Bank statement shows standing order received £400 (not in cash book), bank charges £35 (not in cash book) and an unpresented cheque of £500. What is the bank statement balance?
questions.rationale: Adjusted cash book = £6,800 + £400 − £35 = £7,165. Add back unpresented cheque £500 to get the statement balance £7,665.

questions.stem: Which of these is a reconciling item that requires NO adjustment to the cash book?
questions.rationale: Timing differences correct themselves when the bank processes them.

questions.stem: A bank statement shows an overdrawn balance of £1,200. There is an outstanding lodgement of £800. What is the cash book balance?
questions.rationale: −£1,200 + £800 = −£400, an overdraft in the cash book.

questions.stem: Why is a bank reconciliation performed regularly?
options: To check for errors and unauthorised transactions
To increase the level of sales made
To reduce the amount of tax payable
To record the depreciation of equipment
questions.rationale: It helps detect fraud and errors on either record.

questions.stem: A cash book balance is £4,500. A direct debit of £90 was recorded in the cash book as £9. What is the corrected cash book balance?
questions.rationale: The payment was understated by £81, so the balance falls from £4,500 to £4,419.

questions.stem: A sale of £150 was entered in the day book but never posted to either ledger. Which type of error is this?
questions.rationale: The transaction was left out entirely, so the trial balance still balances.

questions.stem: A cheque for £400 was entered in the cash book as £40 and in the ledger account as £40. What type of error is this?
questions.rationale: The wrong figure was used in the original record and carried through.

questions.stem: A cash receipt of £600 from a customer was debited to the sales ledger control and credited to the bank. What type of error is this?
questions.rationale: The debit and credit sides were swapped. Correction requires twice the amount.

questions.stem: What is the journal to correct a receipt of £600 that was reversed (debit receivables, credit bank)?
questions.rationale: The wrong entry must be cancelled (£600) and the right one made (£600), so £1,200.

questions.stem: A purchase invoice of £340 was posted to the wrong supplier's account. What is the effect on the purchases ledger control account?
questions.rationale: The total of the control account is correct. Only two individual accounts are wrong.

questions.stem: Which of the following errors would be corrected without using a suspense account?
options: A transposition error posted to one side
One side of a journal omitted
Rent debited to the wrong expense account
questions.rationale: A suspense account is only needed when one side of the entry is wrong or missing.

questions.stem: An employee earns £2,000 gross. Employee pension is 5% and income tax is £260. NIC is £120. What is the net pay?
Which of these is paid by the employer in addition to wages?
questions.rationale: Employer NIC is an extra cost to the business.

questions.stem: Overtime is paid at time-and-a-quarter and the basic hourly rate is £16. What is the overtime rate?
A salaried employee earns £30,000 a year paid monthly. What is the monthly gross pay?
Payroll entries: gross wages £5,000, employee deductions £1,100, employer NIC £400. What is the credit to bank when net pay is paid?
Why must payroll records be kept confidential?
options: To reduce the wages paid to employees
To avoid the business paying employer NIC
They contain personal and sensitive data
To increase the tax collected by HMRC
questions.rationale: Data protection law requires personal data to be kept secure.

questions.stem: Which of these is a control over cash receipts?
options: Banking all receipts intact and promptly
Allowing one person to count and bank
questions.rationale: Intact banking prevents misuse and creates an audit trail.

questions.stem: A purchase order should be authorised by:
options: Any employee who needs the goods quickly
A manager with the appropriate authority
The supplier who will deliver the goods
The customer who ordered the finished product
questions.rationale: Authorisation limits reduce unauthorised spending.

questions.stem: A control that restricts who can view or change data in the accounting system is a:
questions.rationale: Access controls use user IDs and passwords.

questions.stem: Regularly backing up accounting data helps with:
options: Reducing the VAT payable on each return
Speeding up the sales made to customers
Recovery after data loss or corruption
Increasing the profit earned by the business
questions.rationale: Backups protect against failure, theft and ransomware.

questions.stem: Prenumbered documents such as invoices help to:
options: Avoid the need to issue credit notes
Reduce the amount of VAT charged to customers
Speed up the payment received from customers
Make sure all documents are accounted for
questions.rationale: Gaps in the sequence are easy to spot.

questions.stem: A purchases ledger control account is credited with credit purchases of £30,000 and debited with payments of £27,000 and returns of £1,500. Opening balance was £6,000 credit. What is the closing balance?
Receipts from customers of £18,000 are posted to the sales ledger control account as:
questions.rationale: Cash received reduces receivables, so the control account is credited.

questions.stem: The sales ledger control account is overstated by £300 because a credit note was posted to the wrong side. What should be done?
options: Correct the control account and investigate the individual accounts
questions.rationale: A posting error should be traced and corrected so that the control account and ledger agree.

questions.stem: Which entry would be made in the sales ledger control account for bad debts written off of £500?
questions.rationale: The receivable is removed, so receivables control is credited.

questions.stem: Discount allowed to customers of £220 is recorded in the sales ledger control account as:
questions.rationale: Discounts allowed reduce the amount owed by customers.

questions.stem: A list of all customers' balances is called:
questions.rationale: It is reconciled to the sales ledger control account.

questions.stem: An asset costing £4,500 is bought on credit from a supplier but wrongly recorded in purchases. What is the correcting journal?
questions.rationale: Move the cost out of purchases and into the asset account.

questions.stem: A business writes off an obsolete asset with a net book value of £700. What is the journal?
options: Debit loss on disposal £700, credit asset £700
Debit asset £700, credit loss on disposal £700
questions.rationale: The asset is removed and the loss is an expense.

questions.stem: The owner takes a business laptop worth £800 for personal use. What is the journal?
questions.rationale: An asset is withdrawn by the owner, reducing capital through drawings.

questions.stem: Opening journal entries for a new business include which of the following?
options: Debit assets, credit liabilities and capital
questions.rationale: The accounting equation is established with assets as debits and liabilities and capital as credits.

questions.stem: A journal entry should be supported by:
options: A narrative and authorisation, plus source documents where possible
questions.rationale: This provides an audit trail.

questions.stem: A bank statement balance is £5,400 credit (in funds). Unpresented cheques are £1,100 and outstanding lodgements £600. What is the cash book balance?
A cash book is £2,300 in funds. Bank interest of £40 appears on the statement only. What is the corrected cash book balance?
questions.rationale: Interest received increases the balance.

questions.stem: A dishonoured cheque from a customer of £250 is recorded in the cash book as:
questions.rationale: The earlier receipt is reversed on the credit side of the cash book.

questions.stem: A cash book balance of £3,000 does not agree to the statement balance of £3,450. Unpresented cheques are £700 and a bank error charged £250 incorrectly. Which statement is correct?
options: The cash book is correct once the unpresented cheques and the bank error are considered
questions.rationale: £3,450 − £700 + £250 = £3,000. The reconciliation agrees to the cash book.

questions.stem: A bank statement shows a direct debit for insurance not in the cash book. What should the business do?
options: Contact the bank to remove it
Record it in the cash book
questions.rationale: The business has a payment not yet recorded.

questions.stem: Why might the bank statement show a higher balance than the cash book?
options: A customer's cheque was dishonoured by the bank
Bank charges are on the statement but not the cash book
Unpresented cheques have been entered in the cash book but not yet cleared
Outstanding lodgements are in the cash book but not yet credited
questions.rationale: Cheques already deducted in the cash book have not yet left the bank account, so the statement balance is higher.

questions.stem: Which type of error occurs when a transaction is entered in the wrong account of a different class, such as wages in the asset account?
questions.rationale: The principle of classification is breached.

questions.stem: The sales day book total was overstated by £100. What is the effect on the trial balance?
options: It still balances if both sides were posted from the total
questions.rationale: Both the debit to receivables and the credit to sales would be overstated.

questions.stem: A debit of £150 was posted to the correct account twice and there was no matching credit. What is the effect on the trial balance?
questions.rationale: An extra debit has been posted with no matching credit.

questions.stem: Suspense account has a credit balance of £480. It is caused by a purchases invoice of £480 not posted to the supplier's ledger. Which entry clears suspense?
questions.rationale: The missing credit is recorded in the supplier account and the suspense debit clears the balance.

questions.stem: An error of commission would:
options: Not affect the trial balance totals
questions.rationale: The amount is posted to the wrong account but on the correct side.

questions.stem: An employee receives net pay of £1,650 after deductions of £450. What is the gross pay?
What is a payslip?
options: A document showing gross pay, deductions and net pay
questions.rationale: Employers must give each employee a payslip.

questions.stem: Which of these is paid by the employer to HMRC but is NOT a deduction from the employee's pay?
questions.rationale: It is an additional cost to the employer.

questions.stem: A company pays gross wages of £12,000. Employer NIC is £1,400. What is the total employment cost?
Gross pay £2,500, income tax £380, NIC £190, pension (employee) £125, and employer pension £100. What is the net pay?
questions.rationale: £2,500 − £380 − £190 − £125 = £1,805. Employer pension is not deducted.

questions.stem: Why should a person who authorises payments not also be able to set up new suppliers?
options: To reduce the risk of fraud by splitting incompatible duties
questions.rationale: Segregation lowers the chance of fictitious suppliers.

questions.stem: A bank reconciliation is a:
questions.rationale: It identifies differences after they have occurred.

questions.stem: A strong password policy is an example of:
questions.rationale: It stops unauthorised use of systems.

questions.stem: Which control would stop a purchase being made without approval?
options: Requiring a signed purchase order from an authorised person
questions.rationale: Authorisation before ordering is a preventive control.

questions.stem: A sales ledger control account has opening balance £22,000 debit. Credit sales £75,000, receipts £70,000, sales returns £3,000, bad debts written off £1,000. What is the closing balance?

The sum of customer balances is £14,230 and the control account balance is £14,330. A £100 cheque from a customer was posted to the customer's account but not to the control account. What should be done?
questions.rationale: The receipt reduces what customers owe. The control account is overstated by £100.

questions.stem: A contra entry is recorded when:
options: The same party is both a customer and a supplier and balances are offset
A supplier is paid by BACS
questions.rationale: Offsetting reduces both receivables and payables.

questions.stem: Which of these is recorded in a purchases ledger control account as a debit?
questions.rationale: Payments reduce the liability.

questions.stem: A control account is useful because it:
options: Gives a total balance that can be checked against the ledger listings
questions.rationale: It supports error detection.

questions.stem: The owner introduces £2,000 of his own computer equipment. What is the journal?
questions.rationale: The business receives an asset and capital increases.

questions.stem: Which of these transactions would normally NOT need a journal entry?
options: A credit sale of goods to a customer
Opening balances for a new business
questions.rationale: Routine credit sales are recorded in the sales day book.

questions.stem: A journal writes off an obsolete machine with cost £5,000 and accumulated depreciation £4,000. What is the journal?
options: Debit accumulated depreciation £4,000, debit loss on disposal £1,000, credit machinery cost £5,000
questions.rationale: Remove cost and depreciation. The NBV £1,000 is a loss.

questions.stem: The cash book shows £1,500 in funds. The statement shows a charge of £30 and a credit transfer from a customer of £200 not in the cash book. What is the adjusted cash book balance?
A cheque for £75 paid to a supplier has not appeared on the bank statement. It is:
questions.rationale: The supplier has not yet banked it.

questions.stem: A customer's cheque of £500 has been paid in but not yet credited by the bank. It is:
questions.rationale: It is in the cash book but not on the statement.

questions.stem: Cash book balance £2,200. Adjustments: bank charges £25, direct debit £140 and a standing order from a customer £90 are not in the cash book. What is the corrected balance?
A bank reconciliation statement starts with the:
questions.rationale: It reconciles to the cash book balance.

questions.stem: An error of omission means:
options: A transaction is left out of the records altogether
questions.rationale: Both debit and credit are missing.

questions.stem: Which of these will cause the trial balance to be out of balance?
options: A cost posted to the wrong expense account
A debit entry posted twice with no corresponding credit
A sale recorded as a purchase
questions.rationale: Only one-sided errors cause imbalance.

questions.stem: A suspense account balance should be:
options: Cleared as soon as the errors are identified
questions.rationale: Suspense is a temporary account.

questions.stem: A transposition error occurs when:
options: Digits are swapped, such as £540 recorded as £450
questions.rationale: The difference is divisible by 9.

questions.stem: An employee works 40 hours at £12 and 5 hours at time-and-a-half. What is the gross pay?
Net pay is the amount:
options: Paid to the employee after deductions
questions.rationale: Gross pay less deductions.

questions.stem: Employer NIC is £320, employee NIC £200, PAYE £450 and pension (employee) £100 for the month. How much must be paid to HMRC?
questions.rationale: PAYE £450 + employee NIC £200 + employer NIC £320 = £970. The pension goes to the scheme.

questions.stem: Which document is given to an employee at the end of the tax year?
questions.rationale: It summarises pay and tax for the year.

questions.stem: A manager reviews and approves each invoice before payment. This is:
questions.rationale: Approval prevents unauthorised payments.

questions.stem: Locking the stockroom is an example of:
questions.rationale: It prevents theft.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a benefit of regular training for accounting staff?
questions.rationale: Competent staff reduce risk.

questions.stem: Which rate of VAT applies to most goods and services in the UK?
questions.rationale: The standard rate is 20%. The reduced rate is 5% and some items are zero-rated.

questions.stem: Which of the following is normally zero-rated for VAT in the UK?
options: Most food for human consumption (not restaurant meals)
questions.rationale: Most basic food is zero-rated. The business can still reclaim input VAT on its costs.

questions.stem: What is the difference between zero-rated and exempt supplies?
options: A business making zero-rated supplies can reclaim input VAT, but one making only exempt supplies generally cannot
There is no difference between them for VAT purposes
Zero-rated supplies do not have to be recorded
Exempt supplies are taxed at the reduced rate of 5%
questions.rationale: Zero-rated supplies are taxable at 0% so the business can recover input VAT. Exempt supplies are outside the VAT charge and input VAT is usually not recoverable.

questions.stem: A business must register for VAT if its taxable turnover in the last 12 months exceeds the registration threshold. What is the UK threshold from 1 April 2024?
questions.rationale: The threshold rose from £85,000 to £90,000 on 1 April 2024. A business can also register voluntarily.

questions.stem: A business must notify HMRC of the need to register for VAT within:
options: The end of the tax year in which it is exceeded
30 days of the end of the month in which the threshold was exceeded
questions.rationale: Registration must be notified within 30 days of the end of the month the threshold was exceeded.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a requirement of a valid VAT invoice?
questions.rationale: A VAT invoice must show the supplier's VAT number, date, description, amounts and VAT rate.

questions.stem: A business sells goods for £1,000 plus VAT at 20%. The customer is offered a 4% prompt payment discount. If the customer takes the discount, what is the VAT?
A business buys a car for use by the owner for business and private use. Can input VAT be reclaimed?
options: Yes, but only 50% of the VAT can be reclaimed
Generally not, VAT on cars with private use is blocked
Only if the car cost more than £20,000
Yes, all of the VAT can be reclaimed
questions.rationale: VAT on the purchase of a car is generally blocked where there is any private use.

questions.stem: A business is VAT registered and entertains UK customers at a cost of £500 plus VAT of £100. What is the VAT treatment?
options: Input VAT of £100 can be reclaimed
Input VAT of £100 cannot be reclaimed
questions.rationale: Input VAT on business entertainment of UK customers is blocked.

questions.stem: VAT returns are normally submitted:
questions.rationale: Most businesses file VAT returns every quarter, and must file online.

questions.stem: A VAT quarter has output VAT of £14,000 and input VAT of £9,500. What is the VAT payable?
A VAT return shows a net amount payable of £3,200 for the quarter ended 31 December. By when must the return and payment normally be made (electronic payment)?
options: 7 February (one month and seven days after the quarter end)
questions.rationale: Online returns and payments are due one month and 7 days after the end of the period.

questions.stem: Which box of the VAT return shows total sales excluding VAT?
questions.rationale: Box 1 is VAT due on sales, Box 4 is VAT reclaimed on purchases, Box 6 is total sales ex VAT and Box 7 is total purchases ex VAT.

questions.stem: Which box of the VAT return shows the VAT reclaimed on purchases?
questions.rationale: Box 4 is VAT reclaimed on purchases and other inputs.

questions.stem: In a VAT return, Box 3 is £16,000 and Box 4 is £11,000. What is Box 5?
questions.rationale: Box 5 is the net amount: Box 3 (total VAT due) minus Box 4 (VAT reclaimed) = £5,000.

questions.stem: A business discovers it understated output VAT by £1,500 in the last return. What can it do?
options: Ignore it permanently as it is a small amount
Resubmit all returns for the last 4 years
Correct it on the next VAT return if the net error is below the reporting limit
Deduct the amount from the payroll payment
questions.rationale: Net errors up to £10,000 (or 1% of Box 6 up to £50,000) can be corrected on the next return.

questions.stem: Which VAT penalty approach applies where a return or payment is late (points system)?
options: An immediate penalty of 100% of the VAT due
A custodial sentence for any late submission
No penalty is applied until the third late return
A point is awarded for each late return, with a financial penalty once the threshold is reached
questions.rationale: HMRC's points-based penalty applies to late submissions, and late payment attracts interest and penalties.

questions.stem: Under cash accounting for VAT, output VAT is accounted for when:
options: The goods are ordered by the customer
The invoice is issued to the customer
The end of the accounting year is reached
Payment is received from the customer
questions.rationale: Cash accounting ties VAT to the receipt and payment of cash, helping with cash flow and bad debts.

questions.stem: What is a main benefit of cash accounting?
options: The business can claim a higher amount of input VAT
VAT is paid to HMRC earlier than normal
The business files fewer returns each year
Automatic VAT relief for irrecoverable debts
questions.rationale: VAT is only due once the customer pays, so an unpaid debt carries no VAT cost.

questions.stem: Under the flat rate scheme, VAT payable is calculated as:
options: A fixed percentage of VAT-inclusive turnover
Output VAT minus input VAT for the period
A percentage of the purchases for the period
20% of the profit for the period
questions.rationale: A fixed rate set by HMRC for the trade sector is applied to gross turnover. Input VAT is generally not reclaimed.

questions.stem: A business in the flat rate scheme with a flat rate of 10% has VAT-inclusive turnover of £48,000. What VAT is payable?
questions.rationale: 10% × £48,000 = £4,800. The percentage applies to gross (VAT-inclusive) turnover.

questions.stem: Under annual accounting, a business normally:
options: Submits one return a year and makes interim payments
Is exempt from charging VAT on its sales
questions.rationale: Interim payments are made on account and a single annual return is submitted.

questions.stem: What is the VAT treatment of bad debt relief?
options: VAT can be reclaimed after 6 months from the due date if the debt is written off
VAT is reclaimed directly from the customer
VAT can never be reclaimed on a bad debt
VAT can be reclaimed immediately when an invoice is raised
questions.rationale: The debt must be over 6 months old (from the later of payment due date or supply), unpaid and written off.

questions.stem: What does PAYE stand for?
questions.rationale: PAYE is HMRC's system for collecting income tax and NIC from employment income.

questions.stem: Employers must report each payment to employees to HMRC:
options: Once a month, after the payment has been made
On or before the payment date, using Real Time Information (RTI)
Only when tax has been deducted from the payment
At the end of the tax year only
questions.rationale: A Full Payment Submission (FPS) is sent on or before each payday.

questions.stem: Which form shows an employee's total pay and deductions for the whole tax year?
questions.rationale: Employers must give a P60 to each employee at the end of the tax year (by 31 May).

questions.stem: Which form is used to report an employee's taxable benefits in kind, such as a company car?
questions.rationale: Employers report benefits on P11D forms after the tax year and pay Class 1A NIC.

questions.stem: A new employee gives no P45 and has no tax code. What starter information is used to decide the tax code?
options: A payslip from the previous year
questions.rationale: The starter checklist (replacing the old P46) records whether this is their only job and is used to work out the correct code.

questions.stem: A tax code of 1257L normally means:
options: The employee has no personal allowance
Tax is charged at 20% on all pay
An emergency basic rate code is in use
questions.rationale: Dropping the final letter and adding a zero gives the tax-free amount for the year.

questions.stem: An employee has gross pay of £3,000 per month. The monthly free pay under their tax code is £1,047.50. Tax is 20% on the next £3,141.67 of monthly taxable pay. What is the income tax?
Employer's NIC is paid by:
options: HMRC on behalf of the employer
The employee out of their net pay
The pension provider on behalf of the employee
The employer on top of the employee's gross pay
questions.rationale: It is a business cost on earnings above the secondary threshold.

questions.stem: An employee earns £2,000 in the month and the employer pays 15% employer NIC above £417 (monthly secondary threshold). What is the employer's NIC?
An employee has gross pay £2,400. Taxable pay for tax is £1,500 at 20% and NIC is 8% on £1,200 of earnings subject to NIC. What are the total deductions for income tax and NIC?
Which of these is a statutory payment made by an employer that can be partially reclaimed from the government?
questions.rationale: Employers can recover most statutory payments by reducing PAYE payments to HMRC.

questions.stem: PAYE and NIC deducted from employees (plus employer NIC) are usually paid to HMRC by:
options: The 1st day of the tax year
The end of the tax year only
The 5th of the same month in which wages are paid
The 22nd of the following month (electronic payment)
questions.rationale: Payments are normally due by the 22nd after the end of the tax month when paid electronically.

questions.stem: Under auto-enrolment, which statement is correct?
options: Employees cannot opt out once they are enrolled
Eligible employees must be automatically enrolled in a workplace pension and can opt out
Employers do not have to make any contribution
Only directors of the company must be enrolled
questions.rationale: Eligible employees must be enrolled, and employers must contribute at least the minimum.

questions.stem: How long must VAT records normally be kept?
questions.rationale: VAT-registered businesses must keep records for 6 years (10 years for some schemes).

questions.stem: Which of these is a benefit of submitting returns and payments on time?
questions.rationale: Late submissions and payments can lead to penalties and interest charges.

questions.stem: Under Making Tax Digital for VAT, VAT-registered businesses must:
options: Keep digital records and submit returns using compatible software
Submit a paper return once each year
Keep their records for a single year only
File a return only when HMRC asks for one
questions.rationale: MTD for VAT applies to all VAT-registered businesses, whatever their turnover.

questions.stem: A careless inaccuracy in a VAT return gives rise to a penalty. What is the maximum penalty percentage of the potential lost revenue for a careless error?
questions.rationale: Careless inaccuracies attract up to 30%. Deliberate but not concealed is up to 70% and deliberate and concealed up to 100%.

questions.stem: A business sells goods for £2,400 including VAT at 20%. What is the VAT?
A supplier invoice shows net £850 and VAT at 20%. What is the total payable?
questions.rationale: VAT £170. Total £1,020.

questions.stem: A sale is £600 net plus VAT at 5%. What is the total?
questions.rationale: VAT £30. Total £630.

questions.stem: Total purchases in a quarter including VAT at 20% are £14,400. All are standard-rated. What is the input VAT?
Standard-rated sales net £60,000, zero-rated sales £10,000, standard-rated purchases net £25,000, all at 20%. What is the VAT payable?
questions.rationale: Output VAT £12,000 (zero-rated has none). Input VAT £5,000. Payable £7,000.

questions.stem: A business has exempt sales only. Which statement is correct?
options: It cannot register for VAT and cannot reclaim input VAT
It can reclaim all of its input VAT
It charges VAT at 20% on its sales
It charges VAT at the zero rate on its sales
questions.rationale: Exempt supplies are outside the VAT system.

questions.stem: A business sells a product for £1,200 net to an overseas customer outside the UK and exports it. What VAT rate usually applies?
questions.rationale: Exports of goods are normally zero-rated with evidence of export.

questions.stem: A credit note for £120 net is issued to a customer. What is the effect on the VAT return (VAT at 20%)?
questions.rationale: A credit note reverses part of the sale and its output VAT.

questions.stem: A business takes advantage of a 10% settlement discount on a £1,000 net invoice with VAT at 20%. What is the VAT on the sale?
questions.rationale: VAT is calculated on the discounted price: £900 × 20% = £180.

questions.stem: Which of the following may VAT-registered businesses reclaim?
options: VAT on goods and services bought for business purposes
VAT on cars used partly for private journeys
VAT on purchases made for private use
VAT on the entertainment of UK clients
questions.rationale: Input VAT is reclaimable only if it relates to business use.

questions.stem: A business deregisters from VAT when its turnover falls below the deregistration threshold. What is the current threshold?
questions.rationale: The deregistration threshold is £88,000 from 1 April 2024.

questions.stem: A business expects turnover over £90,000 in the next 30 days alone. By when must it register?
options: By the end of that 30-day period
There is no requirement to register
After a further 30 days have passed
questions.rationale: The forward-looking test requires registration if turnover is expected to exceed the threshold in the next 30 days.

questions.stem: What is the tax point for a supply of goods usually?
options: The date on which payment is received only
The date of delivery or the date the invoice is issued, whichever is earlier
The last day of the accounting year
The date on which the goods were ordered
questions.rationale: Basic tax point is the delivery date, which an earlier invoice or payment can override.

questions.stem: An invoice is issued 10 days after delivery. When is the tax point (assuming no payment before)?
options: The date the customer placed the order
The delivery date in all cases
Within 14 days after delivery, the invoice date is the tax point
questions.rationale: If an invoice is issued within 14 days of the basic tax point, the invoice date becomes the tax point.

questions.stem: A VAT registration number is issued by:
questions.rationale: HMRC registers businesses for VAT.

questions.stem: Which of these is exempt from VAT?
questions.rationale: Insurance, postal services by Royal Mail and certain finance and education are exempt.

questions.stem: Which of these supplies is zero-rated?
questions.rationale: Children's clothes, most food and books are zero-rated.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT required on a simplified VAT invoice for sales up to £250?
questions.rationale: A less detailed invoice can be issued for small retail supplies.

questions.stem: A VAT-registered business sells services to a VAT-registered business in the UK. Which VAT treatment applies?
options: The supply is exempt from VAT
No VAT is charged as both are registered
VAT is charged at the zero rate
VAT is charged at the standard rate
questions.rationale: UK B2B supplies of standard-rated services attract VAT.

questions.stem: Box 1 of the VAT return shows:
options: VAT due on sales and other outputs
Total value of sales excluding VAT
Total value of purchases excluding VAT
questions.rationale: Box 1 is output VAT.

questions.stem: On a VAT return, the figure for total purchases excluding VAT is entered in:
questions.rationale: Box 7 is total purchases and expenses, excluding VAT.

questions.stem: A business has Box 1 of £18,000 and Box 4 of £21,000. What is Box 5 and what does it mean?
questions.rationale: Box 5 shows the difference. Box 4 exceeds Box 3 so a refund is due.

questions.stem: If a VAT return is submitted late, the business may receive:
options: No consequences if payment is made later
A lower rate of VAT on future sales
A penalty point and possible interest
questions.rationale: Late submissions are managed using a points system.

questions.stem: A VAT return is for the quarter ended 30 June. When is it due (online)?
questions.rationale: One month and 7 days after the period end.

questions.stem: Under the flat rate scheme with a rate of 8% and gross turnover of £60,000, VAT payable is:
Which VAT scheme is most suited to a small business that wants simple calculations and does not buy many goods?
questions.rationale: The flat rate scheme saves record-keeping but input VAT is generally not reclaimed.

questions.stem: Who can use cash accounting for VAT?
options: Businesses with estimated VAT taxable turnover of £1.35 million or less
Only businesses with turnover above £10 million
questions.rationale: The scheme is limited to smaller businesses.

questions.stem: A business using cash accounting makes a sale of £1,200 plus VAT in March but receives payment in May. In which VAT return is the output VAT included?
questions.rationale: Under cash accounting VAT is due when cash is received.

questions.stem: Which of these is a statutory deduction from an employee's pay?
questions.rationale: Statutory deductions are those required by law.

questions.stem: Which of these is a voluntary deduction?
options: Workplace pension contribution (where the employee opts to pay more)
questions.rationale: Voluntary deductions include extra pension and charity giving.

questions.stem: Student loan deductions from pay are collected by:
options: The employer through payroll, then paid to HMRC
The bank where the employee holds an account
The employee paying the loan company directly
Companies House on behalf of HMRC
questions.rationale: Employers deduct repayments based on the employee's plan.

questions.stem: An employee earning £3,500 per month has tax of £450 and NIC of £210 and pays £150 into a pension. What is the net pay?
Which authority must employers report payroll to?
questions.rationale: Employers report pay and deductions to HMRC under RTI.

questions.stem: An FPS (Full Payment Submission) must contain:
options: Only the total payroll cost for the period
Pay and deductions for each employee paid
Only the VAT number of the business
Only the bank details of the employer
questions.rationale: An FPS is submitted every time employees are paid.

questions.stem: An employee's net pay is £1,800. Deductions were tax £320, NIC £140 and pension £90. What was the gross pay?
Which is the employer's obligation when an employee asks for a payslip?
options: To provide a written or electronic payslip on or before payday
To provide it within one year of the request
To refuse the request until the end of the year
To provide it only when asked by HMRC
questions.rationale: Employees have a legal right to an itemised payslip.

questions.stem: A new employee earns £2,000 per month and has the standard tax code. If paid monthly, the monthly free pay is approximately:
Employer's NIC is 15% above £417 per month. A member of staff earns £1,417. What is the employer's NIC?
A P11D reports:
options: Benefits and expenses provided to employees
The VAT due on the business's sales
The corporation tax due for the year
The pay of an employee for the month
questions.rationale: Benefits such as company cars and private medical cover are reported on a P11D.

questions.stem: The tax year for PAYE runs from:
questions.rationale: Employers' payroll records follow the tax year.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best way to reduce the risk of VAT errors?
options: Ignoring the invoices that are difficult to code
Check coding and rates before submitting the return
Estimating every figure on the return
Submitting the return late to allow more time
questions.rationale: Accurate records and reviews reduce errors.

questions.stem: HMRC can inspect VAT records:
options: Only once in the life of the business
Only with an order from a court
Never, as the records are private
At any reasonable time with notice
questions.rationale: Businesses must make records available.

questions.stem: A business deliberately under-declares output VAT to save money. HMRC's maximum penalty rate could be:
options: Nothing, if the VAT is paid later
Up to 100% of the VAT lost
questions.rationale: Deliberate and concealed behaviour attracts the highest penalty band.

questions.stem: A business that wrongly charged VAT on an exempt supply should:
options: Keep the VAT and tell nobody
Charge additional VAT on the next invoice
Ignore the error and keep the VAT collected
Correct the error and issue credit notes as needed
questions.rationale: VAT charged in error must be accounted for or corrected.

questions.stem: Which of these records must be kept for VAT?
options: Sales and purchase invoices and a VAT account
Social media posts about the business
Staff holiday rotas and shift patterns
Marketing plans for the next year
questions.rationale: The VAT account summarises the VAT position.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sensible way to store VAT records?
options: Not stored once the return is filed
In a public folder open to anyone online
Securely, in a form that is easy to retrieve
In a rubbish bin once they are entered
questions.rationale: Records must be retained securely and be accessible.

questions.stem: A customer pays £1,800 including VAT at 20% for services. What is the net value of the sale?
A business buys stationery for £60 plus VAT at 20%. How much input VAT can it reclaim?
Standard-rated sales net £48,000; zero-rated sales £12,000; exempt sales £6,000; all VAT at 20%. What is the output VAT?
questions.rationale: Output VAT arises only on standard-rated sales: £48,000 × 20% = £9,600.

questions.stem: A sale of goods £2,000 net has a 2% settlement discount offered. If the customer takes it, what is the VAT?
An invoice for £750 plus VAT at 5% is issued. What is the total?
The VAT fraction for 5% reduced rate supplies, to find VAT from a gross amount, is:
A business sells to a customer outside the UK and the goods are exported. The VAT rate on the supply is usually:
questions.rationale: Exports are normally zero-rated with proof of export.

questions.stem: Which supplies are outside the scope of VAT?
questions.rationale: Employment income is outside the scope of VAT.

questions.stem: A business that is VAT registered must show on its invoices its:
questions.rationale: Every VAT invoice must show the supplier's VAT number.

questions.stem: Penalties for VAT registration late are linked to:
options: The VAT due since the date registration should have taken place
questions.rationale: HMRC charges a percentage of the VAT due.

questions.stem: A VAT registered business can voluntarily deregister if:
options: Its turnover is expected to fall below the deregistration threshold
questions.rationale: The deregistration threshold is lower than the registration threshold.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a taxable supply for VAT?
questions.rationale: A taxable supply includes standard, reduced and zero-rated goods and services.

questions.stem: The VAT return for the quarter shows output tax £11,800 and input tax £8,200. What is the Box 5 figure and the position?
A VAT return shows Box 6 total sales ex VAT. This includes:
options: Standard, reduced, zero-rated and exempt supplies
questions.rationale: Box 6 includes all sales excluding VAT.

questions.stem: Errors in prior returns of less than the reporting limit can be corrected:
questions.rationale: Below the limit, adjustments can be made on the next return.

questions.stem: A business files its VAT return on 12 August for the quarter ended 30 June. What is the position?
options: It is late, as the deadline was 7 August
questions.rationale: The return was due one month and 7 days after the period end.

questions.stem: VAT returns are submitted to:
questions.rationale: HMRC administers VAT.

questions.stem: A business can join the flat rate scheme if its expected taxable turnover in the next 12 months, excluding VAT, is no more than:
questions.rationale: The flat rate scheme is aimed at smaller businesses with turnover up to £150,000.

questions.stem: In the flat rate scheme, the VAT payable is based on:
options: Gross turnover multiplied by a fixed percentage
questions.rationale: The percentage depends on the trade sector.

questions.stem: A business in the flat rate scheme at 12% with gross turnover of £30,000 for the quarter pays HMRC:
Which of these is NOT taxable benefit in kind?
options: A company car for private use
A mobile phone provided for business use
questions.rationale: Business-use mobile phones are exempt.

questions.stem: Class 1A NIC is payable on:
questions.rationale: It is paid by the employer.

questions.stem: An employee's gross annual pay is £36,000. Using a personal allowance of £12,570 and 20% tax on the rest (basic rate band not exceeded), what is the annual income tax?
An employee earns £2,800 per month. Monthly free pay £1,047.50 and tax at 20%. What is monthly tax?
A P45 is given to an employee by:
options: Their former employer when they leave
questions.rationale: It shows pay and tax to date and is passed to the new employer.

questions.stem: Real Time Information requires employers to report pay:
questions.rationale: Employers send an FPS on or before each payday.

questions.stem: Employee NIC is calculated on:
options: Earnings between the primary threshold and the upper earnings limit at the main rate
questions.rationale: Earnings above the upper limit are charged at a lower rate.

questions.stem: A business pays PAYE of £4,000, employee NIC of £1,500 and employer NIC of £1,800 for the month. How much is paid to HMRC?
VAT records may be kept in electronic form if:
options: They are accessible and meet Making Tax Digital requirements
questions.rationale: MTD requires digital records and software.

questions.stem: An error on a VAT return was careless and HMRC is told promptly. The penalty is likely to be:
questions.rationale: Prompt voluntary disclosure reduces penalties.

questions.stem: Which of these is a common cause of VAT errors?
options: Using the wrong VAT rate on a sale or purchase
questions.rationale: Rates should be checked for each supply.

questions.stem: A business's VAT-inclusive takings from standard-rated sales are £7,200. What is the VAT?
Net purchases £5,000 standard-rated and £2,000 zero-rated. What is the input VAT at 20%?
questions.rationale: Only standard-rated purchases carry VAT: £5,000 × 20% = £1,000.

questions.stem: A business sells goods for £500 net each to 40 customers at 20% VAT. Customers who pay within 7 days (half of them) get a 4% prompt-payment discount. What is the total output VAT, assuming all take the discount if eligible?
Total VAT paid on purchases for the quarter is £3,450 and VAT charged on sales is £5,100. What is VAT payable?
A sale of £3,000 is made to a customer in the EU and goods are exported with proof. The VAT charged is:
questions.rationale: Exports are zero-rated.

questions.stem: Which supply is exempt from VAT?
options: Postal services provided by Royal Mail (universal service)
questions.rationale: Some postal services are exempt.

questions.stem: Input VAT can generally be reclaimed on:
options: Business purchases used to make taxable supplies
questions.rationale: VAT must relate to taxable business use.

questions.stem: A VAT invoice must show:
questions.rationale: Required for the customer to reclaim VAT.

questions.stem: A VAT-registered business must keep VAT records for:
questions.rationale: Some records may need longer.

questions.stem: A business is partially exempt if it:
options: Makes both taxable and exempt supplies
questions.rationale: Input VAT recovery must be apportioned.

questions.stem: Box 4 of a VAT return is:
questions.rationale: It is input VAT.

questions.stem: The VAT return deadline for the quarter ended 31 March is normally:
questions.rationale: One month and 7 days after the period end.

questions.stem: Payment of VAT due should be made:
options: By the same date as the return (for electronic payments)
questions.rationale: Late payment can bring penalties.

questions.stem: A return shows Box 1 £9,400, Box 2 £0, Box 4 £6,700. What is Box 3 and Box 5?
questions.rationale: Box 3 = Box 1 + Box 2. Box 5 = Box 3 − Box 4.

questions.stem: The main advantage of annual accounting is:
options: One return per year and simpler administration
questions.rationale: It reduces compliance effort.

questions.stem: Under the flat rate scheme, a business with gross turnover £50,000 and rate 7% pays:
A business may choose cash accounting to:
options: Pay VAT only when it has received cash from customers
questions.rationale: It helps cash flow.

questions.stem: Which deduction is a voluntary deduction from pay?
questions.rationale: Voluntary deductions are chosen by the employee.

questions.stem: An employee's gross pay is £2,400. Deductions: tax £280, NIC £130, pension £120. What is net pay?
Employers must keep payroll records for at least:
questions.rationale: HMRC may check records.

questions.stem: Employee earns £4,000 per month; employer NIC is 15% above £417 per month. What is employer NIC?
An employee's statutory sick pay is paid by:
questions.rationale: Employers pay SSP to eligible employees.

questions.stem: A P60 shows:
options: Pay and deductions for the whole tax year
questions.rationale: It is issued by 31 May.

questions.stem: A new employee gives a P45 from their previous job. The employer uses it to:
options: Set up the correct tax code and record earnings to date
questions.rationale: It includes tax code and pay to date.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sensible internal control over VAT?
options: Reviewing the VAT return before submission
questions.rationale: Review reduces errors.

questions.stem: A careless inaccuracy in a VAT return will lead to:
options: A penalty based on the extra tax due
questions.rationale: Penalties depend on behaviour.

questions.stem: A business spots a net underpayment of £800 on a prior return and the error is below the limit. What should it do?
options: Adjust on the next VAT return
questions.rationale: Corrections below the limit can be made on the next return.
